docs.title: Neuro Scutbook
docs.text:
A bedside neurology reference for MDs, NPs, PAs, and medics — how to work up and manage a patient with neurological symptoms in the clinic, ER, or on the wards, the way a neurology consult would. Every topic pairs a prescriptive consult workflow with a plain-language evidence brief and a standardized military-medicine layer.

Headache triage Acute stroke Military medicine

Fastest way in

Press / anywhere and type a symptom, drug, or trial name.

Disclaimer — read first

This site is educational clinical decision-support. It is not a substitute for professional clinical judgment, formal consultation, or individual medical advice, and it does not establish a provider–patient relationship. Dosing, protocols, and military standards change — verify everything against current guidelines, product labeling, and the governing regulation before acting on it. Use reflects your own professional responsibility.

    The question providers actually get stuck on: do I board this Soldier, when, and am I the one who starts it? Answered from AR 40-501, AR 40-502, DA Pam 40-502, DoDI 6130.03, and DoDM 1332.18 — including the MAR2-versus-DES fork, who signs, the real day thresholds, and the full IDES timeline.

docs.title: How to use this
docs.text:
• On call or at the bedside? Open the topic and read top-to-bottom: red flags → rapid approach → workup → tiered Step 1→2→3 order sets with doses → disposition.
  • Prescribing? Look for the TRICARE box wherever drugs appear — preferred versus PA-gated, and what the authorization needs.
  • Studying or teaching? Jump to the Discover brief at the bottom of each page for the evidence and the key trials.
  • Search — press / anywhere and type a symptom, drug, or trial name.

How current is this?

Every page carries a visible Last reviewed stamp and a Verified footer that states what was checked against source, what is conference or press-release data rather than peer-reviewed, and what still needs confirmation before you act on it. Where a recommendation rests on observational rather than randomized evidence, the page says so.

39 pages across headache, cerebrovascular disease, seizure, traumatic brain injury, demyelinating disease, neuromuscular-junction disorders, and military medicine — with more topics added one at a time, each updated to current evidence before it goes up.

docs.title: How to add a topic
docs.text:
Every clinical page follows the "Headache" format — the tiered, prescriptive style used across the Headache and Stroke pages. The canonical reference implementation is docs/headache/migraine.md; the fill-in skeleton is includes/topic-template.md. To add a page:

  1. Copy includes/topic-template.md to docs/<area>/<topic>.md.
  2. Fill in each section. Delete sections that truly don't apply, but keep the order and the format hallmarks below.
  3. Add the page to the nav: list in mkdocs.yml.
  4. Preview locally (mkdocs serve), build with mkdocs build --strict, then commit and push — the site redeploys automatically.

docs.title: Format hallmarks (the "Headache" style — don't drop these)
docs.text:
• Prescriptive, not just comprehensive. The reader should know exactly what to do at each step — this is "what the neurologist wants you to do first, second, third."
  • A "The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)" numbered block near the top of management.
  • Tiered !!! orderset boxes — Step 1 → 2 → 3 — with a DOSE on every drug and an explicit "what defines failure / when to escalate" between tiers.
  • Decision tables (comorbidity → agent, situation → target) and === "tabs" for parallel option sets.
  • A !!! tip "TRICARE — …" box wherever drugs are prescribed — name the preferred/no-PA go-to vs the PA-gated agents (and what the PA requires); always tell the reader to verify at the TRICARE Formulary Search.
  • The standardized !!! military box (fixed 5 fields).
  • A "📚 Discover" evidence brief, linked References, and a *Verified MON YYYY: …* footer that states what was source-checked and flags anything that could not be confirmed.

docs.title: The standard sections (in order)
docs.text:
1. Title + Last reviewed: MON YYYY stamp
  2. One-liner + who it's for

  4. Diagnosis / classification (quote criteria exactly)
  5. Rapid approach (numbered)
  6. The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
  7. Workup (labs / imaging / LP — an !!! orderset if there's a mandatory set)
  8. Management — tiered !!! orderset Step 1→2→3 with doses, decision tables, Avoid box
  9. TRICARE prescribing box (!!! tip) wherever drugs appear
  10. Disposition
  11. Military box (!!! military)

  13. References + *Verified MON YYYY* footer

docs.title: Custom callout boxes
docs.text:
This site defines two custom admonitions in addition to the Material defaults:

!!! danger "🚩 Red flags"
    Emergent / must-not-miss items.

!!! orderset "Step 1 — first-line"
    Copy-pasteable, dosed orders. Tier as Step 1 → 2 → 3.

!!! tip "TRICARE — <topic> prescribing"
    Preferred/no-PA go-to vs PA-gated agents; verify at the TRICARE Formulary Search.

!!! military "Military medicine — <topic>"
    The five fields: deployability, profile, EPTS/LOD, retention, MEB/IDES.

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
• Copyright: write Discover briefs in your own words and cite. Source PDFs are a reading list — never paste from Continuum, UpToDate, or similar.
  • Currency: update content to current evidence before stamping a review date. No hand-waved dates.
  • De-identify: no PII, no real lot numbers, no patient specifics.
  • Military content: published-doctrine level only; verify against current AR 40-501 / DoDI 1332.18 / aeromedical policy; nothing sensitive.
  • Disclaimer: the site-wide educational-use disclaimer applies to every page.

docs.title: Approach to cognitive impairment
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

One-liner: cognitive complaints are common and most of them are not neurodegenerative disease — so the job is to separate the treatable from the degenerative, name the syndrome before you name the disease, and only then decide whether a biomarker changes anything.

Who this is for: the provider handed "memory problems" in clinic, and the one who has to decide whether this is depression, drugs, sleep apnoea, a rapidly progressive dementia that needs admitting tonight, or Alzheimer's disease. In a military setting the same complaint usually arrives as post-concussive cognitive symptoms in a young service member — that is a different problem and lives on the TBI cognitive page.

🚩 Red flags — do not work this up as slow neurodegeneration

Pattern Worry Do now Progression over weeks to months, not years Rapidly progressive dementia — CJD, autoimmune encephalitis, malignancy, infection Admit or expedite. Go to rapidly progressive dementia Age <65, especially <60 Young-onset — FTD, genetic, autoimmune, metabolic, HIV, neurosyphilis Broader work-up; refer to behavioural neurology Early falls, parkinsonism, or visual hallucinations Dementia with Lewy bodies Do not give a typical antipsychotic — see the sensitivity warning Personality or conduct change dominating memory Frontotemporal dementia Collateral history is the test; imaging supports Gait disturbance early, urinary incontinence, "magnetic" gait NPH, vascular, B12 deficiency, cord pathology Imaging + B12/copper; consider gait-responsive causes Fluctuating consciousness, inattention, acute onset Delirium — but ask what is causing it Find the cause; do not diagnose dementia in a delirious patient. Autoimmune encephalitis, CNS infection and non-convulsive status all present exactly this way — "it's delirium" is a description, not a diagnosis. If there is no obvious precipitant, or it does not clear, go to rapidly progressive dementia Headache, seizure, focal deficit, papilloedema Mass, subdural, vasculitis Image before anything else

Two rules that prevent most diagnostic errors: never diagnose dementia during a delirium, and never diagnose Alzheimer's disease in a patient you have not screened for depression, drugs, sleep apnoea and thyroid or B12 deficiency.

docs.title: Delirium, MCI, dementia — get the level right first
docs.text:
Onset Attention Course Consciousness Delirium Hours–days Impaired — the defining feature Fluctuating Altered Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) Months–years Usually intact Slowly progressive Normal Dementia (major neurocognitive disorder) Years Intact until late Progressive Normal
  • MCI = objective cognitive decline with preserved independence in instrumental activities. Dementia = cognitive decline that interferes with independence. The line is functional, not a test score, and the collateral historian draws it, not the patient.
  • MCI is not a disease — it is a stage with many causes, and the numbers are worth carrying: over a mean 5 years, roughly 41.5% convert to dementia in clinic populations (27% in population-based samples), about half stay stable, and 8.7% revert to normal in clinics — 28.2% in population samples. Annual conversion is 3–10% in the community, 10–15% in specialty clinics.
    • Reversion is not the all-clear. In one cohort 65% of reverters ultimately progressed. Tell patients they are at elevated risk, screen for treatable causes, and reassess at 6–12 months.
  • Subjective cognitive decline (complaint without objective deficit) carries a modestly increased risk but is not a diagnosis. Follow it; do not work it up as disease.

docs.title: Name the syndrome before you name the disease
docs.text:
The single most useful diagnostic move is to ask which cognitive domain went first, and take that answer from someone who lives with the patient.

Leading domain Think first Page Episodic memory (repeats questions, loses the thread of recent events) Alzheimer's disease AD Visuospatial, attention that fluctuates, visual hallucinations Dementia with Lewy bodies DLB/PDD Behaviour, personality, disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy Behavioural-variant FTD FTD Language — effortful speech, or loss of word meaning Primary progressive aphasia FTD Processing speed and executive function, stepwise or with vascular risk Vascular cognitive impairment Vascular Any of the above, but over weeks to months Rapidly progressive dementia RPD

Mixed pathology is the norm, not the exception, particularly over 80 — vascular disease and Alzheimer's pathology coexist far more often than either occurs alone. Say "predominantly X" rather than pretending to a single diagnosis you cannot support.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Rule out delirium — then ask what caused it. Acute, fluctuating, inattentive → find the cause. This is where the pathway forks, not where it stops: if there is no obvious precipitant, if it does not clear with treatment of one, or if there are seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability or fever, that is rapidly progressive dementia until proven otherwise — and the window is measured in weeks.
  2. Take a collateral history. Non-negotiable. What went first, when, and what can they no longer do? A patient's own account of their memory is the least reliable data in the encounter.
  3. Screen objectively — MoCA or MMSE, plus a functional scale. Record the raw score and the education adjustment.
  4. Screen the treatable contributors before anything expensive: depression, medications, sleep apnoea, alcohol, thyroid, B12. Most "reversible dementia" is one of these.
  5. Lab panel + structural imaging (MRI preferred) — see Workup.
  6. Decide the syndrome from the leading domain, and route to the disease page.
  7. Only then ask whether a biomarker changes management. It usually does not, unless anti-amyloid therapy is genuinely on the table.
  8. Address safety and capacity from the first visit — driving, firearms, finances, medications, and the caregiver.
  9. Military disposition — and note that dementia is disqualifying upon diagnosis, which is unlike almost everything else in this reference.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
Every patient — the baseline set

  • Labs: CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12 (add methylmalonic acid if borderline), HbA1c, lipids. Add: HIV and RPR/treponemal testing where risk or young onset.
  • Structural imaging — MRI brain without contrast is preferred (CT only if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable). You are looking for hippocampal and lobar atrophy patterns, vascular burden, subdural collections, hydrocephalus, and mass lesions.
  • Medication review — every visit. See the Avoid box.
  • Depression screen (PHQ-9 or GDS) and a sleep apnoea screen (STOP-BANG).
  • Objective cognitive testing — MoCA is more sensitive than MMSE for MCI and for executive and visuospatial deficits; MMSE is more familiar and better validated longitudinally. Use one consistently and record the version.

Add when the picture demands it

  • Young onset (<65), atypical, or rapid → expand: autoimmune and paraneoplastic panels, heavy metals, copper/ceruloplasmin, ammonia, EEG, CSF. See RPD.
  • Neuropsychological testing — when the syndrome is unclear, when the deficit is mild and the stakes are high (capacity, occupation, a service member's fitness), or to establish a baseline before treatment.
  • EEG — suspected seizures, fluctuation, or RPD.
  • DaT-SPECT — supports DLB when parkinsonism is equivocal.
  • Polysomnography — REM sleep behaviour disorder, or suspected OSA.

Reversible and contributing causes — screen before you diagnose

Be honest about what "reversible" means. Potentially reversible causes account for 9–23% of dementia depending on setting and definition — but only about 11% actually resolve, and only 3% fully. The commonest genuinely reversible contributors are medications (28.2%), depression (26.2%) and metabolic disorders (15.5%).

So the screen is not mandatory because reversal is likely. It is mandatory because contributors are common, and every one you fix makes the patient better than they would otherwise have been. B12 deficiency and hypothyroidism usually contribute rather than reverse once neurodegeneration is established; NPH, subdural haematoma and neurosyphilis genuinely can reverse if caught early.

  • Depression — the classic mimic. Prominent complaint with relatively preserved objective performance, poor effort, "I don't know" answers. Treat and reassess.
  • Medications — anticholinergics (oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, tricyclics), benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, high anticholinergic burden overall.
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea and chronic sleep deprivation.
  • Alcohol and other substances.
  • B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism.
  • Normal pressure hydrocephalus — gait first, then urinary, then cognition. Gait must lead.
  • Subdural haematoma — especially in an anticoagulated or fall-prone patient.
  • Neurosyphilis, HIV, and in the right setting CNS Whipple, Lyme.
  • Hearing and vision loss — under-treated, and they masquerade as cognitive decline.

docs.title: Biomarkers — what they answer, and when to ask
docs.text:
The question a biomarker answers is narrow: "is Alzheimer's pathology present?" It does not tell you the syndrome, it does not exclude co-pathology, and in most patients it does not change what you do. Order it when the answer would change management.

Test What it shows Practical note Plasma p-tau217 Alzheimer's pathology, with the best performance of the blood markers Pooled sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 88.7%, AUROC 91.1%. Accuracy 89–91% in secondary care but 85% in primary care — and lower again over age 80 (83%). Unaffected by CKD, diabetes, sex or ApoE genotype CSF Aβ42/40 ratio + p-tau181 or p-tau217 Amyloid and tau pathology Long-established; requires LP Amyloid PET Fibrillar amyloid burden Confirms pathology; required or expected before anti-amyloid therapy Tau PET Tau distribution and stage Correlates with symptoms better than amyloid does FDG-PET Regional hypometabolism pattern Helps separate AD from FTD when the clinical picture is ambiguous DaT-SPECT Presynaptic dopaminergic deficit Supports DLB; does not diagnose AD

Use a two-cutoff rule, and know what is actually FDA-cleared

A single cutoff throws away accuracy. Using two — one to rule in, one to rule out, with the 12–17% who land in between going on to CSF or PET — raises accuracy to 92–94% in both primary and secondary care. Report results that way rather than as a binary.

The first and so far only FDA-cleared blood-based IVD is the p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio on the Lumipulse platform (Fujirebio), for detecting AD pathology in symptomatic patients. The other assays in circulation — PrecivityAD2, ALZpath, Lilly — are laboratory-developed tests without IVD clearance. That distinction matters for what you can defend ordering.

Testing asymptomatic people is not recommended outside research.

A positive amyloid biomarker is not a diagnosis of dementia

Amyloid pathology is common in cognitively normal older adults, and the prevalence rises steeply with age: ~12% at 50, 18% at 60, 25% at 70, 33% at 80, 43% at 90. ApoE ε4 homozygotes reach 15% by roughly age 40.

A positive test in a patient without objective impairment tells you about risk, not disease — and it cannot be un-told. Do not order amyloid biomarkers in a patient you would not treat, and counsel before you test, not after.

This is also why the 2024 biological definition of Alzheimer's disease is contested. Under the Alzheimer's Association Revised Criteria (2024) — which replace the 2018 NIA-AA research framework — an abnormal Core 1 biomarker is sufficient for diagnosis without symptoms. Applied literally to the prevalence figures above, that makes a third of cognitively normal 80-year-olds "cases." Several expert groups argue it should stay in the research domain. This site's position: characterise the symptomatic, do not diagnose the asymptomatic.

docs.title: Management — the frame
docs.text:
Disease-specific treatment lives on the disease pages: Alzheimer's (including anti-amyloid therapy), DLB/PDD, FTD, vascular. What follows applies to everyone.

Step 1 — the things that work regardless of diagnosis

  • Stop or reduce the cognition-toxic drugs. Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, opioids where possible. This is the highest-yield prescribing act on the page.
  • Treat the contributors — depression, sleep apnoea, pain, hearing and vision loss. Hearing loss is the single largest modifiable dementia risk factor in the Lancet Commission's accounting (9% population-attributable fraction) — but be precise about what the evidence supports. ACHIEVE, the first RCT, was negative overall and positive only in a prespecified higher-risk subgroup; observational ASPREE data found 33% lower 7-year dementia risk with hearing aids. Correcting hearing is risk-modifying, not a treatment for established dementia — offer it on that basis.
  • Vascular risk factor control — BP, lipids, diabetes, smoking. Relevant in every dementia, not just vascular, because mixed pathology is the norm.
  • Exercise, social engagement, and structured routine.
  • Caregiver support and education from the first visit — caregiver burden predicts institutionalization more reliably than the patient's test score.

Avoid — and this list is as important as anything you prescribe

  • Benzodiazepines — worsen cognition, increase falls, and are hard to stop.
  • Anticholinergics — oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, tricyclics, older antipsychotics. Cumulative anticholinergic burden is a modifiable risk.
  • Typical antipsychotics in suspected DLB — severe sensitivity reactions.
  • Antipsychotics generally for behavioural symptoms — all carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Non-pharmacological management first, every time.
  • Do not treat an amyloid biomarker. Treat a patient with a syndrome.

docs.title: Safety, capacity and the conversation
docs.text:
• Driving — ask at every visit, and ask the collateral historian separately. A dementia diagnosis alone does not mandate cessation, and the AAN parameter gives usable thresholds:
    • CDR 0.5 (questionable/very mild) — may still drive, assess individually.
    • CDR 1 (mild dementia) — substantially higher crash risk; on-road test pass rates are only 41–76%. Strongly counsel toward stopping.
    • CDR ≥2 (moderate) — incompatible with safe driving, across every guideline.
    • Reassess every 6 months in anyone still driving. Raise concern faster for caregiver worry, any crash or ticket, self-restricted driving patterns, or aggressive driving.
    • DLB and FTD impair driving fitness more severely at milder stages — visuospatial, motor and behavioural deficits do not track CDR. Do not apply the AD thresholds to them.
    • Know your state reporting requirements.
  • Firearms — in a military and veteran population this must be asked directly and early, framed as storage planning while the patient can still participate in the decision.
  • Finances — vulnerability to fraud and financial mismanagement often precedes the diagnosis.
  • Advance planning and capacity — the window for the patient to express their own wishes closes. Raise durable power of attorney and advance directives at the first visit, not the fifth.
  • Say the diagnosis. Patients and families overwhelmingly want to be told. Vague euphemism transfers the burden of uncertainty onto the family without sparing anyone.

TRICARE — cognitive impairment work-up

  • The symptomatic drugs are generic and formulary — donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine, memantine. Start there; nothing on this page requires a prior authorization.
  • The expensive decisions are diagnostic, not therapeutic. Amyloid PET, tau PET and plasma biomarker assays are where coverage questions arise, and coverage has moved quickly — check current policy before you order, not after.
  • Anti-amyloid monoclonals are a different order of magnitude — high-cost specialty infusions with their own coverage, site-of-care and MRI-monitoring requirements. Those are covered on the Alzheimer's page.
  • Neuropsychological testing frequently needs authorization; the referral question and the clinical justification matter more than the CPT code.
  • Verify current coverage at the TRICARE Formulary Search and with the regional contractor before counselling — DoD P&T revises criteria without notice.

Military medicine — cognitive impairment and dementia

Framework — verify against current AR 40-501, DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 and Vol 2, DoDI 1332.18 and service aeromedical policy. See Profiles, MEB/MAR2 & deployability. This box carries the section-wide framing; the disease pages carry only what differs.**

  • Get the population right first. True neurodegenerative dementia is rare on active duty. In an MTF the overwhelming majority of dementia care is for retirees and dependents, where the questions are diagnostic, caregiver and coverage questions rather than fitness ones. In a young service member, cognitive complaints are far more likely to be post-concussive, sleep, mood, substance or medication-related — start at TBI — cognitive, not here. The two pages where this changes are FTD and rapidly progressive dementia.
  • Retention — this is the inverse of every other neurology page on this site. DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d covers "permanent or progressive cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or other dementias" and states it "is not compatible with retention, and the Service should initiate appropriate medical and personnel actions upon diagnosis. Paragraph 5.26.a. does not apply." That sentence appears exactly twice in all of para 5.26 — here and at epilepsy, 5.26.k. There is no persists-despite-treatment prong to argue and no MRDP to wait out. Do not import the reasoning from MG, LEMS or botulism, where the 5.26.a gate is the whole argument.
  • What the standard turns on is "permanent or progressive," not the word "dementia." The gate has moved from treatment response to diagnostic certainty — and that is the only defence the Soldier has left. A referral built on a screening score and a worried spouse will not survive review, and the cost of being wrong is a career. Before the word enters the record, the note must carry: collateral history from someone who sees the Soldier daily; formal neuropsychological testing, not a MoCA; structural imaging; documented exclusion of depression, medication effect (anticholinergics, sedatives, opioids, antiseizure drugs), sleep apnoea and sleep debt, substance use, thyroid and B12; and evidence of decline over time or irreversibility — because that is the element 5.26.d actually names.
  • Army hook — cite the DoD paragraph as the operative one. The AR counterpart is the catch-all AR 40-501 3-31k, which expressly reaches "alteration of consciousness, speech, personality, or cognitive and mental function" rising to the para 3-1 definition. But note the mismatch and handle it explicitly: 3-31k carries its own "after adequate treatment… residual symptoms" gate that 5.26.d waives. Cite 5.26.d as the standard that acts on diagnosis and 3-31k + 3-1 as the Army definition of the disqualifying condition — not the reverse. Where a named subparagraph fits the underlying disease better, use it alongside: 3-31d (basal ganglia/cerebellar degeneration, Parkinson's named) for DLB/PDD; 3-31f (stroke with residuals) for vascular; 3-31j (TBI) where head injury is the substrate.
  • Profile (DA Form 3349) — the primary factor is P, not S. DA Pam 40-502 defines P — physical capacity or stamina as including "conditions of the… nervous system", and confines S to "personality, emotional stability, and psychiatric diseases." A neurodegenerative dementia is a nervous-system disease: profile it P, adding S only where personality change, disinhibition or emotional instability is a separately limiting feature (bvFTD, DLB neuropsychiatric symptoms). AR 40-501 itself writes neurologic profiles as P-3. Temporary while the work-up and treatable-cause trial run; permanent once the diagnosis is established — and a permanent 3 or 4 is itself the DES referral (AR 40-501 3-4). Section 4 limits must speak in functional terms to weapons access, driving and vehicle operation, independent duty, supervisory and financial responsibility, and safety-sensitive tasks.
  • EPTS / LOD. Insidious onset makes dating genuinely hard, and the earliest evidence is usually not in the medical record — review OERs/NCOERs, ACFT trend, counselling statements (DA Form 4856) and prior PHAs, and date the first attributable functional change. Remember the 6-month rule: for conditions predating enlistment, accession standards govern the first 6 months of active service (EPSBD); after that, retention standards apply. In young-onset cases ask specifically about family history — several dementias are autosomal dominant — and genetic testing in a service member follows counselling and a considered decision, not curiosity.
  • MEB / DES — the referral sequence, in order. (1) Work the differential and treat the reversible contributors on a temporary profile, linking every extension. (2) When the diagnosis is established to the standard above, that is the trigger — no 12-month administrative MRDP to run out, no clinical-stability argument to make. (3) Write the permanent P-3 in e-Profile with functional Section 4 limits; that profile is the referral (AR 40-501 3-4). (4) An approval authority second-signs, and that signature starts the DES clock. MAR2 is not the pathway here — MAR2 exists for Soldiers who meet retention standards but cannot perform their PMOS, and a Soldier meeting 5.26.d does not meet them. Sending this case to MAR2 delays a board the Soldier is entitled to. Whether the Soldier is found fit is the PEB's decision — write the standard and the evidence, never the outcome.
  • Deployability: non-deployable — and not primarily because of the memory. Impaired judgment under stress, weapons access, and no capacity for independent or unsupervised duty, against an operational environment whose specific stressors — sleep deprivation, heat, dehydration, altered routine, unfamiliar surroundings — reliably worsen cognition and precipitate delirium. The 72-hour deploy-on-receipt-of-mission expectation (AR 40-501 3-1) cannot be met. Practically: forward locations cannot deliver neuropsychological reassessment, MRI-based monitoring or caregiver structure, and the agents used for neuropsychiatric symptoms bring their own controlled-substance and monitoring problems.
  • Aeromedical: disqualifying, and AR 40-501 names it. AR 40-501 4-27i disqualifies "history of degenerative or demyelinating process. Such as multiple sclerosis, dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or basal ganglia disease" for flying duty Classes 1, 2, 2F, 2P, 3 and 4. 4-27h adds "history of organic mental syndromes… until reviewed by the USAAMA" — which is where the USAAMA routing comes from. On the accession side the imported paragraph is DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 para 6.26.d, "history of neurodegenerative disorders" — not 6.26.q, whose exemplars are non-degenerative chronic disorders. Ground the aircrew member and route to USAAMA; the same logic applies to ATC and UAS duties.
  • The TBI overlap needs saying plainly. Service members with repetitive head-impact exposure ask whether they are developing CTE. Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research construct, CTE is a post-mortem neuropathological diagnosis, and neither can be diagnosed in a living patient. Counsel honestly, treat the treatable contributors, and see TBI — work-up and return to duty.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
The field changed at the point of diagnosis before it changed at the point of treatment. For thirty years Alzheimer's disease was a clinical diagnosis confirmed at autopsy. Now amyloid and tau pathology can be detected in life — first with PET, then CSF, and now with blood-based markers led by plasma p-tau217, which performs closest to the CSF standard. That has two consequences the clinic feels immediately: the diagnosis can be biologically confirmed rather than inferred, and it can be confirmed in people whose symptoms do not warrant treatment. A test that is easy to order is easy to over-order, and the pretest probability in front of you determines whether the result means anything.

Anti-amyloid therapy is real, modest, and demanding. Lecanemab and donanemab genuinely remove amyloid and genuinely slow decline — by margins that are statistically robust and clinically modest — at the cost of ARIA, infusion or injection burden, ApoE ε4 genotyping, and serial MRI. Whether that trade is worth it is a conversation, not a protocol, and it belongs to the patient. The details, including the ARIA monitoring schedule and the interaction with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, are on the Alzheimer's page and the CAA page.

Meanwhile the highest-yield interventions remain unglamorous. Deprescribing anticholinergics and benzodiazepines, treating sleep apnoea, correcting hearing loss, managing vascular risk, and supporting the caregiver do more for more patients than anything in the biomarker column — and they work regardless of which protein is misfolding.

Key sources: NIA-AA diagnostic framework; DLB consensus criteria; FTD and PPA consensus criteria; VASCOG/AHA vascular cognitive impairment criteria; FDA labelling for the anti-amyloid monoclonals and the symptomatic agents.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Lecanemab (LEQEMBI) FDA label, effective 2026-07-21 — boxed ARIA warning, ApoE ε4 testing, MRI schedule, and the IQLIK autoinjector dosing. DailyMed
  2. Donanemab (Kisunla) FDA label, effective 2025-12-30 — titration schedule and ARIA monitoring. DailyMed
  3. Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine, memantine — current FDA labels; dosing on the Alzheimer's page.
  4. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy — this site, for Boston v2.0 criteria and the ARIA relationship.
  5. AR 40-501 para 3-31k, 3-1, 3-4, 4-27; DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d ("Paragraph 5.26.a. does not apply") — the upon-diagnosis carve-out.

Verified August 2026: reviewed as part of a whole-section pass — one scripted label diff across all six pages, one OpenEvidence round, and two reviewer agents. All drug dosing in this section is taken from current FDA labels, not from memory. Corrections applied here: the 2024 Alzheimer's Association Revised Criteria replace the NIA-AA framework (and the page now states the position that they should characterise the symptomatic, not diagnose the asymptomatic); plasma p-tau217 performance figures and the two-cutoff rule, with the Lumipulse p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio identified as the only FDA-cleared blood IVD; amyloid prevalence in cognitively normal adults by age; MCI conversion and reversion rates, including that 65% of reverters ultimately progress; reversible dementia corrected downward — 9–23% potentially reversible but only ~11% actually resolve; hearing loss reframed as risk-modifying (ACHIEVE was negative overall); and AAN driving thresholds by CDR stage. The delirium red flag was rewritten after a safety review found it routed rapidly-progressive patients off the pathway. The military box was rebuilt from verbatim regulation — see below.

Military content verified verbatim from source PDFs this pass: DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 5.26.d reads "permanent or progressive cognitive impairment… Paragraph 5.26.a. does not apply" — confirmed to appear exactly twice in all of para 5.26, at dementia and epilepsy. The profile factor was corrected from S to P (DA Pam 40-502 assigns the nervous system to P; S is personality and emotional stability). AR 40-501 3-31k carries its own "after adequate treatment" gate that 5.26.d waives — so 5.26.d is cited as operative. Aeromedical corrected to AR 40-501 4-27i, which names dementia and Alzheimer's outright, with DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 6.26.d as the accession paragraph — not 6.26.q, which does not fit. MAR2 is affirmatively not the pathway for an established dementia.

Not independently verified: TRICARE formulary tier, PA criteria and site-of-care rules; USAAMA adjudication practice and Aeromedical Policy Letters; non-Army service standards (these boxes are Army-framed); and Reserve/Guard pathways, which differ materially and are not addressed.

docs.title: Alzheimer's disease
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

Part of Approach to cognitive impairment.

One-liner: the commonest cause of dementia — an amyloid and tau proteinopathy that classically presents as progressive episodic memory loss and is now, for the first time, both biologically confirmable in life and modifiably treatable, at a cost in monitoring, money and risk that has to be discussed rather than assumed.

Who this is for: the provider deciding whether this is Alzheimer's disease at all, what to start, and — the genuinely new question — whether this specific patient should be offered an anti-amyloid antibody, which is a decision about eligibility, risk tolerance and logistics as much as diagnosis.

🚩 Before you call it Alzheimer's

Pattern Worry Do Weeks-to-months progression Rapidly progressive dementia Expedite; do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor and follow up in 6 months Visual hallucinations, fluctuation, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder Dementia with Lewy bodies Antipsychotic sensitivity — get this right before anyone prescribes Behaviour or language first, memory relatively spared FTD Collateral history; FDG-PET can help Age <65 Young-onset AD, genetic, or a non-AD cause Broader work-up; genetic counselling if familial pattern On an anti-amyloid antibody, now with new focal deficit or headache ARIA Urgent MRI. ARIA-E mimics ischaemic stroke — consider it before thrombolysis

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
The framework changed in 2024, and it is contested. The Alzheimer's Association Revised Criteria (2024) replace the 2018 NIA-AA research framework and the 2011 NIA-AA clinical guidelines — NIA now holds an advisory role only. The change is not cosmetic:

  • AD is now defined biologically. An abnormal Core 1 biomarker — amyloid PET, an approved CSF assay, or plasma p-tau217 — is sufficient for diagnosis without symptoms.
  • Core 2 biomarkers (tau PET, biofluid tau) provide prognostic staging.
  • The "N" (neurodegeneration) was removed from the core criteria.
  • The clinical stage (asymptomatic, MCI, mild/moderate/severe) is recorded separately from the biology.

This is genuinely controversial, and the page takes a position

Defining a disease by a biomarker in a person without symptoms means a substantial number of cognitively normal older adults meet criteria for "Alzheimer's disease" — see the amyloid prevalence figures on the hub. Several expert groups argue the 2024 criteria should stay in the research domain for now.

Practical position for this page: use the biological criteria to characterise a symptomatic patient, not to diagnose an asymptomatic one. Do not tell a person without cognitive impairment that they have Alzheimer's disease on the strength of a blood test.

The classic clinical syndrome:

  • Episodic memory first — repeating questions, losing recent conversations, misplacing items, relying increasingly on notes and on a spouse. Impaired encoding, not just retrieval: cueing and recognition do not rescue the memory the way they do in depression or in subcortical disease.
  • Then word-finding difficulty, visuospatial disorientation (getting lost on familiar routes), and executive decline.
  • Insight is often reduced early, which is why the collateral history is the diagnostic instrument.

Atypical presentations exist and are missed: posterior cortical atrophy (visual complaints with normal eyes), logopenic primary progressive aphasia, a dysexecutive/frontal variant, and a corticobasal syndrome that is sometimes AD pathology. Young onset skews atypical.

What a biomarker adds — and what it does not

A positive amyloid biomarker tells you AD pathology is present. It does not tell you the patient's symptoms are caused by it, and it does not exclude co-pathology — mixed vascular and Lewy pathology is common, especially over 80.

The order of operations matters: establish the syndrome and exclude the treatable contributors first (see the hub); test biology only when the answer changes management. The clearest indication to test is a genuine intention to offer anti-amyloid therapy, which requires confirmed amyloid pathology before initiation.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm it is dementia or MCI, not delirium or depression, and that the treatable contributors have been screened. See the hub.
  2. Confirm the syndrome is amnestic-predominant — or recognise one of the atypical variants.
  3. Structural imaging — MRI to support the pattern and, critically, to establish the vascular and microhaemorrhage baseline that governs anti-amyloid eligibility.
  4. Decide whether anti-amyloid therapy is genuinely on the table — stage, comorbidity, anticoagulation, MRI findings, logistics, and the patient's own values. If it is not, do not order amyloid biomarkers.
  5. If it is: confirm amyloid pathology, test ApoE ε4 genotype, baseline MRI, and counsel on ARIA before the first dose.
  6. Start symptomatic therapy — a cholinesterase inhibitor, adding memantine as disease advances. This is independent of, and additive to, any decision about anti-amyloid therapy.
  7. Treat the modifiable contributors and vascular risk — they matter here as much as anywhere.
  8. Address safety, capacity, driving and caregiver support from the first visit.
  9. Military disposition — dementia is disqualifying upon diagnosis; see the military box.

docs.title: Symptomatic therapy — start here for essentially everyone
docs.text:
Step 1 — cholinesterase inhibitor

Modest, real, symptomatic benefit. Not disease-modifying. Choose on tolerability and route; there is no persuasive efficacy difference between them.

  • Donepezil — 5 mg PO once daily in the evening. After 4–6 weeks, increase to 10 mg daily (the usual maintenance). In moderate-to-severe disease the label permits 23 mg daily after at least 3 months at 10 mg — the added benefit is marginal and the cholinergic side effects are not; most patients should stay at 10.
  • Rivastigmine — oral 1.5 mg PO BID, increasing by 1.5 mg BID at minimum 2-week intervals to 3, 4.5 and up to 6 mg BID as tolerated.
    • Patch: start 4.6 mg/24 h, increase after ≥4 weeks to 9.5 mg/24 h — the minimum effective dose — and after a further ≥4 weeks to a maximum of 13.3 mg/24 h. Rotate sites; the patch has less GI intolerance than the capsule and is the pragmatic choice for many patients.
    • Rivastigmine also carries a Parkinson's disease dementia indication — relevant on the DLB/PDD page.
  • Galantamine ER — 8 mg PO daily in the morning, increasing after ≥4 weeks to 16 mg/day, and after a further ≥4 weeks to a maximum of 24 mg/day. Take with food and maintain fluid intake. Do not exceed 16 mg/day in moderate hepatic impairment.
  • Counsel on the side effects that cause discontinuation — nausea, diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss, vivid dreams, bradycardia and syncope, and increased urinary urgency. Titrate slowly; most intolerance is a titration problem.
  • Check the pulse before and during treatment. These drugs are cholinergic — bradycardia, heart block and syncope are real, and a patient who falls after starting one should have the drug reconsidered before the fall is attributed to the dementia.

Step 2 — add memantine as disease advances

  • Memantine — 5 mg PO once daily, increasing in 5 mg increments at intervals of at least one week to 10, 15 and a target of 20 mg/day (10 mg BID). Labelled for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease.
  • Reduce the dose in severe renal impairment.
  • Combination with a cholinesterase inhibitor is standard in moderate-to-severe disease and is generally well tolerated — memantine's side-effect profile is much lighter than the cholinergic agents'.

docs.title: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies — the decision, then the protocol
docs.text:
This is a shared decision, not a reflex — and eligibility is narrow

Both approved agents are indicated only for patients in the MCI or mild dementia stage — the population studied. They were not studied in moderate or severe disease and should not be started there.

Confirm before anyone commits:

  • Amyloid pathology is confirmed (PET or CSF) — this is a label requirement, not a nicety.
  • ApoE ε4 genotype is known. Homozygotes — roughly 15% of AD patients — have a substantially higher incidence of ARIA, including symptomatic, serious and severe radiographic ARIA. Test before initiating, and counsel before testing, including what a result means for blood relatives.
  • A recent baseline MRI has been reviewed, and the exclusions are numeric: more than 4 microhaemorrhages, or any single macrohaemorrhage, excludes treatment. Pre-existing microhaemorrhage or superficial siderosis raises ARIA risk. This is where cerebral amyloid angiopathy and this page meet; read that page's ARIA section before your first patient.
  • Anticoagulation is a relative contraindication — increased ARIA-H risk, and intracerebral haemorrhages >1 cm, some fatal, have occurred in this drug class.
  • Cognitive staging is documented — MCI or mild dementia, typically MMSE ~22–30.
  • The infrastructure exists — infusion or injection capacity, and MRI access on the required schedule. Starting without the monitoring is worse than not starting.

Lecanemab (Leqembi) — dosing and monitoring

  • Intravenous: 10 mg/kg over approximately 1 hour every 2 weeks.
  • Subcutaneous (LEQEMBI IQLIK autoinjector): 500 mg once weekly.
  • After 18 months, either continue the starting regimen or transition to maintenance: IV 10 mg/kg every 4 weeks, or SC 360 mg once weekly.
  • MRI schedule: baseline, then after 1, 2, 3 and 6 months of treatment.
  • Enhanced clinical vigilance for ARIA during the first 14 weeks.
  • Infusion-related reactions — slow or stop the infusion; consider premedication with antihistamine, NSAID or corticosteroid at subsequent doses.

Donanemab (Kisunla) — dosing and monitoring

  • Intravenous over approximately 30 minutes every 4 weeks, titrated: infusion 1 — 350 mg; infusion 2 — 700 mg; infusion 3 — 1,050 mg; infusion 4 and beyond — 1,400 mg.
  • That titration is not arbitrary — it is a safety intervention. TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 6 showed the modified schedule cut ARIA-E from 24.2% to 15.6% and symptomatic ARIA-E from 4.8% to 2.8%, while still clearing amyloid. Do not compress it.
  • Consider stopping once amyloid plaques are reduced to minimal levels on amyloid PET — a genuinely different treatment philosophy from lecanemab's open-ended maintenance, and worth explaining to patients as a potential finite course.
  • Confirm amyloid pathology before initiating; baseline MRI and serial monitoring as labelled.

If ARIA occurs — what to actually do

Management is driven by severity and whether the patient has symptoms. Radiographic ARIA is common; most of it is asymptomatic and does not end treatment.

Situation Action Asymptomatic, mild Continue treatment with MRI surveillance Asymptomatic, moderate Suspend; resume by shared decision after radiographic resolution Symptomatic, mild or moderate Suspend. Consider IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily × 3–5 days, then an oral prednisone taper. Monthly MRI until resolution. Avoid anticoagulants and thrombolytics Severe, or recurrent ARIA Permanently discontinue. Corticosteroids; inpatient management
  • Recurrence after resumption runs 13.8–25.6% — factor that into the shared decision rather than treating resumption as a return to baseline.
  • Incidence for orientation: ARIA-E in 12.6% with lecanemab and 24.0% with donanemab at standard dosing; roughly 70% of ARIA is asymptomatic. ApoE ε4 homozygotes run far higher — up to 55% in high-dose aducanumab trials.

ARIA — boxed warning for the whole class

Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities: ARIA-E (oedema, sulcal effusion) and ARIA-H (microhaemorrhage, superficial siderosis).

  • Usually early, usually asymptomatic — but serious and life-threatening events occur, and ARIA can be fatal. Intracerebral haemorrhages >1 cm, some fatal, have been observed.
  • ApoE ε4 homozygotes are at higher risk across every severity category.
  • Pre-existing microhaemorrhage or superficial siderosis raises the risk of both ARIA-E and ARIA-H.
  • The cross-specialty point that matters most: ARIA-E causes focal neurologic deficits that mimic ischaemic stroke. Before giving thrombolysis to any patient on this drug class, consider whether the deficit is ARIA-E. Make sure your stroke service knows which of your patients are on these agents — see acute ischaemic stroke.
  • Any new neurologic symptom on treatment gets an MRI, and management is dictated by ARIA type, severity and whether symptoms are present.

docs.title: Behavioural and psychological symptoms
docs.text:
Non-pharmacological first — every time

Identify the trigger: pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, hunger, boredom, overstimulation, fear, a changed routine, or a caregiver approach that is escalating rather than de-escalating. Most agitation has a cause that is not psychiatric, and the medication that works best is usually the one you stop.

  • Structure, routine, daylight, activity, and caregiver coaching.
  • Review every medication — anticholinergics and benzodiazepines make this worse.
  • Treat pain empirically in a patient who cannot report it. Scheduled paracetamol is an underused agitation intervention.

If medication is genuinely necessary — there are now TWO approved options

  • Dextromethorphan/bupropion (Auvelity) — FDA indication for agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer's disease added in 2026. The first non-antipsychotic approved for this indication, which means it does not carry the antipsychotic class mortality warning — the main reason to consider it first in a patient where that warning is the sticking point. Dosing for the agitation indication was not label-verified for this page — check the current label before prescribing.
  • Brexpiprazole (Rexulti) — approved May 2023. 0.5 mg PO once daily on days 1–7; increase to 1 mg once daily on days 8–14; then 2 mg once daily from day 15 — the recommended target. May increase to a maximum of 3 mg once daily after at least 14 days on clinical response. Maximum 2 mg/day in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh ≥7). Not indicated for as-needed ("prn") use — do not write it that way.
    • Carries the antipsychotic class boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Document the discussion, use the lowest effective dose, and set a review date to stop.
    • Trial effect was roughly a 5-point greater reduction on the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory versus placebo over 12 weeks — real, and worth stating plainly to a family deciding whether the mortality warning is acceptable.
  • Depression is common and treatable — an SSRI is often more useful than an antipsychotic. Citalopram has the best agitation trial evidence (CitAD, at 30 mg/day) — but that dose exceeds the FDA maximum of 20 mg/day in patients over 60 because of QT prolongation. That is an awkward gap between the evidence and the label; sertraline is the conservative default, and escitalopram is under study.
  • Avoid benzodiazepines. They worsen cognition, increase falls, and are difficult to stop.

Avoid

  • Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs — cognition, falls, dependence.
  • Anticholinergics — oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, tricyclics. Reducing anticholinergic burden is one of the few genuinely disease-relevant prescribing acts available.
  • Typical antipsychotics, and any antipsychotic in suspected DLB.
  • Anti-amyloid antibodies in moderate or severe dementia — outside the studied population.
  • Starting an anti-amyloid antibody without MRI capacity for the required schedule.
  • Ordering an amyloid biomarker in a patient you would not treat.

TRICARE — Alzheimer's prescribing

  • The symptomatic agents are generic and formulary — donepezil, rivastigmine (oral and patch), galantamine, memantine. Start here; expect no prior authorization.
  • Anti-amyloid monoclonals are high-cost specialty biologics and should be assumed prior-authorization-gated. Expect requirements mirroring the label: confirmed amyloid pathology, MCI or mild dementia stage, ApoE ε4 genotyping, baseline MRI, and a documented monitoring plan. They are infused agents and run through the medical benefit, so the authorization question includes site of care as well as the drug.
  • The MRI schedule is part of the cost. Baseline plus scans at 1, 2, 3 and 6 months is four to five studies in the first half-year — build that into the authorization request rather than discovering it at the second scan.
  • Brexpiprazole is a branded specialty agent; expect PA and expect the criteria to require a documented AD diagnosis and failed non-pharmacological management.
  • Verify current status and criteria at the TRICARE Formulary Search before counselling — DoD P&T revises tiers and criteria without notice. TRICARE-specific coverage for anti-amyloid therapy and for amyloid PET was not independently verified for this page.

Military medicine — Alzheimer's disease

The section-wide framing — retention under 5.26.d acting on diagnosis, the profile, EPTS/LOD, the referral sequence and aeromedical — is on the hub. Only the deltas are here.

  • Population: beneficiaries, not Soldiers. Active-duty AD is rare and, when it occurs, is young-onset and often familial — so genetic counselling is in scope and should precede any testing.
  • Army hook is the plain catch-all — AR 40-501 3-31k + para 3-1. No better-named subparagraph exists for AD.
  • The anti-amyloid delta is a beneficiary problem, not a fitness one. Two things an MTF must plan for: the MRI monitoring burden at a facility without ready capacity, and the fact that ARIA-E mimics ischaemic stroke. If you have beneficiaries on these drugs, your emergency department — and any remote or deployed facility they might present to — needs to know it before the thrombolysis decision.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Amyloid is necessary and insufficient — and the drugs prove both halves. For decades the amyloid hypothesis was argued from genetics and pathology while every therapeutic test of it failed. Lecanemab and donanemab settled the mechanistic question: remove amyloid and decline slows. They also settled the magnitude question less comfortably. Lecanemab slowed CDR-SB decline by 0.45 points over 18 months — about 27%, or roughly 4–5 months of delayed progression. Donanemab managed 0.67 points (36%) in the low/medium-tau population and 0.70 (29%) overall at 76 weeks, and reduced the risk of progressing from MCI to mild dementia by 33%, and mild to moderate by 50%. Those are real, reproducible, and small. Whether they are worth biweekly infusions, serial MRI, genotyping and a boxed warning is not a question medicine can answer on the patient's behalf — but it is a question that deserves the actual numbers rather than an adjective.

And the class has already lost a member. Aducanumab was withdrawn from the US market in November 2024 — a commercial decision rather than a safety or efficacy one, but a reminder that approval is not permanence. Anti-tau therapies have produced no positive phase 3 to date.

The honest framing for the clinic is a trade, not a breakthrough. These drugs slow a trajectory; they do not restore function or stop the disease. The patients most likely to benefit — early, biologically confirmed, without significant vascular or microhaemorrhage burden, with the support to attend monitoring — are a minority of the people who will ask about them. Saying so clearly is part of the job, and so is not letting a patient outside that group feel they have been denied something.

Meanwhile the diagnostic revolution may matter more than the therapeutic one. Plasma p-tau217 brings biological confirmation within reach of a blood draw. That is transformative for specialist triage and dangerous as a screening test — amyloid pathology exists in cognitively normal older adults, and a positive result cannot be withdrawn once given. The discipline the field needs is about who gets tested, not about what the assay can detect.

And the unglamorous interventions keep outperforming. Deprescribing anticholinergics and benzodiazepines, treating sleep apnoea and hearing loss, controlling vascular risk, and supporting caregivers still deliver more benefit to more patients than anything in the biologics column.

Key sources: FDA labelling for lecanemab and donanemab; NIA-AA diagnostic and staging framework; FDA labelling for the cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine and brexpiprazole.

  2. Donanemab (Kisunla) FDA label, effective 2025-12-30 — 350/700/1,050/1,400 mg titration and the stop-on-amyloid-clearance provision. DailyMed
  3. Donepezil, rivastigmine (capsule and transdermal), galantamine ER, memantine — current FDA labels; all dosing on this page is taken from them.
