Not independently verified:* the Auvelity dosing for the agitation indication (not label-pulled — check the label before prescribing*); TRICARE coverage for anti-amyloid therapy and amyloid PET; and the military paragraph citations beyond those verified on the hub.

docs.title: Frontotemporal dementia
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

Part of Approach to cognitive impairment.

One-liner: a group of young-onset degenerative syndromes that begin with behaviour, personality or language rather than memory — frequently misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness for years, frequently inherited, and the dementia most likely to present in someone still working.

Who this is for: the provider seeing a 45–65-year-old whose personality has changed, whose job performance has collapsed, or whose speech is failing — and who has already been through psychiatry. In a military population this is the one degenerative dementia that can genuinely present on active duty.

🚩 The pattern that should stop you calling it psychiatric

Finding Why it matters Personality change in a 50-year-old with no psychiatric history New-onset primary psychiatric illness in mid-life is uncommon. Late-onset "depression" that is really apathy, or "mania" that is really disinhibition, is bvFTD until proven otherwise Loss of empathy, socially inappropriate behaviour, loss of insight Not a mood disorder. The family, not the patient, brings the complaint New compulsive or ritualised behaviour; dietary change, especially carbohydrate craving Highly characteristic and rarely volunteered — ask Progressive language failure with preserved memory Primary progressive aphasia Any of the above + fasciculations, weakness, dysphagia FTD–ALS overlap. Look for it deliberately; it changes prognosis and counselling entirely A parent or sibling with young-onset dementia, ALS, or "early Alzheimer's" Up to a third of FTD is autosomal dominant — take a three-generation family history

The commonest error is years of psychiatric treatment before anyone images the brain. In a mid-life patient with new behavioural change and declining function, imaging is not over-investigation.

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
Behavioural-variant FTD (bvFTD) — the commonest form. Diagnosis rests on early and progressive change in behaviour or personality, with features drawn from: disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative, stereotyped or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality and dietary change, and a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. Supportive imaging shows frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy or hypometabolism.

Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) — language is the earliest and most prominent deficit:

Variant Core deficit Typical pathology Nonfluent/agrammatic Effortful, halting speech; agrammatism; apraxia of speech Usually FTD (tau) Semantic Loss of word meaning; impaired naming and single-word comprehension; surface dyslexia Usually FTD (TDP-43) Logopenic Word-finding pauses, impaired sentence repetition Usually Alzheimer's disease — see AD

The logopenic caveat matters: a PPA syndrome does not mean FTD pathology. If the variant is logopenic, the underlying disease is most often AD, and that changes both prognosis and whether amyloid biomarkers are worth pursuing.

FTD–ALS overlap: motor neuron disease develops in a meaningful minority of FTD patients, and cognitive/behavioural change occurs in a substantial proportion of ALS patients. Examine for fasciculations, wasting, weakness, brisk reflexes and bulbar signs at every visit — the finding transforms the conversation about prognosis and about advance planning.

Genetics — ask, then decide whether to test

A family history of dementia is reported in up to 40% of FTD, with clear autosomal dominant inheritance in roughly 10–30%. Three genes account for the large majority — about 60% of familial cases: C9orf72 (also the commonest genetic cause of ALS, and the classic FTD–ALS link), MAPT (tau) and GRN (progranulin).

  • Take a three-generation family history, and ask specifically about ALS and about psychiatric illness — affected relatives are often mislabelled.
  • Genetic testing is a counselling event, not a lab test. It has implications for adult children, for insurance, and — in a service member — potentially for career. Refer to genetic counselling before testing, not after the result.

What supports the diagnosis: MRI showing frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric; FDG-PET showing frontotemporal hypometabolism, which is particularly useful when MRI is equivocal and when the question is FTD versus AD; and neuropsychological testing showing a dysexecutive or language-led profile with relatively preserved episodic memory. Amyloid biomarkers are useful mainly to argue against AD in an ambiguous case.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Take the collateral history. In bvFTD the patient's account is not merely unreliable — the loss of insight is a diagnostic feature.
  2. Image early. MRI brain; add FDG-PET if the clinical picture is ambiguous or the MRI is unremarkable.
  3. Examine for motor neuron signs — and repeat it at follow-up.
  4. Neuropsychological testing to establish the profile and a baseline.
  5. Take a three-generation family history; refer to genetic counselling if the pattern suggests inheritance.
  6. Stop the drugs that will not help and may harm — cholinesterase inhibitors, antipsychotics where avoidable.
  7. Treat the behaviour that most endangers the patient or the family, non-pharmacologically first, then an SSRI.
  8. Address safety early and bluntly — driving, firearms, finances, and the patient's capacity to make major decisions, which is often already impaired at diagnosis.
  9. Support the caregiver. Caregiver burden in bvFTD exceeds that in AD at equivalent stages, because behaviour is harder to live with than forgetfulness.
  10. Military disposition — and this is the dementia most likely to arise on active duty.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
There is no disease-modifying treatment for FTD. Everything below is symptomatic, and the most valuable interventions are non-pharmacological.

Step 1 — non-pharmacological, and deprescribing

  • Identify triggers and restructure the environment. Behaviour in bvFTD is often stimulus-driven and routine-dependent; changing the environment works better than changing the neurochemistry.
  • Caregiver education is the intervention. Families need to hear that the behaviour is the disease, not a choice and not a personality flaw — that reframing changes outcomes.
  • Stop cholinesterase inhibitors if someone has started one. They are not indicated in FTD, do not help, and may worsen behavioural symptoms — a common inherited error from an assumed Alzheimer's diagnosis.
  • Memantine is not indicated in FTD and has not shown benefit.
  • Review every sedating and anticholinergic drug.

Step 2 — if medication is needed for behaviour

  • SSRIs are the usual first choice for disinhibition, compulsive and repetitive behaviours, overeating and irritability. Sertraline is the pragmatic default; citalopram carries dose-dependent QT prolongation. All are off-label for FTD.
  • Trazodone is used for agitation and sleep, also off-label. It carries the antidepressant class boxed warning for suicidal thoughts and behaviours in young adults — which matters more here than in late-life dementia, because FTD patients are frequently under 65 and sometimes under 55.
  • Antipsychotics: avoid where possible. The boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis applies, and patients with FTD may be unusually sensitive to extrapyramidal effects. If genuinely required, use the lowest dose of an atypical for the shortest time, with a documented review date.
  • Do not treat apathy with a stimulant reflexively — the evidence is thin and the cardiovascular and behavioural risks are real.

Avoid

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors — no benefit, possible worsening.
  • Memantine — no demonstrated benefit in FTD.
  • Antipsychotics as a default for behaviour — boxed warning, extrapyramidal sensitivity.
  • Benzodiazepines — disinhibition can worsen.
  • Assuming a PPA syndrome is FTD — the logopenic variant is usually Alzheimer's disease.
  • Genetic testing without counselling, particularly in a service member.

TRICARE — FTD prescribing

  • There is no disease-modifying therapy to authorize, and the symptomatic agents — SSRIs, trazodone — are generic and formulary. The prescribing side of this page is inexpensive.
  • The cost and coverage questions here are diagnostic and supportive, not pharmaceutical: FDG-PET, neuropsychological testing, genetic testing and counselling, speech and language therapy for PPA, and — the largest by far — long-term care and caregiver support for a patient who may be decades from retirement age.
  • Young-onset disease creates benefit problems that older-onset disease does not — dependent children, a working spouse, and an active-duty or recently separated status that determines which system the family lands in. Involve case management early; this is the single most useful thing an MTF can do for these families.
  • Verify current coverage at the TRICARE Formulary Search and with the regional contractor. Not independently verified for this page.

Military medicine — frontotemporal dementia

Section-wide framing on the hub. Only the deltas are here — and this is the page where they matter most.

  • This is the one degenerative dementia that genuinely presents on active duty. Peak onset spans the late 40s to early 60s — squarely within a senior NCO or field-grade career.
  • The realistic presentation is a disciplinary or performance problem, not a medical one. Uncharacteristic misconduct, financial irresponsibility, inappropriate remarks, apathy read as laziness, or a collapse in evaluation reports. A previously exemplary senior Soldier whose conduct changes in mid-life deserves a neurological thought before an administrative one. By the time the diagnosis is made, the record may already contain adverse actions the disease caused.
  • The documentation problem is the screening instrument. In bvFTD, judgment and impulse control are impaired before cognition tests abnormal — a MoCA of 27 does not exclude it, and normal screening does not rebut the diagnosis. What carries a board is a formal executive and behavioural neuropsychological battery plus collateral and command corroboration, which is also what satisfies the AR 40-501 3-1a limb (duty interference "as substantiated by the Soldier's commander or supervisor") while a screening score is normal.
  • Profile: P primary, with S carried explicitly — disinhibition and personality change are exactly what DA Pam 40-502 puts under S. Section 4 must reach weapons access, financial responsibility and supervisory authority.
  • EPTS/LOD is most contested here. Symptoms precede diagnosis by years and the evidence sits in evaluation reports and financial or disciplinary records, not in medicine.
  • Where misconduct has already occurred, the interaction between the medical diagnosis and any administrative or UCMJ action is a legal and command question, not a medical one — document the neurological findings and their timeline factually and promptly, and let the appropriate authorities weigh them. Do not editorialise about culpability in the medical record.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
FTD is the dementia that arrives disguised as a character change. Because the earliest damage is to the frontal and anterior temporal regions that govern behaviour, empathy and language rather than memory, the first people to notice are a spouse, a supervisor or a bank — not a doctor, and not the patient, whose loss of insight is itself part of the syndrome. The result is a diagnostic delay measured in years, frequently spent in psychiatric care, and often accompanied by damage to relationships, finances and careers that a timely diagnosis would have limited.

It is also the dementia with the most genetics. A large minority is autosomal dominant, and C9orf72 links it to ALS — which is why the motor examination belongs in every FTD visit and why the family history is a clinical instrument rather than a formality. That inheritance turns the diagnosis into a family event, which is exactly why testing belongs downstream of counselling.

And it is the dementia where treatment has least to offer and management has most. There is no disease-modifying therapy, cholinesterase inhibitors do not help and may harm, and antipsychotics carry real risk. What does change outcomes is unglamorous: naming the disease early, restructuring the environment, coaching the family to stop attributing the behaviour to choice, protecting the patient's finances and safety while there is still something to protect, and supporting a caregiver whose burden is measurably heavier than in Alzheimer's disease.

Key sources: international consensus criteria for behavioural-variant FTD and for the primary progressive aphasias; FTD genetics literature for C9orf72, MAPT and GRN.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rascovsky K, et al. International consensus criteria for behavioural-variant FTD (FTDC), 2011 — still current; no revision has been published.
  2. Gorno-Tempini ML, et al. Classification of primary progressive aphasia and its variants, 2011 — still the standard three-variant framework, including the logopenic–Alzheimer's association.
  3. Sertraline, trazodone, atypical antipsychotics — current FDA labels; all use in FTD is off-label, and the antipsychotic class boxed warning applies. DailyMed
  4. Alzheimer's disease — this site, for the logopenic-variant overlap and the amyloid biomarker discussion.
  5. TBI — work-up & return to duty — this site, for the CTE/TES boundary.
  6. AR 40-501 para 3-31k, 3-1, 3-4, 4-27; DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d.

Verified August 2026: corrections applied — trazodone's antidepressant boxed warning was missing entirely and has been added, which matters more here than in late-life dementia because FTD patients are frequently under 65; the criteria citations are now named and confirmed current (Rascovsky 2011 for bvFTD, Gorno-Tempini 2011 for the PPA variants, neither revised); and the genetics figures were refined — family history in up to 40%, clear autosomal dominant in ~10–30%, with C9orf72/MAPT/GRN accounting for about 60% of familial cases. A military review confirmed the disciplinary-presentation framing and the UCMJ/culpability boundary as sound and appropriately bounded, and added the documentation point that normal screening does not rebut the diagnosis — a MoCA of 27 does not exclude bvFTD, and a board reading only the MoCA will get it wrong. Profile factor corrected from S to P primary, with S carried explicitly.**

Not independently verified:* SSRI and trazodone dosing in FTD — deliberately not quoted*, because all use here is off-label and the doses were not label-pulled; the claim that cholinesterase inhibitors may worsen FTD behaviour (confirmed as current consensus, not as trial evidence); the comparative caregiver-burden claim; and TRICARE criteria.

docs.title: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

Part of Approach to cognitive impairment.

One-liner: an α-synucleinopathy producing fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder — commonly misdiagnosed as Alzheimer's disease, and the one dementia where giving the wrong drug can kill the patient.

Who this is for: anyone about to prescribe an antipsychotic to an older adult with dementia, anyone puzzled by a patient whose cognition swings between visits, and anyone who has been told a patient "has Alzheimer's but sees things."

🚩 Neuroleptic sensitivity — the reason this page exists

Severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions occur in a large minority of DLB patients, and they can be irreversible or fatal. (The figure often quoted is "up to about half"; the Fourth Consensus Criteria list neuroleptic sensitivity as a supportive clinical feature and deliberately assign no percentage, because exposure is inconsistent and definitions vary. Treat it as common enough to change your prescribing, not as a number to quote.) The reaction is acute onset or worsening of parkinsonism, rigidity, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability — a neuroleptic-malignant-like syndrome.

  • Never give haloperidol or another typical antipsychotic to a patient with suspected DLB.
  • Atypicals are safer, not safe. The risk is reduced, not abolished — quetiapine and clozapine are the least-worst options, and olanzapine and risperidone are not.
  • This is a bedside emergency-department problem, not just a clinic one. The commonest way the harm happens is an agitated older patient in an ED or on a ward getting IM haloperidol before anyone takes a Parkinson's or hallucination history.
  • Ask the two questions before any antipsychotic in an older adult: do they have parkinsonism? and do they see things that are not there?

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
Core features — fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness; recurrent, well-formed, detailed visual hallucinations; REM sleep behaviour disorder, which may precede cognitive decline by years; and spontaneous parkinsonism.

Supportive and biomarker findings include severe neuroleptic sensitivity, autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary problems), repeated falls, syncope, hyposmia, depression, apathy and systematised delusions; reduced dopamine transporter uptake on DaT-SPECT; abnormal MIBG cardiac scintigraphy; and polysomnographic confirmation of REM sleep without atonia.

DLB vs Parkinson's disease dementia — the same biology, split by a clock

The distinction is conventional, not biological: the "1-year rule." If dementia begins before or within 1 year of parkinsonism, call it DLB; if parkinsonism has been established for more than a year before dementia, call it Parkinson's disease dementia.

Treat them essentially the same. The rule exists for research consistency and matters clinically mostly because it shapes what the family has already been told.

What gets it missed:

  • Fluctuation is mistaken for delirium — or for a patient "having a good day."
  • Memory is often relatively preserved early, so an amnestic screen looks reassuring. Visuospatial and attentional testing is where DLB shows up — pentagon or cube copy, clock draw, and sustained attention tasks.
  • Hallucinations are under-reported because patients with insight find them frightening to disclose. Ask directly, and ask the collateral historian.
  • RBD is dismissed as "vivid dreams." Ask whether the patient acts out dreams, and whether the bed partner has moved to another room or been injured.
  • Mixed AD and Lewy pathology is common — a positive amyloid biomarker does not exclude DLB.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Ask the two safety questions — parkinsonism? visual hallucinations? — and flag neuroleptic sensitivity prominently in the record before anything else happens.
  2. Take the collateral history, specifically for fluctuation, hallucinations, and dream enactment.
  3. Test visuospatial and attentional domains, not just memory.
  4. Screen for and treat orthostatic hypotension — it drives falls, and it is treatable.
  5. Deprescribe — anticholinergics, dopamine blockers (including antiemetics), benzodiazepines.
  6. Start a cholinesterase inhibitor. This class works better here than in Alzheimer's disease.
  7. Treat the symptom that most impairs function, one at a time: hallucinations, RBD, parkinsonism, orthostasis, or sleepiness.
  8. Address falls, driving and caregiver support. Do not apply the Alzheimer's driving thresholds here — DLB impairs driving fitness more severely at milder stages, because visuospatial, attentional and motor deficits do not track a global staging score.
  9. Military disposition — dementia is disqualifying upon diagnosis; see the military box.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — deprescribe, then treat orthostasis

  • Stop dopamine-blocking antiemetics — metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are common, avoidable causes of acute deterioration. Use ondansetron instead.
  • Stop anticholinergics — oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, tricyclics. They worsen cognition and hallucinations in a disease already defined by cholinergic deficit.
  • Stop or minimise benzodiazepines and sedating agents — falls, confusion.
  • Treat orthostatic hypotension — liberalise salt and fluid unless contraindicated, compression, elevate the head of the bed, and review antihypertensives, which are often no longer needed. Orthostasis is a major and reversible contributor to falls here.

Step 2 — cholinesterase inhibitor (the cornerstone in DLB/PDD)

The cholinergic deficit in Lewy body disease is more profound than in Alzheimer's, and the response — particularly for hallucinations, apathy and fluctuation — is often better.

  • Rivastigmine — the agent with an FDA indication for mild-to-moderate dementia associated with Parkinson's disease. Oral: 1.5 mg PO BID, increasing by 1.5 mg BID at minimum 2-week intervals to a maximum of 6 mg BID as tolerated.
    • Patch: 4.6 mg/24 h, increasing after ≥4 weeks to 9.5 mg/24 h (the minimum effective dose) and after a further ≥4 weeks to 13.3 mg/24 h. The patch is often better tolerated and is the pragmatic first choice.
  • Donepezil — 5 mg PO once daily, increasing to 10 mg daily after 4–6 weeks. Widely used in DLB, though its labelled indication is Alzheimer's-type dementia — off-label here, and worth saying so.
  • Watch the pulse. Cholinergic bradycardia matters more in a population already prone to syncope and falls.

Step 3 — treat the dominant symptom

Visual hallucinationsREM sleep behaviour disorderParkinsonismExcessive daytime sleepiness
  • First, remove the cause — anticholinergics, dopaminergic drugs, infection, dehydration, poor lighting, visual impairment. Correct the glasses and turn a light on before reaching for a drug.
  • Optimise the cholinesterase inhibitor — often sufficient.
  • If hallucinations are distressing or dangerous and non-drug measures fail: quetiapine at a low starting dose, or clozapine, which has the better evidence in Parkinson's disease psychosis but requires absolute neutrophil count monitoring. Both are off-label for DLB. Start low, go slow, review to stop.
  • Try the cholinesterase inhibitor first. Consensus is explicit that ChEIs should precede any antipsychotic for psychosis and agitation in DLB — they can substantially reduce hallucinations and delusions, and they carry none of the sensitivity risk.
  • Pimavanserin (Nuplazid) — 34 mg PO once daily, no titration. Carries the antipsychotic class boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Its FDA indication is hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson's disease psychosis — using it in DLB is off-label, and the page should not pretend otherwise. A basket trial in dementia-related psychosis was positive and stopped early for success, but the FDA did not grant a broad dementia-related psychosis indication — it remains PD psychosis only.
  • All antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, and pimavanserin is included.
  • Not every hallucination needs treating. A patient with insight who is not distressed by benign, non-threatening imagery may be better served by explanation than by a drug.
  • Make the bedroom safe first — remove hard and sharp objects, pad or lower the bed, consider separate beds. This is the intervention that prevents injury.
  • Melatonin is the usual first pharmacological choice, and is preferred over clonazepam in this population because of falls, sedation and cognitive effects.
  • A benzodiazepine (clonazepam) works but is the wrong drug class in a falls-prone, cognitively impaired patient — last resort only, lowest possible dose, explicit review date. Neither melatonin nor clonazepam is FDA-labelled for RBD; doses are deliberately not quoted here pending review.
  • Carbidopa/levodopa is the treatment, but the response is typically less robust than in Parkinson's disease and it can worsen hallucinations and confusion. Dosing is deliberately not quoted here — it is titrated to motor response in a population where the psychiatric ceiling, not the motor benefit, sets the dose.
  • Treat only if the motor symptoms are functionally limiting, use the lowest effective dose, and titrate slowly with an explicit warning to the family about psychiatric worsening.
  • Avoid dopamine agonists, amantadine and anticholinergic antiparkinsonian drugs — all worse for cognition and hallucinations than levodopa.
  • Screen for and treat sleep apnoea, and review sedating medications first.
  • Sleepiness is intrinsic to the disease and often the symptom families find hardest; scheduled activity and light exposure help more than stimulants.

Avoid

  • Haloperidol and all typical antipsychotics — severe sensitivity reactions, potentially fatal. Flag this in the allergy field, not the progress note.
  • Olanzapine and risperidone — worse tolerated here than quetiapine or clozapine.
  • Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine — dopamine blockers hiding in the antiemetic order set.
  • Anticholinergics of any kind, including for bladder symptoms.
  • Benzodiazepines — except a deliberate, reviewed clonazepam trial for injurious RBD.
  • Dopamine agonists, amantadine, anticholinergic antiparkinsonian agents.
  • Surgery without a plan — anaesthesia, opioids and antiemetics all conspire here. Tell the surgical and anaesthetic teams the diagnosis in advance.

TRICARE — DLB/PDD prescribing

  • The workhorses are generic and formulary — rivastigmine (capsule and patch), donepezil, memantine, carbidopa/levodopa, melatonin. Nothing in the first two steps should require a prior authorization.
  • Quetiapine and clozapine are generic; clozapine's constraint is the ANC monitoring and registry requirement, not the formulary.
  • Pimavanserin is a branded specialty agent — assume prior authorization, and note that a PA written for DLB rather than Parkinson's disease psychosis is off-label and should be argued as such, with the literature and the clinical rationale, rather than filed as a formulary request.
  • Verify current status at the TRICARE Formulary Search before counselling. TRICARE-specific criteria were not independently verified for this page.

Military medicine — DLB and PDD

Section-wide framing on the hub. Only the deltas are here.

  • The military value of this page is safety, not disposition. These are beneficiary-age diseases; active-duty cases would be extraordinary. What matters is stopping an MTF, ED, peri-operative or deployed provider who has never met the patient from giving haloperidol or another D2 blocker. Flag neuroleptic sensitivity on the problem list and in the allergy field, not in a progress note.
  • Named Army hook beats the catch-all: AR 40-501 3-31d — "progressive degenerative disorders of the basal ganglia and cerebellum, including Parkinson's disease" — cited alongside 3-31k. Aeromedical 4-27i names Parkinson's disease and basal ganglia disease directly.
  • Profile is unambiguously P (parkinsonism, orthostasis, falls), with S added for the neuropsychiatric burden.
  • Do not apply the Alzheimer's driving thresholds — DLB impairs driving fitness more severely at milder stages.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Two diseases, one protein, and a rule invented for tidiness. DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia share α-synuclein pathology, cholinergic depletion and clinical phenomenology; the 1-year rule that separates them is a research convention, not a biological boundary. It survives because it lets trials enrol consistent populations — but at the bedside the treatment is the same, and pretending otherwise mostly confuses families who have already been given one label.

The cholinergic deficit is deeper here than in Alzheimer's, and it shows. Cholinesterase inhibitors, whose effect in AD is genuinely modest, often produce visible improvement in DLB — particularly in hallucinations, apathy and the fluctuation itself. That is the closest thing to a mechanistically satisfying treatment response in the dementias, and it argues for starting one early rather than reserving it.

And the most important fact on the page is a prohibition. Neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB is not a side effect to weigh against benefit — it is a potentially fatal, sometimes irreversible reaction affecting a large minority of patients. Most of the harm is preventable by two questions asked before an antipsychotic is written for any older adult. This is the rare instance where the diagnosis matters most to the clinician who has never heard of the patient.

Key sources: DLB consortium consensus criteria; FDA labelling for rivastigmine and pimavanserin; the antipsychotic class boxed warning for dementia-related psychosis.

docs.text:
1. Rivastigmine (capsule and transdermal) FDA labels — the Parkinson's disease dementia indication and the titration schedules quoted on this page.
  2. Pimavanserin (Nuplazid) FDA label, effective 2026-06-18 — 34 mg once daily, indicated for Parkinson's disease psychosis; DLB use is off-label. DailyMed
  3. Donepezil, memantine — current FDA labels; use in DLB is off-label.
  4. McKeith IG, et al. Fourth Consensus Report of the DLB Consortium, 2017 — still current. REM sleep behaviour disorder was elevated to a core clinical feature in this edition; neuroleptic sensitivity is listed as supportive, with no percentage assigned. Criteria for prodromal DLB (MCI-LB) have since been published; a biological staging framework based on CSF α-synuclein has been proposed but is not yet in the diagnostic criteria.
  5. AR 40-501 para 3-31k, 3-1, 3-4, 4-27; DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d.

Verified August 2026: rivastigmine and pimavanserin dosing and indications are from current FDA labels. Corrections applied: the neuroleptic-sensitivity frequency was softened — the Fourth Consensus Criteria (McKeith 2017) list it as a supportive feature and assign no percentage, so "up to about half" is presented as the commonly quoted figure rather than a criterion; cholinesterase inhibitors are now stated as first-line for psychosis and agitation, ahead of any antipsychotic; pimavanserin's boxed warning is attached to the drug, and the page now records that a dementia-related-psychosis basket trial was positive but the FDA did not grant a broad indication; and the Alzheimer's driving thresholds are explicitly disclaimed here, because DLB impairs driving fitness at milder stages. The Army hook was corrected to the named AR 40-501 3-31d, and the profile factor from S to P.**

Not independently verified: the comparative tolerability ranking among atypical antipsychotics (supported but on a weak evidence base); melatonin and clonazepam dosing in RBD, deliberately not quoted because neither is FDA-labelled for it; carbidopa/levodopa dosing, titrated to a psychiatric rather than motor ceiling; and TRICARE criteria.

docs.title: Rapidly progressive dementia
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

Part of Approach to cognitive impairment.

One-liner: dementia evolving over weeks to months rather than years — a presentation that is not a variant of the degenerative dementias but a separate emergency, because a meaningful proportion of causes are treatable and the window closes.

Who this is for: anyone whose "memory clinic" referral has deteriorated between the referral and the appointment. The question is never "which dementia is this" — it is "what treatable thing am I about to miss."

🚩 Treat this as an emergency, not a clinic problem

Any of these means admit or expedite, today:

  • Cognitive decline over weeks to a few months, particularly with a datable onset.
  • Myoclonus, ataxia, or new visual disturbance with cognitive decline.
  • Seizures, especially faciobrachial dystonic seizures.
  • New psychiatric presentation with movement disorder, autonomic instability or hyponatraemia.
  • Fever, headache, or systemic illness with cognitive change.
  • Known cancer, immunosuppression, or new focal deficit.

The single most important decision is early: is this autoimmune? Autoimmune encephalitis is the commonest treatable cause of rapidly progressive dementia, and outcome depends on how quickly immunotherapy starts. Waiting for antibody results before treating is the classic and costly error.

Do not anchor on prion disease. CJD is the famous cause; it is not the commonest, and treating it as the default costs treatable patients their window.

docs.title: The differential — work it systematically
docs.text:
A structured sweep prevents the two failure modes: missing a treatable cause, and over-investigating a degenerative one. Work these categories deliberately rather than by association.

Category Examples Clues Autoimmune / paraneoplastic Anti-NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GAD65; paraneoplastic (Hu, Ma2, CV2); steroid-responsive encephalopathy with autoimmune thyroiditis Seizures, psychiatric onset, movement disorder, autonomic instability, hyponatraemia (LGI1), faciobrachial dystonic seizures (LGI1) Infectious HSV, VZV, HIV, neurosyphilis, PML, fungal, TB, Whipple, Lyme, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis Fever, immunosuppression, exposure, CSF pleocytosis Neoplastic CNS lymphoma, intravascular lymphoma, gliomatosis, carcinomatous meningitis Focal signs, imaging, weight loss, systemic disease Toxic / metabolic B12, thiamine (Wernicke), thyroid, hepatic, renal, hyponatraemia, heavy metals, drugs Nutrition, alcohol, dialysis, polypharmacy Vascular Vasculitis, CADASIL, CAA-related inflammation, multiple emboli, endocarditis Headache, stepwise decline, systemic inflammation, murmur Prion Sporadic CJD, variant, familial, iatrogenic Myoclonus, ataxia, akinetic mutism, characteristic MRI Systemic / iatrogenic Sarcoid, SLE, medication effect, chemotherapy or immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity Systemic features, drug timeline

Two that are missed most often, for opposite reasons

  • Wernicke encephalopathy — missed because it is looked for only in overt alcoholism. Consider it in bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, malignancy, malnutrition and prolonged vomiting. If it crosses your mind, give thiamine — the treatment is safe and the damage is not reversible once established.
  • Autoimmune encephalitis — missed because the presentation is psychiatric and the patient goes to psychiatry. A first psychotic episode with seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability, or a rapidly abnormal course is not primary psychiatric illness.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
Step 1 — the immediate set, in parallel, not in sequence

  • MRI brain with and without contrast, including DWI and FLAIR. DWI is essential — the cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restriction of prion disease live there, and it will also show the medial temporal changes of autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
  • EEG — non-convulsive status is a treatable cause of subacute decline and is invisible without it. Also looks for the periodic patterns of prion disease and the extreme delta brush described in NMDAR encephalitis.
  • Lumbar puncture — cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, cytology and flow cytometry, infectious studies, and paired serum and CSF autoimmune/paraneoplastic panels. Send CSF for both — serum alone misses cases, and CSF alone misses others.
  • Bloods: CBC, CMP, thyroid function and TPO antibodies, B12 and thiamine, ESR/CRP, ANA and ENA, ANCA, HIV, RPR/treponemal, and drug/toxicology as indicated.
  • Malignancy screen — CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and consider whole-body FDG-PET where paraneoplastic disease is suspected. Testicular ultrasound and pelvic imaging as appropriate.

Step 2 — targeted, when the picture points

  • Prion-specific: CSF RT-QuIC — the assay that changed this diagnosis. It detects the misfolded prion protein directly. Second-generation CSF RT-QuIC: sensitivity 92–97%, specificity 99–100% — and it has superseded 14-3-3 as the test of choice, since 14-3-3 is a non-specific marker of neuronal injury that produced both false alarm and false reassurance.
    • But know where it is weaker. Sensitivity is highest for MM1/MV1 and VV2 subtypes and falls for MV2 (75–93%) and MM2 (44–78%) — so a negative RT-QuIC does not exclude CJD, particularly in an atypical phenotype. False positives occur at <1%.
    • 14-3-3 and total tau remain useful as routine tests, particularly where RT-QuIC is not available. Do not discard them; demote them.
    • Olfactory mucosa RT-QuIC reaches ~96% sensitivity and ~100% specificity where it is offered.
  • Brain biopsy — reserved for when the treatable causes have been pursued and a diagnosis would change management, most often suspected CNS vasculitis, lymphoma or CAA-related inflammation. A negative biopsy does not exclude.
  • Genetic testing — familial prion disease, CADASIL, and the young-onset degenerative dementias.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm the tempo. Weeks to months, with a datable onset, from a collateral historian.
  2. Admit, or expedite to the point of functional admission. This does not work as a series of outpatient appointments.
  3. Run Step 1 in parallel — MRI, EEG, LP with paired panels, bloods, malignancy screen.
  4. Give thiamine now if there is any nutritional risk. Do not wait.
  5. Ask the autoimmune question explicitly, and answer it against a threshold rather than a feeling. The Graus 2016 criteria exist precisely so this decision can be made without antibodies — subacute onset (<3 months) of working-memory deficit, altered mental status or psychiatric symptoms, PLUS at least one of: new focal CNS findings, unexplained seizures, CSF pleocytosis, or MRI features suggestive of encephalitis — with reasonable exclusion of alternatives. If that is met, you have enough to treat.
  6. If autoimmune encephalitis is plausible, start immunotherapy — do not wait for antibodies. Antibody results take days to weeks; outcome tracks time to treatment.
  7. Look for the tumour, and keep looking if the first screen is negative and suspicion persists.
  8. Only when the treatable causes are excluded should the conversation turn to prion or degenerative disease.
  9. Prognosis and planning — for prion disease especially, the trajectory is fast and families need honesty early.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Before the first dose of high-dose steroid — three things, every time

  1. Is aciclovir running? Start it first in any febrile or possibly infectious encephalopathy. Steroids into untreated HSV, TB, cryptococcus or a parasitic CNS infection is how a survivable illness becomes a fatal one.
  2. Has the LP been done, and the CSF sent for cytology and flow cytometry? Steroids clear the CSF, abolish the pleocytosis and destroy the cytology yield within 24–48 hours. Tap first if you can tap at all.
  3. Is there an enhancing mass lesion that could be lymphoma? If so, talk to neurosurgery and haematology before the steroid, not after. Steroids melt primary CNS lymphoma — the lesion vanishes, the biopsy becomes non-diagnostic for weeks to months, and the patient loses the time. A dramatic steroid response is not evidence for autoimmune encephalitis; PCNSL does exactly the same thing.

None of these is a reason to delay treatment in a patient without a mass lesion. They take minutes, not days.

Treat the treatable — and treat empirically where waiting costs more than acting

  • Thiamine — give it on suspicion, before any glucose, parenterally, and give the TREATMENT dose, not the 100 mg maintenance dose.
    • Thiamine 500 mg IV over 30 minutes every 8 hours for 2–3 days, then 250 mg IV/IM daily for 5 days, then oral. Continue while the diagnosis remains plausible.
    • If 500 mg cannot be stocked, the floor is 200 mg IV three times daily — never 100 mg once. 100 mg IV is prophylaxis, not treatment.
    • Watch the vial arithmetic: thiamine is stocked at 100 mg/mL, so a 500 mg dose is 5 mL — five vials. Drawing one vial is the commonest way this is under-dosed.
    • Give magnesium alongside — thiamine-dependent enzymes are magnesium-dependent, and replacement fails in hypomagnesaemia.
    • Do not withhold glucose from a hypoglycaemic patient while hunting for thiamine. Give thiamine first or simultaneously; do not let the sequencing rule cause a hypoglycaemic death.
  • Aciclovir empirically for any febrile or subacute encephalopathy where HSV is on the list. Start it before the LP if the LP will be delayed.
    • Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours — dosed on ideal body weight in obesity, renally adjusted, infused over ≥1 hour, with generous IV hydration. The drug is crystal-nephrotoxic if run fast into a dry patient.
    • Duration 14–21 days once confirmed. Do not treat a 3-day course.
    • A negative CSF HSV PCR in the first 72 hours of symptoms does NOT exclude HSV encephalitis — and that is exactly the window in which a page telling you to move fast gets the LP done. A bloody tap also inhibits the PCR. If suspicion persists, continue aciclovir and repeat the LP at 3–7 days.
    • The cost of continuing is trivial; the cost of stopping on a false negative is the patient.
  • Autoimmune encephalitis — first-line immunotherapy started on clinical grounds: methylprednisolone 1,000 mg IV daily × 3–5 days (the regimen used throughout this site), IVIG, and/or plasma exchange, alone or in combination, per your neuroimmunology pathway. Read the checklist below before the first steroid dose. Escalate to second-line (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) if the response is inadequate — early escalation is associated with better outcomes. Regimens are not dosed on this page because they were not label-verified at drafting; use your institutional protocol or the current consensus guidance.
  • Remove the tumour where a paraneoplastic cause is found — in ovarian teratoma-associated NMDAR encephalitis, resection is part of the treatment, not just the oncology.
  • Treat the infection, the metabolic derangement, or the drug — obvious, and still missed.
  • Non-convulsive status — treat as status epilepticus.

Avoid

  • Waiting for antibody results before starting immunotherapy in a plausible case. This is the single commonest management error in this presentation.
  • Giving 100 mg IV thiamine and calling it treated. That is the prophylactic dose.
  • Stopping aciclovir on a single negative HSV PCR drawn in the first 72 hours.
  • Starting high-dose steroids before aciclovir is running in a febrile encephalopathy, or before tissue where an enhancing mass lesion could be lymphoma.
  • Anchoring on CJD. It ends the search prematurely, and the search is where the treatable patients are found.
  • Attributing a first psychiatric presentation with neurological signs to psychiatry without excluding autoimmune encephalitis.
  • Glucose before thiamine in a malnourished patient.
  • Ordering 14-3-3 as the prion test. It lacks specificity; RT-QuIC is the test.
  • Brain biopsy before the non-invasive treatable work-up is complete.

TRICARE — rapidly progressive dementia

  • This is an inpatient problem, and the inpatient benefit covers it. Do not delay MRI, LP, EEG or empiric treatment for an authorization.
  • The specialty items to anticipate are the autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panels (send-out, expensive, and frequently queried), CSF RT-QuIC (sent to a specialist prion laboratory), whole-body FDG-PET for occult malignancy, and IVIG or plasma exchange — which run through the medical benefit and, in the outpatient continuation phase, need authorization.
  • Second-line immunotherapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) is high-cost, off-label for most autoimmune encephalitis indications, and should be argued as off-label medical necessity with literature support, not filed as a formulary request.
  • Verify current coverage at the TRICARE Formulary Search and with the regional contractor before counselling — DoD P&T revises criteria without notice. Not independently verified for this page.

Military medicine — rapidly progressive dementia

Framework — verify against current AR 40-501, DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 and Vol 2, DoDI 1332.18, and applicable force-health-protection guidance. See Profiles, MEB/MAR2 & deployability.

  • This is the one page in this section that is genuinely an active-duty problem. Autoimmune encephalitis and CNS infection are diseases of young adults, and a service member with a subacute psychiatric-then-neurological presentation is a realistic scenario in a way that Alzheimer's disease is not.
  • The military-specific risk is a psychiatric admission. A young service member with new psychosis, agitation or behavioural change is very likely to reach behavioural health before neurology. Autoimmune encephalitis presenting to a military behavioural health service and treated as a primary psychiatric illness is the failure mode this page exists to prevent. Seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability, hyponatraemia, or a course that does not behave like psychiatry should trigger neurology and an LP.
  • Disposition follows the cause and the residual deficit, not the presentation — and the regulation says so on its face. DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d reaches "permanent or progressive cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or other dementias." A treatable autoimmune encephalitis or CNS infection with expected recovery is neither permanent nor progressive, so 5.26.d does not engage at all until permanence or progression is established. That is a textual argument, not a clinical judgement call — make it.
    • Until then the ordinary route applies: temporary profile, linked extensions, MRDP (clinical, or the 12-month administrative point), then the retention question under AR 40-501 3-31k → para 3-1 — or 3-31i if seizures persist — gated normally by 5.26.a.
  • MEB / MAR2 — and here, unlike the rest of this section, MAR2 is genuinely on the table. These Soldiers may recover into a Soldier who meets retention standards but cannot perform their PMOS — which is a MAR2, an administrative review, not a disability process. Refer to the DES only if residual impairment fails 3-31k → 3-1 at MRDP. Do not refer before MRDP; recovery here runs for months.
  • Profile: temporary through the diagnostic work-up, treatment and recovery — which can run many months. Link every extension; do not close it at hospital discharge, and expect the 12-month administrative MRDP to become the driver in a slow recoverer.
  • EPTS / LOD: onset is datable here, unlike the degenerative dementias, which makes LOD relatively straightforward. Document the exposure or trigger where one exists, and, in infectious cases, whether it was deployment-associated — that determination has downstream consequences.
  • Deployability: non-deployable during work-up, treatment and recovery. Reassess against documented cognitive recovery, seizure freedom and medication requirement, not against discharge from hospital.
  • Aeromedical: grounded; USAAMA adjudicates, and a seizure or a residual cognitive deficit will each independently keep an aircrew member grounded.
  • The CBRN and outbreak angle — a cluster of subacute encephalopathy in a deployed or garrison population is a public health event, not a series of individual cases. Notify preventive medicine and the public health emergency officer, as for botulism.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Speed changes the differential completely. A dementia that takes years is almost always degenerative; a dementia that takes weeks is a different problem with a different question. The whole value of separating rapidly progressive dementia as a category is that it forces the clinician to stop pattern-matching against Alzheimer's disease and start a systematic hunt — because a meaningful fraction of these patients have something that can be treated, and the treatment window is measured in weeks.

Autoimmune encephalitis reorganised this field twice. First by revealing that a large group of patients previously labelled psychiatric, or written off as viral encephalitis of unknown cause, had identifiable antibody-mediated disease. Then by establishing that outcome depends on time to immunotherapy — which means the correct clinical behaviour is to treat on clinical suspicion and let the antibody result arrive later. That is uncomfortable, and it is right.

And prion diagnosis finally became reliable. For years the CSF test in use was 14-3-3, a non-specific marker of neuronal injury that generated both false alarm and false reassurance. RT-QuIC detects the misfolded prion protein itself, and its specificity transformed a diagnosis that had previously rested on pattern recognition and time. The clinical consequence is not therapeutic — there is still no treatment — but a confident, earlier diagnosis spares families a futile investigative marathon and lets planning begin while it can still involve the patient.

Key sources: consensus criteria for autoimmune encephalitis; CSF RT-QuIC validation literature for sporadic CJD; the rapidly progressive dementia differential literature.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Autoimmune encephalitis clinical approach and consensus criteria — the "treat on clinical grounds" principle and the syndrome definitions summarised above. Citation not verified for this draft.
  2. CSF RT-QuIC for sporadic CJD — the assay that superseded 14-3-3. Citation and performance figures not verified for this draft.
  3. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy–related inflammation — this site, which carries the CAA-ri regimen.
  4. Status epilepticus — this site, for non-convulsive status.
  5. AR 40-501 para 3-31k, 3-1, 3-4, 4-27; DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d.

Verified August 2026: this page was the subject of a dedicated safety review, and it changed the most. The drafting decision to quote no doses at all was judged correct for IVIG, plasma exchange, rituximab and cyclophosphamide — and wrong for thiamine, aciclovir and corticosteroids. Three specific hazards were found and fixed. Thiamine now carries a treatment dose (500 mg IV q8h), because the site's own status epilepticus page prescribed 100 mg IV — the exact maintenance dose this page warned against — and that page has been corrected in the same pass. Aciclovir now carries 10 mg/kg IV q8h and the warning that a negative CSF HSV PCR in the first 72 hours does not exclude HSV encephalitis, because the previous wording ("while PCR is pending") read as a stop condition. A pre-steroid checklist was added, because the page's own differential includes primary CNS lymphoma and its Avoid box was pushing readers toward steroid-before-tissue. The Graus 2016 threshold now replaces "answer it clinically," and RT-QuIC is stated with its real performance (sens 92–97%, spec 99–100%, but 44–78% in MM2, so a negative does not exclude; 14-3-3 and t-tau retained where RT-QuIC is unavailable).

A military review confirmed the disposition argument and strengthened its basis: 5.26.d reaches only "permanent or progressive" cognitive impairment, so it does not engage at all in a treatable encephalitis with expected recovery — a textual argument, not a judgement call. MAR2 is genuinely on the table here, unlike elsewhere in this section, and that bullet was missing.

Not independently verified:* IVIG, plasma exchange, rituximab and cyclophosphamide regimens — deliberately still not quoted*, and routed to institutional protocol for the reasons above; the differential categories and their relative frequencies; and TRICARE criteria.

docs.title: Vascular cognitive impairment
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

Part of Approach to cognitive impairment.

One-liner: cognitive impairment caused by cerebrovascular disease — the only common dementia with a genuinely modifiable cause, which is why it is worth identifying even when it coexists with Alzheimer's pathology, as it usually does.

Who this is for: the provider looking at a scan full of white matter change wondering whether it explains the patient, and the one deciding what to actually do about it. The answer is mostly on the stroke prevention page — this page is about recognising the syndrome and knowing which lever to pull.

🚩 What changes the plan

Pattern Worry Do Cognitive decline within 3–6 months of a stroke Post-stroke cognitive impairment Formal cognitive assessment — it is routinely missed in stroke follow-up Lobar microbleeds and superficial siderosis Cerebral amyloid angiopathy — not just "small vessel disease" Changes anticoagulation decisions and anti-amyloid eligibility. Apply Boston v2.0 Young patient, migraine with aura, family history, confluent anterior temporal white matter change CADASIL and other monogenic small vessel disease Genetic referral; do not write it off as hypertensive change Gait disturbance leading, urinary symptoms, "magnetic" gait NPH vs vascular vs both These overlap and coexist; do not assume Rapid stepwise decline with headache or systemic features Vasculitis, endocarditis, hypercoagulable state Go to rapidly progressive dementia

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
The requirement is a plausible causal link, not merely coexistence. White matter hyperintensities are near-universal in older adults; finding them does not make the dementia vascular.

What supports a vascular contribution:

  • A temporal relationship — decline beginning within months of a clinical stroke, or a stepwise rather than smoothly progressive course.
  • A matching cognitive profile — processing speed and executive dysfunction lead, with memory relatively better preserved and, critically, helped by cueing (a retrieval rather than encoding failure — the opposite of Alzheimer's).
  • Imaging burden proportionate to the deficit — strategic infarcts (thalamus, angular gyrus, caudate, genu of internal capsule), multiple lacunes, or confluent white matter hyperintensity, not a few scattered dots.
  • Corroborating findings — gait disturbance, early urinary urgency, pseudobulbar affect, focal signs.

Subtypes worth distinguishing because they behave differently: post-stroke cognitive impairment; subcortical ischaemic small vessel disease, the commonest and most insidious; multi-infarct; strategic single infarct; hypoperfusion; and haemorrhagic, which brings CAA into the frame.

Mixed is the default, not the exception

Over 80, coexisting Alzheimer's and vascular pathology is the commonest finding at autopsy, and the two are more than additive — vascular burden lowers the threshold at which Alzheimer's pathology produces symptoms.

Practical consequence: a patient can have both, and treating the vascular half is worthwhile even when the amnestic syndrome points to AD. "Mixed dementia" is an honest diagnosis, not a hedge — and it justifies both a cholinesterase inhibitor and aggressive vascular risk reduction.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm the syndrome is executive- and speed-led, and that memory improves with cueing.
  2. Image, and read the scan properly — burden, location, strategic infarcts, and the microbleed pattern. Lobar microbleeds mean CAA, which changes decisions.
  3. Work the stroke aetiology if there has been a clinical event — this is a stroke work-up, not a dementia work-up.
  4. Attack the modifiable risk factors hard. This is the therapeutic core of the page.
  5. Screen for and treat depression and apathy — both are more common here than in AD and both are treatable.
  6. Consider a cholinesterase inhibitor where mixed pathology is likely.
  7. Rehabilitate — gait, falls, and cognitive rehabilitation where available.
  8. Military disposition — dementia is disqualifying upon diagnosis; the vascular risk factors have their own retention implications.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — vascular risk factor control (this is the treatment)

Full regimens are on the stroke prevention page; this is the cognitive-specific framing.

  • Blood pressure control is the single best-supported intervention for preventing and slowing vascular cognitive impairment. Target per current stroke-prevention guidance. Avoid over-treatment causing orthostatic hypotension in a falls-prone older patient — check standing pressures.
  • Lipids, diabetes, smoking cessation, atrial fibrillation detection and anticoagulation — as for secondary stroke prevention.
  • Antithrombotics per the stroke indication, not for the dementia. There is no indication for antiplatelet therapy to treat cognitive impairment itself, and in a patient with lobar microbleeds or suspected CAA the calculus shifts toward harm.
  • Physical activity — supported for both vascular and cognitive endpoints.

Step 2 — symptomatic and supportive

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not FDA-labelled for vascular dementia. Their use here is off-label, and the effect where present is small. The defensible case is probable mixed pathology, where you are treating the Alzheimer's component — say that explicitly rather than treating "vascular dementia" with an AD drug.
  • Treat depression and apathy — both common post-stroke and both under-treated. An SSRI is the usual choice.
  • Gait, falls and continence — physiotherapy, falls assessment, home safety.
  • Pseudobulbar affect — recognise it and explain it to the family; it is distressing and frequently mistaken for depression.

Avoid

  • Treating white matter hyperintensities as a diagnosis. They are a finding; the patient is the diagnosis.
  • Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy prescribed for cognition — no indication, and real harm where CAA is present.
  • Aggressive BP lowering without checking standing pressures — orthostatic hypotension causes falls and may worsen cerebral hypoperfusion.
  • Anticholinergics and benzodiazepines — as everywhere in this section.
  • Assuming "vascular" excludes Alzheimer's. It usually does not.

TRICARE — vascular cognitive impairment

  • Everything with evidence behind it is generic and formulary — antihypertensives, statins, metformin, antiplatelets, and the SSRIs. This is the cheapest dementia to treat well, because the treatment is cardiovascular risk management.
  • Anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation follow the stroke pages; DOAC tier and PA status change, so verify.
  • Cholinesterase inhibitors used off-label for presumed mixed pathology are generic and unlikely to be challenged, but document the mixed-pathology reasoning rather than coding an AD indication you have not established.
  • Cardiac rehabilitation, physiotherapy and falls programmes are usually the higher-value authorization requests here.
  • Verify current status at the TRICARE Formulary Search. Not independently verified for this page.

Military medicine — vascular cognitive impairment

Section-wide framing on the hub. Only the deltas are here.

  • This is the one page in the section where 5.26.d is often NOT the operative standard. Below the dementia threshold this is an ordinary post-stroke disposition running MRDP → the MAR2-versus-DES fork, gated normally by 5.26.a. Only when permanent or progressive cognitive impairment is established does 5.26.d take over and the gate disappear.
  • Named Army hook: AR 40-501 3-31f — "stroke… when residuals affect performance" — cited ahead of 3-31k, with DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 5.26.b as the DoD floor.
  • The risk factors carry their own standards. The stroke, the hypertension and the atrial fibrillation each have retention implications independent of the cognition — cite them separately; see stroke.
  • The realistic active-duty case is post-stroke cognitive impairment in a 40s–50s service member, not late-life small vessel disease. Formal cognitive assessment is routinely omitted from stroke follow-up — and in a service member that omission decides whether a real deficit is documented before a return-to-duty decision. Test it deliberately.
  • This is the only page in the section where the military box can legitimately be about prevention. Blood pressure, lipids, tobacco and weight management in mid-career service members are cognitive interventions as well as cardiovascular ones.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
The only dementia you can meaningfully prevent. Alzheimer's disease has a modifiable component; vascular cognitive impairment is mostly modifiable component. Blood pressure control has the strongest supporting evidence, and the interventions are the same ones already being pushed for cardiovascular reasons — which makes this the rare neurology page whose main therapeutic message is "do the cardiology properly."

The diagnostic trap is the scan. White matter hyperintensities are so prevalent in older adults that finding them explains nothing on its own, and "small vessel disease" has become a radiological shrug that closes down thinking. The discipline is to ask whether the burden and location are proportionate to the deficit and its profile — and to notice when the microbleed pattern is lobar, because that is cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which changes anticoagulation decisions and anti-amyloid eligibility rather than just adding a descriptor.

And the honest position on most older patients is "mixed." Coexisting Alzheimer's and vascular pathology is the commonest autopsy finding above 80, and the two interact — vascular burden lowers the threshold at which amyloid and tau produce symptoms. That is not a diagnostic failure to apologise for; it is a reason to treat both halves, and it is why the vascular risk factors deserve attention in every dementia clinic, not just this page.

Key sources: vascular cognitive impairment consensus criteria; the stroke-prevention evidence base as carried on the stroke prevention page; Boston v2.0 criteria for CAA.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Stroke prevention (primary and secondary) — this site; the regimens behind Step 1 live there and are verified on that page.
  2. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy — this site; Boston v2.0 criteria and the lobar-microbleed significance.
  3. Vascular cognitive impairment criteria — there is no single universally adopted edition. The two most commonly cited are the VASCOG criteria (Sachdev et al., 2014) and the AHA/ASA statement (Gorelick et al., 2011). Cite whichever you use, and say that no consensus standard exists.
  4. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine — current FDA labels; no vascular dementia indication exists and use here is off-label.
  5. AR 40-501 para 3-31k, 3-1, 3-4, 4-27; DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.d.

Verified August 2026: no doses are quoted on this page by design — the vascular risk-factor regimens defer to stroke prevention, which is separately verified, and the cholinesterase inhibitors are named only to say their use here is off-label with no vascular dementia indication. Corrections applied: the criteria citation is now explicit — there is no universally adopted edition, and VASCOG (Sachdev 2014) and AHA/ASA (Gorelick 2011) are the two to cite. A military review established that this is the one page in the section where 5.26.d is often not the operative standard: below the dementia threshold this runs as an ordinary post-stroke disposition through MRDP and the MAR2-versus-DES fork, gated normally by 5.26.a. The named Army hook is AR 40-501 3-31f (stroke with residuals), and the profile factor was corrected to P.**

Not independently verified: the blood-pressure evidence claims and mixed-pathology prevalence statements (both confirmed as current consensus in the evidence round, neither traced to a primary source here); the strategic-infarct locations; and TRICARE criteria.

docs.title: Headache — overview & triage
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

The first job in any headache patient is not to diagnose migraine — it is to exclude a secondary headache that will hurt the patient if you miss it. Triage on red flags first, then treat the primary headache.

Scale of the problem (GBD 2023): headache disorders affect ~2.9 billion people and are the 6th leading cause of health loss worldwide, with ~2× the disability burden in women. Tension-type headache is the most prevalent (~25%), but migraine causes ~90% of headache disability — and medication overuse drives a large share of both, so the MOH screen below earns its place.

🚩 Red flags — the full SNNOOP10 screen (any hit changes your pathway)

Flag Worry Do now S — Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss) Meningitis, abscess, systemic illness Labs, LP (image first if focal/↓LOC/papilledema) S — Secondary risk factors (HIV, immunosuppression) Opportunistic infection, abscess LP + targeted imaging N — Neoplasm history Brain metastasis, primary tumor MRI brain with contrast N — Neurologic deficit / ↓ consciousness / seizure Mass, stroke, encephalitis MRI (CT if emergent) O — Onset sudden / thunderclap (max <1 min) SAH, RCVS, dissection, CVST, apoplexy Non-contrast CT (6-h rule below) → LP/CTA/MRV O — Older age (new/progressive >50) GCA, mass ESR/CRP (start steroids if GCA likely), MRI P — Pattern change / progressive New secondary process Re-work up as a new headache P — Papilledema ↑ICP (IIH, mass, CVST) MRI + MRV, then LP with opening pressure P — Positional — worse standing Low pressure (SIH — CSF leak) MRI (pachymeningeal enhancement/brain sag) → blood patch P — Positional — worse lying / on waking High pressure (IIH, mass) MRI/MRV → LP opening pressure P — Precipitated by Valsalva / exertion / sex SAH, RCVS, posterior-fossa lesion CT + CTA head/neck; MRI P — Pregnancy / puerperium Pre-eclampsia, CVST, RCVS, PRES, apoplexy See the pregnancy box below P — Painful red eye ± autonomic features Acute angle-closure glaucoma (fixed mid-dilated pupil, nausea — vision loss in hours), cavernous sinus, Tolosa-Hunt, pituitary Check IOP / ophthalmology STAT; MRI P — Post-traumatic onset Structural injury / PTH Head-CT rule; see PTH page P — Pathology of the immune system Opportunistic infection, PML, lymphoma LP + MRI with contrast P — Painkiller overuse or a new drug MOH; drug effect Medication review; count acute-med days

Reassuring: an established, stereotyped, self-resolving headache with a normal exam and no red flags — that is where primary headache lives.

Thunderclap workup — the 6-hour CT rule

  • Non-contrast CT within 6 h of onset is ~99% sensitive for SAH — a negative CT in a neurologically intact patient presenting <6 h reasonably excludes SAH without an LP (2023 AHA/ASA).
  • >6 h from onset: CT sensitivity falls (~86–97%) — do an LP for xanthochromia if suspicion remains, and CTA/MRV for RCVS/dissection/CVST.
  • The Ottawa SAH Rule (100% sensitive) can screen out low-likelihood patients before imaging.

When NOT to image (AHS Grade A) — avoid the reflex MRI

Neuroimaging is not needed for headaches consistent with migraine when the neurologic exam is normal and there are no atypical features or red flags (AHS 2020). The prevalence of a significant intracranial abnormality in that group is ~0.2%. Over-imaging drives cost, incidental findings, and anxiety — reserve it for a red-flag hit (relevant where imaging access is limited, e.g., deployed/austere settings).

On the horizon (not clinic-ready): blood biomarkers (GFAP, neurofilament light) are being studied to separate serious secondary from primary headache — promising, not yet validated for use.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Screen for red flags (SNNOOP10 table). Any hit → secondary work-up pathway.
  2. Normal exam + no red flags? Classify the primary headache by phenotype.
  3. Route to the diagnosis:
    • Recurrent, moderate–severe, disabling, ± photophobia/phonophobia/nausea/aura → Migraine (if it reached neurology, it is almost never "just tension")
      • Quick screen — ID Migraine (<2 min, AHS-endorsed): in the last 3 months, did headaches (1) limit your activities ≥1 day? (2) cause nausea? (3) make you sensitive to light? ≥2 "yes" → migraine (≈84% sensitive, 93% PPV).
      • "Sinus headache" is migraine until proven otherwise — up to 88% of self-diagnosed sinus headaches meet migraine criteria (recurrent, predictable, photophobia/nausea, normal exam → migraine, not antibiotics).
    • Headache during or after SARS-CoV-2 infection → treat by phenotype (usually migraine- or tension-type-like); COVID is a recognized trigger for NDPH — re-work up if the pattern changes.
    • Bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild–moderate, NOT worsened by activity, no nausea → tension-type headache — analgesics (ibuprofen, high-dose acetaminophen) ± amitriptyline if frequent (VA/DoD 2023). But if it's disabling or frequent enough to reach you, reconsider migraine.
    • Severe unilateral attacks with ipsilateral autonomic features (tearing, ptosis, rhinorrhea), restless/agitated → Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (cluster, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT/SUNA)
    • Brief, electric, triggered stabs in a trigeminal division → Trigeminal neuralgia — and remember MS can present this way
    • Neck-driven pain with reduced cervical range of motion, reproducible from the neck → cervicogenic headache — manual therapy/PT ± nerve blocks (a top-3 secondary headache per VA/DoD; common in service members with neck trauma/load-bearing)
    • Headache ≥15 days/month with acute-med overuse → Medication overuse headache
    • Daily and unremitting from a remembered onset, no prior headache history → New daily persistent headache
    • Headache after head/neck trauma → Post-traumatic headache

docs.title: Don't-miss secondary headaches (quick recognition)
docs.text:
RCVS — recurrent thunderclaps, and do NOT give steroids

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome — the 2nd commonest cause of thunderclap headache after SAH. Recurrent thunderclaps over days–weeks, often triggered by vasoactive drugs, sexual activity, exertion, or the postpartum state; may cause convexity (not basal) SAH, and CTA/MRA shows "string of beads" vasoconstriction. Use the RCVS² score (≥5 → ~90% sensitive/~99% specific; ≤2 excludes it). Steroids worsen RCVS — the key distinction from primary CNS angiitis. Treat with nimodipine + trigger avoidance.

IIH vs SIH — same "positional," opposite pressure and treatment

  • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH — high pressure): young, overweight woman, daily headache + transient visual obscurations + pulsatile tinnitus + papilledema. Dx: MRI/ MRV (exclude mass/CVST) → LP opening pressure >250 mm. Rx: weight loss + acetazolamide; surgery (ONSF, CSF shunt, venous stenting) for progressive vision loss (untreated → permanent visual loss in 15–20%). GLP-1 receptor agonists are an emerging option.
  • Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH — low pressure): orthostatic headache (worse standing, better lying) from a CSF leak; MRI shows pachymeningeal enhancement + brain sag. Rx: epidural blood patch. (Opposite positional pattern and opposite treatment from IIH — don't conflate them.)

GCA — don't wait for the biopsy

New headache >50 with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms, or PMR → ESR/CRP + temporal artery exam. If GCA is likely, start high-dose corticosteroids immediately (vision loss is preventable but irreversible) and arrange temporal-artery biopsy / vascular imaging.

Pregnancy & postpartum headache — a broad, dangerous differential

Secondary causes underlie >⅓ of acute headaches referred for neuro consult in pregnancy. Actively consider: pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, CVST, RCVS, PRES, cervical artery dissection, pituitary apoplexy, and post-dural-puncture headache.

  • Pregnancy-specific red flags: third trimester, elevated BP, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes or creatinine.
  • Imaging: MRI preferred (limit gadolinium); non-contrast CT acceptable in emergencies.
  • Activate a maternal stroke team (vascular neurology + maternal-fetal medicine + obstetric anesthesiology) for stroke-like symptoms (2026 AHA/ASA).

docs.title: History & exam essentials
docs.text:
History — cover the core elements: onset & tempo, character, location, severity, duration & frequency, associated symptoms (aura, nausea, photophobia, autonomic), triggers, medications (including acute-med days/month — the MOH screen), and comorbidities (mood, sleep, prior head/neck trauma). Have every patient keep a headache diary (frequency, duration, acute-med days, triggers) for ≥1 month — it's the single most useful diagnostic and monitoring tool.

Exam: vitals (including BP and temperature), fundoscopy for papilledema, cranial nerves, visual fields, focal motor/sensory screen, gait, neck stiffness, and temporal artery palpation in older patients. A normal neuro exam is a large part of what makes a primary headache diagnosis safe.

The headache vertical is complete: Migraine, Cluster & TACs, Trigeminal neuralgia, Medication overuse headache, New daily persistent headache, and Post-traumatic headache.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Do TP, et al. Red and orange flags for secondary headaches (SNNOOP10 list). Neurology. 2019.
  2. Department of Veterans Affairs / DoD. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Headache (2023) — the current DoD/VA guideline (TTH, cervicogenic, MOH, gepants/ditans, neuromodulation).
  3. GBD 2023 Headache Collaborators. Global burden of headache disorders, 1990–2023. Lancet Neurol. 2025 (~2.9 billion affected; 6th leading cause of health loss).
  4. Robbins MS. Diagnosis and Management of Headache: A Review. JAMA. 2021 ("sinus headache" = migraine pitfall).
  5. Screening & imaging: Schwedt TJ, et al. Routine migraine screening — AHS position statement (Headache 2025) and Lipton RB, et al. ID Migraine validation (Neurology 2003); Evans RW, et al. AHS neuroimaging-for-migraine guideline (Headache 2020 — Grade A, no imaging if normal exam/no flags).
  6. Rocha EA, et al. RCVS² score. Neurology. 2019; Singhal AB. RCVS review. Int J Stroke. 2023.
  7. SAH work-up: 2023 AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline; Dubosh NM, et al. 6-h CT sensitivity (Stroke 2016); Perry JJ, et al. Ottawa SAH Rule / 6-h CT rule (Stroke 2020).
  8. CVT: Saposnik G, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis — AHA scientific statement (Stroke 2024; D-dimer sensitivity falls to ~74% in isolated-headache presentations).
  9. COVID: Mitsikostas DD, et al. Headache attributed to SARS-CoV-2 — systematic review (Eur J Neurol 2024); AAPM&R PASC guidance (2023).
  10. Pregnancy: ACOG Headaches in Pregnancy and Postpartum CPG No. 3 (2022); AHA Maternal Stroke scientific statement (2026).

Verified July 2026: the red-flag screen follows the full SNNOOP10 list (Do 2019); the 6-hour non-contrast CT rule for thunderclap/SAH and the Ottawa SAH Rule reflect the 2023 AHA/ASA SAH guidance; TTH and cervicogenic headache are added per the 2023 VA/DoD Headache CPG; RCVS (RCVS² score, no-steroids rule), the IIH-vs-SIH positional distinction, GCA, and the pregnancy/ postpartum differential follow current review/guideline sources; burden figures are from GBD 2023. ID Migraine (≥2/3 → migraine), the AHS Grade-A "don't image stable migraine" rule, the "sinus headache = migraine" pitfall, post-COVID headache, the headache-diary/structured-history recommendation, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and the emerging (not-clinic-ready) GFAP/NfL biomarker note were added from the cited sources. Specific epidemiologic and score figures were drawn from those sources — confirm before quoting in a formal document.

docs.title: Cluster headache & the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: the TACs are severe, strictly unilateral headaches with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (tearing, conjunctival injection, ptosis/miosis, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema). They are separated from one another — and from migraine — mainly by attack duration, frequency, and treatment response. Get these right and the treatment falls out of the diagnosis.

🚩 Red flags — image every new TAC at least once

Despite the classic teaching that self-resolving attacks are benign, a new TAC deserves an MRI brain (with attention to the pituitary and cavernous sinus) to exclude a secondary mimic — pituitary lesions and posterior-fossa pathology can reproduce a TAC phenotype. Image urgently for: fixed Horner's/other cranial-nerve deficit, abnormal exam, side-locked but atypical features, or thunderclap onset.

docs.title: Diagnose by the clock (ICHD-3)
docs.text:
Disorder Attack length Frequency Signature Treatment key Cluster headache 15–180 min 1 every other day → 8/day Agitated/restless; circadian & seasonal bouts O₂ + SC/nasal triptan; verapamil prevention Paroxysmal hemicrania 2–30 min >5/day (>half the time) Female-predominant Absolute response to indomethacin SUNCT / SUNA 1–600 sec ≥1/day, often many Cutaneous triggers (touch, chewing) Lamotrigine; IV lidocaine for crisis Hemicrania continua continuous continuous + exacerbations Background pain with autonomic flares Absolute response to indomethacin

If a strictly unilateral headache with autonomic features responds completely to indomethacin, it is paroxysmal hemicrania or hemicrania continua — a diagnosis you don't want to miss because it is so treatable (the "indomethacin test").

It's under-diagnosed — that's why the clock matters

Mean delay from onset to correct diagnosis is ~5–6 years; cluster is routinely mislabeled as migraine (~25%), tension-type (~19%), or sinusitis (~14%), and women are misdiagnosed more often than men (~61% vs 46%). If a patient describes strictly unilateral, autonomic, clockwork attacks with agitation — call it cluster and treat it, don't recycle a sinusitis diagnosis.

🚩 Screen for depression and suicidality — the "suicide headache"

Cluster carries a markedly elevated suicide risk — attempted suicide ~3.9× the general population (95% CI 2.6–5.8), independent of comorbid depression, and a 2025 cohort confirmed elevated attempted and completed suicide across headache disorders (strongest in ED/inpatient settings). The driver is demoralization during attacks, not classic depression. Ask every cluster patient about mood and suicidal ideation, and treat the headache aggressively — control is the intervention.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Confirm strictly unilateral pain with ipsilateral autonomic features and a normal interictal exam.
  2. Image once (MRI, pituitary views) to exclude a secondary cause.
  3. Time the attacks → place them in the table above.
  4. Cluster: at the same visit, start all three — an abortive (O₂ + SC/nasal triptan), a transitional bridge, and a preventive. Clusters are too disabling to titrate slowly.
  5. Short-lasting + autonomic: run the indomethacin trial before anything else.

docs.title: Cluster headache — the prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm + image once (MRI with pituitary views).
  2. Abortive: high-flow oxygen + sumatriptan 6 mg SC (or nasal triptan) — script both, including a home oxygen setup.
  3. Bridge: a prednisone taper or a greater occipital nerve block to cover the gap until the preventive works.
  4. Preventive: verapamil (with the ECG protocol) — start the same day.
  5. Episodic cluster not controlled on verapamil: add galcanezumab 300 mg SC monthly.
