  15. AR 40-501 para 3-31e; DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.f (gated by 5.26.a).

Verified July 2026: four FDA-approved agents for AQP4-IgG-seropositive NMOSD — eculizumab, inebilizumab, satralizumab, and ravulizumab (approved 2024, CHAMPION-NMOSD) — with the ravulizumab q8-week versus eculizumab q2-week dosing distinction confirmed. Eculizumab biosimilars Bkemv and Epysqli are approved under a skinny label (PNH and aHUS only) and do NOT carry the NMOSD indication — verified against the FDA announcement. The comparative figures are now attributed to their primary source — Bilodeau et al., Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2026;13(2):e200536, a single-centre retrospective cohort of 176 patients, verified directly from the paper — and the composite endpoint is reported alongside the relapse-free-survival headline, because it materially changes the conclusion: only the C5 inhibitors clearly separate from rituximab (91% vs 55%), while inebilizumab (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.24–3.12) and satralizumab (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.16–2.68) were not statistically superior to rituximab on the composite. One discrepancy is flagged for the reader: a frequently cited figure of >70% hypogammaglobulinaemia on long-term rituximab could not be confirmed in this source, which reports 13% of rituximab treatment periods complicated by hypogammaglobulinaemia (and 28% by serious infection); the page uses the figures verified in the paper. The Bayesian network meta-analysis ranking (J Neurol 2025; 8 RCTs, 851 patients; ravulizumab SUCRA 0.99) is indirect comparison and is labelled as such. TANGO is a phase 2, open-label trial (n=118, six Chinese centres) with a 2025 published correction — tocilizumab is presented as off-label. The 2015 international consensus criteria remain current and are explicitly endorsed by the 2026 MENACTRIMS guidelines; no successor criteria had been published as of this review. Complement-inhibitor discontinuation rebound is described from published case reports and series — the risk is real but not universal (other series report uneventful switches), and the page frames it as requiring a planned bridge rather than as an absolute contraindication to switching. GFAP is explicitly labelled not-yet-standard-of-care. The contraindication of interferon-beta, natalizumab, and fingolimod in NMOSD reflects established case-series evidence. Meningococcal vaccination requirements before complement inhibition follow the agents' boxed warnings. Not independently verified: TRICARE tiers and PA criteria for the individual biologics — verify at the TRICARE Formulary Search. Retention standards quoted from AR 40-501 3-31e and DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 5.26.f/5.26.a, verified against source PDFs; note that NMOSD is not named as a distinct entity in either regulation and is captured under the demyelinating-disorder language — cite it that way rather than implying a dedicated paragraph exists.**

docs.title: Myasthenia gravis
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

One-liner: an antibody-mediated disorder of the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction — fatigable, fluctuating weakness that worsens with use and through the day and recovers with rest. Ocular, bulbar, limb, and — the one that kills — respiratory muscles.

Who this is for: the provider seeing fluctuating diplopia/ptosis or dysphagia in clinic, and the one facing a patient in myasthenic crisis in the ED. MG is a real active-duty diagnosis and a named referral condition under AR 40-501 3-31c — but the ocular-only carve-out means the disposition is not automatic.

🚩 Myasthenic crisis — respiratory failure is the emergency

The threat is the diaphragm, and pulse oximetry will reassure you right up until the patient crashes. Hypoxia is a late sign; hypercapnic fatigue comes first.

Assess ventilation directly, not with the pulse ox — the "20/30/40 rule":

Measure Intubation-range value Forced vital capacity (FVC) <20 mL/kg (or <1 L) Negative inspiratory force (NIF/MIP) worse than −30 cmH₂O Maximal expiratory pressure (MEP) <40 cmH₂O

None of these thresholds is prospectively validated, and MG patients can crash before any of them trends down. FVC and NIF together predict better than either alone. Trajectory beats any single number — a patient whose FVC has fallen 30% in six hours is intubated tonight even if tonight's number looks acceptable. A fall in MEP of ≥30% marks high risk. A supine-vs- seated drop in VC flags diaphragm weakness.

  • Single-breath count — after a deep breath in, sitting upright, count out loud at ~2 counts per second. Reaching ~30 correlates with adequate pulmonary function; ≤20 indicates significant inspiratory muscle weakness (~116 mL of VC per count). A 2023 systematic review puts the normal threshold at ≥25. This is a correlate of VC/NIF, not a validated independent intubation trigger — use it to trigger spirometry, and where spirometry is unavailable.
  • A normal PaCO₂ is not reassuring. A rise from the patient's own baseline (30 → 42) means the diaphragm is failing. Do not wait for hypercapnia by lab reference range.
  • Bulbar failure — can't handle secretions, weak cough, nasal voice — is an independent reason to secure the airway.
  • Low-risk / step-down: VC >20 mL/kg, MEP >40 cmH₂O, NIF better than −40 cmH₂O.

BiPAP can buy time early but fails fast in true respiratory-muscle fatigue. Check a blood gas before you commit: PaCO₂ >45 mmHg at BiPAP initiation was the only predictor of BiPAP failure in a 60-episode cohort, and a trial started before hypercapnia developed prevented intubation and shortened ventilation. A 2023 review cites PaCO₂ >50, pneumonia, and older age as NIV-failure predictors; failure rates reach ~38%. Trial BiPAP in the non-hypercapnic patient — hypercapnia already present argues for intubation. Intubate early in patients with high pre-crisis MGFA class, severe dysphagia, or absent protective reflexes. If you are asking whether to intubate, intubate.

Two intubation traps specific to MG

  • The two paralytic classes go in OPPOSITE directions — do not treat them as one rule.
    • Succinylcholine: MG patients are RESISTANT (fewer endplate receptors; ED95 ≈2.6× normal). If you use it, dose UP — 1.5–2 mg/kg — not down. An under-dosed RSI in a patient with no respiratory reserve is the disaster. Pyridostigmine also inhibits plasma cholinesterase, so block may be prolonged and phase-II block more likely on repeat dosing.
    • Non-depolarizing blockers: MG patients are exquisitely SENSITIVE — 10–50% of the normal dose, titrated to twitch monitoring.
    • Preferred where available: rocuronium 0.6 mg/kg with sugammadex immediately at hand. Tell anesthesia the patient has MG before induction, every time.
  • Do not give IV magnesium to a crashing MG patient (e.g. for a coincident indication) — it blocks neuromuscular transmission and can precipitate or deepen crisis. See the pregnancy/eclampsia caveat in the drug list below.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Recognize the pattern — fatigable, fluctuating, fatigues with use, worse later in the day, spares sensation and reflexes.
  2. If the patient is in or near crisis, stop working down this list. Protect the airway, then go straight to myasthenic crisis. Rapid immunotherapy is started on clinical grounds — do not wait for serology, electrodiagnostics, or chest imaging. Send the serology on the way past; it will not be back for days and it does not change tonight's management.
  3. Send serology — AChR, then MuSK if negative (see below).
  4. Confirm with the pattern + serology; use EDx (RNS, SFEMG) when serology is negative.
  5. Image the mediastinum (CT/MRI chest) — every MG patient needs a thymoma screen.
  6. Treat — symptomatic (pyridostigmine) + immunotherapy; crisis gets IVIG or PLEX.
  7. Screen for precipitants — infection, and the long list of drugs that worsen MG.
  8. Start the military disposition — profile, and the ocular-vs-generalized determination.

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text: The clinical signature is fatigability. Sustained upgaze reproduces ptosis; repeated abduction fatigues an eye; proximal limbs weaken on repetition. Ptosis and diplopia are the commonest presenting features. Sensation, reflexes, and pupils are normal — a fixed pupil or sensory loss argues against MG and for a mimic.

docs.title: Serology — send in this order
docs.text:
Antibody Frequency Notes AChR (acetylcholine receptor) ~85% of generalized MG First test. Highly specific. Titre does not track severity MuSK (muscle-specific kinase) ~5–8% Send if AChR-negative. Distinct phenotype — prominent bulbar/facial/neck/respiratory weakness, and different treatment (see below) LRP4 ~1–3% Send in double-seronegative patients Seronegative remainder Especially ocular-only MG. A negative panel does not exclude MG — lean on EDx, and see the caveat below before calling anyone seronegative

\"Seronegative\" is often an assay limitation, not an absence of antibody

A standard radioimmunoassay misses antibodies that a clustered-AChR cell-based assay (CBA) detects — and those patients respond to antibody-directed therapy like anyone else. Send a clustered-AChR CBA before you label a patient triple-seronegative, because that label changes both the treatment route and, downstream, what a payer will approve.

When serology is negative — electrodiagnostics

  • Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) — a decremental response: "a 10% decrement in amplitude from the first to fourth or fifth intravolley waveform while stimulating at 2–5 Hz" (3 Hz is the usual standard). Hold anticholinesterases ≥12 h and keep the limb warm — cooling masks decrement. The preferred initial electrodiagnostic test, but abnormal in only ~17% of ocular MG vs ~85% of generalized MG.
  • Single-fiber EMG (SFEMG) — increased jitter or impulse blocking. The most sensitive test for MG — ~92% overall, 95–99% in generalized disease with an appropriate muscle, but only ~79% in purely ocular MG — and less specific and operator-dependent. Sensitivity rises with severity and with muscle selection (orbicularis oculi/frontalis for ocular disease). A normal SFEMG in a well-chosen muscle argues strongly against MG only in generalized disease.
  • The ice-pack test (ptosis improves ≥2 mm after 2 min of ice) is a useful, cheap bedside adjunct for ptosis — not a substitute for confirmation.

Every MG patient needs a chest CT/MRI

10–15% of MG patients have a thymoma, and its presence changes management independently of the MG — a thymoma is a surgical indication regardless of MG severity or serostatus. Conversely, thymoma essentially never accompanies MuSK disease. Image the mediastinum in everyone at diagnosis.

docs.title: Ocular vs generalized — the distinction that drives everything
docs.text:
• Ocular MG — weakness confined to lids and extraocular muscles. Often seronegative.
  • How many generalize depends on whether they were treated — quote the right number for the question you are answering:
    • 50–80% in older long-term studies of largely untreated patients.
    • ~28% in contemporary treated cohorts (mean 87-month follow-up; mean time to generalization 24 months).
    • ~39% pooled across 31 studies (95% CI 32–47%), which blends both. Generalization is concentrated in the first 1–2 years; after 2 years of purely ocular disease the risk falls substantially. Risk factors — later onset age, female sex, symptom severity, abnormal RNS, AChR positivity, thymic hyperplasia — are inconsistently replicated.
  • This split is the hinge of both treatment intensity and the military disposition — the regulations disqualify generalized MG but retain disease confined to the extraocular muscles.

docs.title: Stage it — MGFA classification and the treatment target
docs.text:
The trials this page cites are written in this language, so the page uses it too.

Class Definition I Any ocular muscle weakness; may have weakness of eye closure. Strength elsewhere normal II Mild generalized weakness III Moderate generalized weakness IV Severe generalized weakness V Intubation, or NIV to avoid intubation

Subclass a = limb/axial predominant; b = oropharyngeal/respiratory predominant. MGTX enrolled Class II–IV.

  • Treatment goal (MGFA consensus): post-intervention status of minimal manifestation (MM) or better — "no symptoms or functional limitations from MG but some weakness on examination of some muscles" — with no more than grade 1 medication side effects. Aim at this explicitly; it is the endpoint the trials report.
  • Refractory MG (the gate to biologics, and it has a definition): "unchanged or worse after corticosteroids and at least 2 other immunosuppressant agents, used in adequate doses for an adequate duration, with persistent symptoms or side effects that limit functioning." Refer refractory patients to a clinician or centre with MG expertise.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Is the airway safe? Bulbar or respiratory weakness → assess ventilation directly, admit, treat as crisis. Nothing below matters until this is answered. If the answer is no, jump to crisis and start rapid immunotherapy on clinical grounds — steps 2 and 3 do not gate treatment.
  2. Confirm the diagnosis — pattern + serology, EDx if seronegative. Send a clustered-AChR CBA before accepting a seronegative label.
  3. Screen the mediastinum — chest CT/MRI for thymoma.
  4. Start symptomatic control — pyridostigmine (less useful in MuSK disease). If a tolerated dose in the 300–480 mg/day range leaves the patient symptomatic, they are inadequately controlled, not under-dosed — move to immunotherapy rather than pushing higher.
  5. Start immunotherapy — most generalized patients need it; steroids + a steroid-sparing agent. Measure respiratory function before the first steroid dose (see the early-worsening box).
  6. Discuss thymectomy — a separate oncologic indication for any thymoma; for non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG clinicians should discuss it (AAN Level B), with the best randomized evidence in ages 18–50. Not for MuSK or LRP4 disease.
  7. Escalate to targeted biologics when refractory (defined above) or steroid-dependent — FcRn, complement, or anti-CD19. Serostatus decides which are available to you.
  8. Hand the patient a precipitant-drug list and address the military disposition.

docs.title: Myasthenic crisis — acute management
docs.text:
Step 1 — airway and monitoring

  • Admit to an ICU/step-down anyone with a crisis or impending crisis. Manifest crisis warrants ICU or step-down; impending crisis warrants admission somewhere with ICU capability.
  • Serial FVC, NIF and single-breath count — every few hours; trend beats snapshot.
  • Intubate on the 20/30/40 thresholds above, on bulbar failure with secretions, on visible accessory-muscle fatigue, or on a falling trend regardless of absolute number. Do not wait for hypoxia.
  • Hold pyridostigmine in intubated crisis patients — the marginal benefit is outweighed by secretions and mucus plugging, and it confounds assessment of the response to PLEX/IVIG. Restart it before weaning.
  • Do not use IV pyridostigmine (1–2 mg/h; 1 mg IV ≈ 30 mg PO) — discouraged because of fatal arrhythmia risk.
  • Find and treat the precipitant — infection is the commonest; also review every new drug (see the avoid list). Do not withhold antibiotics from a septic MG patient — see the alternatives in that box.

Before you increase pyridostigmine in a weakening patient, ask whether the drug is the cause

Cholinergic crisis is now exceedingly rare — and the modern position is that you no longer differentiate it by giving edrophonium or neostigmine. But excess cholinesterase inhibitor cannot be fully excluded as a cause of worsening, and these drugs increase airway secretions either way. So it is a consideration to rule through, not a coin-flip.

What points to cholinergic toxicity:

  • Muscarinic excess — hypersalivation, bronchorrhea, lacrimation, diaphoresis, miosis, bradycardia, abdominal cramps, diarrhea — plus fasciculations and cramps (nicotinic).
  • Timing. Weakness peaking 30–60 minutes after a dose rather than at trough. This and the response to a pyridostigmine holiday are the most usable discriminators now.
  • Dose. Suspicion rises above ~450 mg/day, where depolarizing block itself causes weakness — and at lower doses in renal impairment, since pyridostigmine is renally cleared. Note that cholinergic overdose is often but not always accompanied by muscarinic signs.

What points to myasthenic crisis: fatigable weakness worsening with repetitive effort, normal reflexes, normal sensation, and absence of autonomic/cholinergic features.

Anticholinergic cover hides exactly the warning signs you need

Glycopyrrolate and hyoscyamine suppress the muscarinic signs without touching the nicotinic component (weakness, fasciculations, cramps). The pyridostigmine label states that using atropine to blunt muscarinic side effects, by masking the signs of overdosage, can lead to inadvertent induction of cholinergic crisis. A patient on scheduled glycopyrrolate can be walked into depolarizing block with a dry mouth.

When it is unclear, holding pyridostigmine is the safe move — it is symptomatic only, and nothing is lost by stopping it while you secure the airway.

No ICU, no spirometer, no IVIG — the far-forward version

Everything above assumes a hospital. If you are in an aid station, afloat, or forward:

  • Single-breath count is your FVC. Count it hourly and write down every value — the trend is the whole signal.
  • Request urgent MEDEVAC the moment the count is ≤20, the patient cannot manage secretions, or the count has fallen at all between checks. Do not wait for a number, and do not wait for daylight.
  • Intubate before transport, not during. A patient who is marginal on the ground is unmanageable in an aircraft or a small boat.
  • State the destination requirement in the evacuation request: the receiving facility needs a ventilator AND access to IVIG or plasma exchange.
  • While waiting: sit them upright, suction, NPO, stop every drug on the avoid list, treat the precipitating infection with a non-avoid-list agent, hold pyridostigmine if there are any muscarinic signs, and do not start high-dose steroids in an unmonitored setting.

Step 2 — rapid immunotherapy: PLEX preferred in crisis, IVIG if PLEX is unavailable

~70% of patients with severe weakness improve with either. But read that number carefully: the randomized equivalence data come from exacerbation, not intubated crisis (Gajdos 1997, n=87, no difference at day 15; Barth 2011, n=84 with QMG >10.5, 69% IVIG vs 65% PLEX). In crisis specifically, the non-randomized evidence favours PLEX — superior severity at 7 days, ventilation status at 2 weeks and 1-month function (Qureshi, n=54); earlier improvement and shorter ICU stay (Wang, n=40); and in a 250-case multicentre cohort, first-line PLEX/immunoadsorption meant significantly less need for invasive ventilation. A 2025 Cochrane review found IVIg may be less beneficial than PLEX with possibly longer hospitalization (very low certainty).

  • Plasma exchange — 5 sessions over 7–10 days, 1.0–1.5 plasma volumes (40–60 mL/kg) each. First-line in crisis absent a contraindication, and particularly effective in MuSK disease. Daily vs alternate-day showed no efficacy difference. Improvement is usually evident by the 2nd–3rd session. Unusable in sepsis; carries haemodynamic and access risk.
  • IVIG 2 g/kg total, divided over 2–5 days. Easier logistically, no vascular access issue. Improvement usually by the 4th–5th day; effect lasts ~4–8 weeks. Off-label — no immune globulin product carries an FDA myasthenia indication. Contraindicated in hypercoagulable states, renal failure, and IgG hypersensitivity.
  • Start or intensify chronic immunotherapy in parallel — IVIG/PLEX is a bridge, not a maintenance plan. Steroids are usually begun or increased now (watch the early-worsening window, below).

IVIG boxed warning — thrombosis and acute renal failure

  • Thrombosis can occur without known risk factors. Risk is higher with estrogen-containing contraception, prolonged immobilization, indwelling central lines, hypercoagulable states, hyperviscosity, and advanced age — several of which describe the hospitalized crisis patient.
  • Renal dysfunction and acute renal failure, more so with sucrose-containing products.
  • Check baseline renal function, ensure adequate hydration, and use the lowest practicable dose and infusion rate in at-risk patients. Watch for aseptic meningitis and haemolysis.

If a patient on a C5 inhibitor gets PLEX or IVIG, you owe them a supplemental dose

This page's own crisis pathway creates exactly this sequence. PLEX, plasmapheresis and IVIG strip circulating drug and abolish complement blockade. Both labels require make-up dosing:

  • Eculizumab — after each PLEX/plasmapheresis session: 300 mg if the last dose was 300 mg, 600 mg if the last dose was ≥600 mg, given within 60 minutes after the session. With scheduled IVIG cycles: 300–600 mg supplemental depending on last dose and IVIG frequency (no supplement for one-off acute rescue IVIG).
  • Ravulizumab — after each PLEX/plasmapheresis: 1,200–1,500 mg by weight band; after completion of an IVIG cycle: 600–1,800 mg by weight band and last dose — both within 4 hours.

Steroid early-worsening in crisis

High-dose corticosteroids cause transient worsening in up to 50% of patients, on average about 5 days after initiation and lasting 1–7 days (occasionally up to 3 weeks) — a real hazard in a patient already near respiratory failure. In severe disease, give PLEX or IVIG first and wait several days for benefit before starting corticosteroids. If worsening does occur in a monitored setting, generally maintain the dose until the patient improves rather than withdrawing it. The full prescribing rules are in Chronic treatment — read them before you write the first dose.

docs.title: Symptomatic
docs.text:
Pyridostigmine — symptom control, not disease modification

  • Pyridostigmine 30–60 mg PO every 4–6 h, titrated to symptoms. Practical ceiling ~360–480 mg/day.
    • The FDA label describes an average dose of 600 mg/day and severe cases up to 1,500 mg/day — that reflects pre-immunotherapy-era practice and is not a modern target. The operative threshold is >450 mg/day, above which depolarizing block itself causes weakness. Lower still in renal impairment** — pyridostigmine is excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney.
  • Extended-release 180 mg at bedtime for overnight and on-waking weakness.
  • Still symptomatic on a tolerated dose in the 300–480 mg/day range? That patient is inadequately controlled, not under-titrated — escalate to immunotherapy, do not push the dose higher. Cholinesterase inhibitors rarely give complete or sustained relief and do not modify disease; immunosuppression is indicated whenever symptomatic treatment alone fails to give a fully satisfactory functional result.
  • Muscarinic side effects — cramping, diarrhea, secretions — are often covered with glycopyrrolate 1 mg PO TID (max 8 mg/day) or hyoscyamine. Both labels list myasthenia gravis as a contraindication; this is accepted off-label practice, so use the lowest effective dose, document the rationale — and read the cholinergic-crisis box above, because this cover masks the warning signs of overdose.
  • Less effective, and often poorly tolerated, in MuSK disease — do not lean on it there.
  • Now supported by Class I evidence. The first placebo-controlled randomized trial (IMPACT-MG, 2026) confirmed benefit across MGII, QMG and MG-ADL. The same trial found that adding amifampridine on top of pyridostigmine did not help and caused more adverse events — the LEMS drug does not transfer to MG.

docs.title: Immunotherapy tiers
docs.text:
First-line immunotherapyRefractory / steroid-dependent — targeted biologics

Measure respiratory function before the first prednisone dose

Steroid-induced worsening hits up to 50% of patients, on average ~5 days after initiation, lasting 1–7 days — and is predicted by bulbar symptoms, older age, and generalized disease.

  • Before the first dose: single-breath count and FVC.
  • Do not start high-dose prednisone as an outpatient in anyone with bulbar or respiratory weakness — those patients are started inpatient, or covered with PLEX/IVIG first, or both. Pulse high-dose methylprednisolone should only rarely be used in MG.
  • Give explicit return precautions: "if your swallowing, speech or breathing gets worse in the next two weeks, come back the same day — do not wait for your follow-up."
  • If worsening occurs in a monitored setting, maintain the dose until improvement rather than withdrawing it.
  • Corticosteroids (prednisone) — the workhorse. Pick a regimen and write it down:
    • Start-low-go-slow (outpatient default, lowest worsening risk): 10–20 mg daily, increased by 5–10 mg every 5–7 days to a target of ~0.75–1 mg/kg/day (typically 40–60 mg daily) or until control. The MGTX protocol used 10 mg on alternate days, increased in 10 mg increments to a maximum of 100 mg alternate-day or 1.5 mg/kg, whichever is lower.
    • Initiate-and-maintain: 20 mg/day, effective in the mycophenolate trials, with early addition of a steroid-sparing agent.
    • High-dose induction (0.75–1.0 mg/kg/day, or 60 mg/day) achieves pharmacological remission in ~28% and marked improvement in a further 53% — but carries the worsening risk, so not outpatient in bulbar or respiratory disease.
    • Then: hold ~1–3 months and taper slowly to the lowest effective dose or alternate-day dosing. Avoid alternate-day dosing in diabetes (glucose swings).
    • Monitor: glucose/HbA1c, BP, weight, K⁺, bone density with vitamin D and calcium, cataract and IOP screening on prolonged use. Contraindicated in systemic fungal infection. Do not stop abruptly after prolonged use — adrenal suppression.
    • Labelled systemic range is 5–60 mg/day; the MG titration schedules above are consensus practice, not label.
    • Azathioprine — best-established. Start 50 mg PO daily (~1 mg/kg/day); after 6–8 weeks increase by 0.5 mg/kg/day at 4-week intervals to a maximum of 2.5 mg/kg/day. Onset is slow — allow a 12-week minimum trial before calling it a failure. Boxed warning: malignancy.
      • Check TPMT and NUDT15 before starting — the current label covers both. Homozygous deficiency of either → use a different agent; heterozygous → reduce the dose; heterozygous for both → reduce further.
      • CBC with platelets weekly × 1 month, twice monthly for months 2–3, then monthly. Add LFTs periodically. Delayed marrow suppression occurs.
      • Allopurinol → reduce azathioprine to one-third to one-quarter of the usual dose. Febuxostat is not recommended. Lower doses in renal impairment.

    • Mycophenolate mofetil — 1,000 mg PO BID typical in MG (off-label); onset over months. Monitor CBC; reduce or interrupt for neutropenia.

      Mycophenolate — boxed warning: embryofetal toxicity. Read before prescribing to any woman of childbearing potential.

      • First-trimester pregnancy loss and multiple congenital malformations. Consider azathioprine instead in anyone who may become pregnant. There is a REMS and a pregnancy registry.
      • Two pregnancy tests (sensitivity ≥25 mIU/mL): immediately before the first dose and again 8–10 days later; repeat at routine follow-up.
      • Contraception from 4 weeks before, throughout, and for 6 weeks after the last dose. Mycophenolate lowers oral-contraceptive efficacy — a barrier method must be added. A woman on a COC alone is not protected.
      • Also boxed: malignancy (lymphoma, skin) and serious infection, including HBV/HCV reactivation.

    Steroid-sparing oral agents — started early to get patients off steroids:

    • Others in selected patients, all off-label in MG:
      • Methotrexate — 7.5–20 mg PO or SC ONCE WEEKLY (never daily) + folic acid 1 mg daily. Monitor CBC, LFTs, creatinine. Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy for non-neoplastic disease (boxed warning); effective contraception in both sexes. Daily-instead-of-weekly dosing errors have killed patients — write the day of the week on the prescription.
      • Tacrolimus — 3–5 mg PO daily, trough-guided (~5–10 ng/mL); monitor levels, K⁺, creatinine, glucose, BP, QTc. Boxed: malignancy and serious infection.
      • Cyclosporine — 3–5 mg/kg/day PO divided BID, trough-guided; monitor creatinine and BP. Boxed: malignancy, serious infection, hypertension, nephrotoxicity.

The class that reorganized MG care. Reserve for inadequate control on, or intolerance of, conventional immunotherapy — and note the serostatus restrictions, which are the practical decision driver.

No class has beaten another head-to-head

A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis (27 randomized trials, n=2,318) found FcRn inhibitors, C5 inhibitors and CD19 depletion statistically indistinguishable on QMG and MG-ADL; a German real-world propensity-matched comparison of C5 vs efgartigimod (n=153) found the same, with insufficient response in 20–49% of patients in both arms. Choose on serostatus, route, dosing architecture and cost — not on presumed potency. Two practical differentiators: cyclical FcRn dosing requires symptom worsening to trigger the next cycle, which creates timing uncertainty, whereas nipocalimab and the complement agents run on fixed schedules; and B-cell depletion accrues effect over time — MINT's AChR-positive benefit widened between week 26 and week 52.

Age floors differ by agent: eculizumab ≥6 y, nipocalimab ≥12 y; ravulizumab, zilucoplan, rozanolixizumab, efgartigimod and inebilizumab are adults only.

FcRn inhibitors (lower total IgG, including pathogenic antibody):

  • Efgartigimod (Vyvgart IV; Vyvgart Hytrulo SC with hyaluronidase) — the serostatus gate is gone: FDA broadened the gMG indication to ALL adult serotypes on 8 May 2026 (AChR+, MuSK+, LRP4+ and triple-seronegative), on the ADAPT SERON trial. It is the only approved agent with no serostatus restriction, and the only approved option for the seronegative patient. Hytrulo also carries a CIDP indication.
    • IV: 10 mg/kg over 1 h once weekly × 4 (a "cycle"); cap at 1,200 mg/dose if ≥120 kg.
    • SC (Hytrulo): 1,000 mg/10,000 U prefilled syringe over 20–30 s once weekly × 4.
    • Subsequent cycles on clinical evaluation.
  • Rozanolixizumab (Rystiggo, SC) — AChR+ or MuSK+. SC infusion once weekly × 6, weight-banded: <50 kg 420 mg; 50–<100 kg 560 mg; ≥100 kg 840 mg. Do not start the next cycle sooner than 63 days from the start of the previous one. Watch for aseptic meningitis — labelled and serious; headache, fever and meningism on treatment warrant workup, not reassurance. Angioedema and rash are also labelled.
  • Nipocalimab (Imaavy) — FDA-approved 29 Apr 2025, AChR+ or MuSK+, adults and adolescents ≥12. 30 mg/kg IV over ≥30 min once, then 15 mg/kg IV over ≥15 min two weeks later and every 2 weeks thereafter. IV only — no SC formulation is approved.
  • Not prescribable, and worth knowing why: batoclimab's phase 3 was positive, but the sponsor is not filing for approval in MG — development moved to the next-generation FcRn blocker IMVT-1402. Do not expect a batoclimab label.
  • All FcRn agents: evaluate and update age-appropriate vaccines before each new cycle; live vaccines are not recommended during treatment, and non-live vaccine responses are blunted — time them to the end of a cycle.

Complement C5 inhibitors (block terminal complement — AChR+ only, since complement damage at the endplate is the AChR mechanism; ineffective in MuSK disease):

  • Eculizumab (Soliris) — 900 mg IV weekly × 4, then 1,200 mg IV at week 5, then 1,200 mg IV every 2 weeks. Do not start at q2wk — that skips the entire induction month. Now also approved in children ≥6 (AChR+, Feb 2025) — the only MG biologic approved in children. Biosimilars are marketed and carry the same gMG indication (BKEMV, interchangeable; EPYSQLI) — expect step-therapy through one.
  • Ravulizumab (Ultomiris) — weight-based load, then q8wk maintenance starting 2 weeks after the load (gMG, ≥40 kg): 40–<60 kg 2,400 → 3,000 mg; 60–<100 kg 2,700 → 3,300 mg; ≥100 kg 3,000 → 3,600 mg.
  • Zilucoplan (Zilbrysq) — SC once daily, weight-banded: <56 kg 16.6 mg; 56–<77 kg 23 mg; ≥77 kg 32.4 mg, self-injected after training. Obtain baseline amylase and lipase before starting — pancreatitis and pancreatic cysts are labelled; stop for suspected pancreatitis.
  • The prescriber must enrol in a REMS for all three. This gates access — start it before the patient needs the drug.

C5 inhibitors — boxed warning: life-threatening and fatal meningococcal infection

  • Vaccinate against serogroups A, C, W, Y and B — that is two separate vaccines (MenACWY + MenB) — ≥2 weeks before the first dose, per current ACIP schedules for complement-inhibitor recipients, which differ from the package insert. MenACWY alone leaves the patient exposed to the serogroup that classically kills them.
  • If therapy is urgent and the patient is not up to date, do not delay two weeks. The labels are explicit: give antibacterial prophylaxis and vaccinate as soon as possible. The risk of delaying therapy can outweigh the infection risk.
  • Vaccination does not eliminate the risk — breakthrough meningococcal disease occurs in vaccinated patients. Counsel on symptoms and evaluate immediately if suspected.
  • Same rules as in NMOSD.

B-cell depletion:

  • Inebilizumab (Uplizna) — anti-CD19. FDA-approved for gMG 11 Dec 2025 (AChR+ or MuSK+, MINT trial); its third indication after NMOSD and IgG4-RD. 300 mg IV, repeat 300 mg IV at 2 weeks, then 300 mg IV every 6 months (infuse over ~90 min; observe ≥1 h after). Note the MuSK-positive QMG difference in MINT was not statistically significant.
    • Before the first dose: HBsAg/anti-HBc, quantitative serum IgG, and TB screening — active hepatitis B and active or untreated latent TB are contraindications.
    • Premedicate every infusion — IV methylprednisolone 80–125 mg + PO diphenhydramine 25–50 mg + PO acetaminophen 500–650 mg.
    • Live vaccines ≥4 weeks before starting, and none afterwards until B-cell repletion. Contraception during and for 6 months after the last dose.
  • Rituximab (anti-CD20) — off-label; no FDA myasthenia indication exists. State the regimen you mean: commonly 375 mg/m² IV weekly × 4, or 1 g IV × 2 doses two weeks apart. Screen HBsAg and anti-HBc before the first dose (boxed warning); the IV product also carries a boxed warning for fatal infusion-related reactions.
    • Particularly effective in MuSK disease, where consensus supports it as an early option rather than a last resort. In AChR-positive generalized MG the consensus position is weaker — an option after failure or intolerance of other agents — but randomized evidence now also supports early rituximab within 1 year of generalized onset, a position the 2025 ABN guidelines have adopted.

docs.title: Serostatus is the practical routing tool
docs.text: Situation Favoured approach AChR+ generalized Pyridostigmine + steroids/steroid-sparing; discuss thymectomy if non-thymomatous; escalate to FcRn, complement, or inebilizumab — the only group with all three classes available MuSK+ Pyridostigmine often poorly tolerated; rituximab early; FcRn (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab) or inebilizumab; complement inhibitors do not work; thymectomy does not help Seronegative generalized Send a clustered-AChR CBA first — most "seronegative" patients are assay-negative, not antibody-negative. If truly triple-seronegative: pyridostigmine + steroids/steroid-sparing (not serostatus-restricted), then efgartigimod — the only FDA-approved biologic for this group (all-serotype label, May 2026). Complement inhibitors, rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab and inebilizumab all remain serostatus-restricted. IVIG/PLEX and off-label rituximab are the fallbacks. Efficacy data in true triple-seronegative disease are small and largely uncontrolled — say so to the patient. Any thymoma Surgical resection regardless of severity or serostatus — but see the exceptions and the timing rule below Ocular-only Pyridostigmine first; add corticosteroids (~15 mg/day is often enough) if symptoms are functionally limiting or troublesome — this is a positive recommendation, not a coin-flip. Whether it prevents generalization is supported by consistent observational data awaiting randomized confirmation Crisis / refractory PLEX first-line in crisis (IVIG if PLEX unavailable); escalate chronic therapy in parallel

docs.title: Thymectomy
docs.text:
Thymoma present → surgical resection, as oncologic surgery: "with rare exceptions, all patients with MG with thymoma should undergo surgery to remove the tumor." Two caveats the word "always" hides:

  • Resection is done to remove the tumour and may not improve the MG. All thymic tissue is removed with it. Incompletely resected thymoma is managed with post-operative radiotherapy/chemotherapy.
  • Exceptions exist: in elderly or multimorbid patients palliative radiotherapy can be considered, and small thymomas may be followed unless enlarging or symptomatic.
  • Timing — thymectomy is elective. It "should be performed when the patient is stable and deemed safe to undergo a procedure where postoperative pain and mechanical factors can limit respiratory function." Do not operate on an unstable myasthenic.

No thymoma → discuss thymectomy in AChR-positive generalized MG. The AAN puts this at Level B — clinicians should discuss it, not "do it." MGTX randomized thymectomy plus prednisone against prednisone alone and found it superior — better time-weighted QMG, lower steroid requirement, less azathioprine and IVIG use, fewer hospitalizations for exacerbation — sustained through 5 years, with an absolute increase in the chance of reaching minimal manifestation status at 36 months of 20% (95% CI 1.6–37%).

  • Age — the number that is usually quoted wrong. MGTX enrolled patients under 65 with disease duration <5 years, but in post hoc analysis neither prednisone dose nor QMG differed between arms in patients ≥50. So: best randomized evidence is ages 18–50, and several consensus documents restrict the recommendation there.
    • Above 50, the randomized evidence does not demonstrate benefit — but observational data do. A multicentre propensity-matched study in late-onset AChR-positive non-thymomatous MG found thymectomy conferred a 2.36-fold higher chance of remission or minimal manifestation status (48.9% vs 23.8% at 24 months; 59.5% vs 28.9% at 36 months), with adverse-event rates comparable to younger patients. A second cohort found HR 3.25 (95% CI 1.31–8.1). Both call for a randomized trial. Some experts consider thymectomy in the 50–65 group especially when thymic hyperplasia is present or biomarkers resemble early-onset disease.
  • Surgical route — counsel the uncertainty, don't resolve it. MGTX used extended transsternal thymectomy. The AAN (Level B) directs clinicians to counsel patients that it is uncertain whether the benefit of extended transsternal thymectomy is also attained by minimally invasive approaches. This is contested — some authorities hold that video- and robot-assisted methods give the same benefit provided all thymic tissue including mediastinal fat is removed. Present both positions.
  • MuSK, LRP4, and agrin antibodies — "current evidence does not support an indication for thymectomy."
  • Purely ocular disease — not routine, and the data are limited, retrospective and largely negative (47 thymectomized ocular patients vs 67 who declined: no difference in stable remission at 100–116 months; another series, remission in 2 of 11). The consensus carve-out is narrow: AChR-positive ocular MG patients who fail anticholinesterases and who prefer not to take, cannot take, or are refractory to immunosuppression may be offered thymectomy.
  • Seronegative generalized MG — thymectomy "may be considered" if immunosuppression fails or is not tolerated.

docs.title: Prescribing for a patient with MG — read before you write
docs.text:
The precipitant list — written for the covering provider, not just the neurologist

Give every patient a copy. But this box is aimed at you — the ED doc reaching for cipro, the anesthesiologist, the OB starting magnesium — who may not know this patient has MG.

Avoid — highest priority:

  • Fluoroquinolones (cipro/levo/moxi/ofloxacin) — FDA boxed warning in MG. Guidance grades them "use cautiously, if at all" — in practice, avoid if any alternative exists.
  • D-penicillamine — causes an MG-like syndrome. Avoid.
  • Botulinum toxin — presynaptic NMJ blocker. Avoid.
  • IV magnesium — treat as contraindicated. See the pregnancy box below.
  • Telithromycin — caused severe, often fatal worsening and was contraindicated; withdrawn from the US market since 2016. Listed for completeness only.

Use only if unavoidable, and watch closely:

  • Aminoglycosides, macrolides (azithro/clarithro/erythromycin), clindamycin, colistin/polymyxins, lincomycin.
  • Beta-blockers, procainamide, quinine/quinidine.
  • Statins — can worsen or unmask MG.
  • Hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine.
  • Live-attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella-zoster, intranasal influenza, oral polio, rotavirus, oral typhoid, smallpox, yellow fever) — these do not affect MG itself but are contraindicated on immunosuppressive treatment. Give age-appropriate vaccines before starting an FcRn blocker, complement inhibitor, or inebilizumab — not after.
  • Iodinated radiologic contrast (older reports; modern agents appear safer) and desferrioxamine.

What to give instead — and the mirror error to avoid:

Reasonable antibiotic alternatives: penicillins and cephalosporins, doxycycline, vancomycin, metronidazole, TMP-SMX. But do not let this list stop you treating a serious infection — untreated sepsis is the commonest cause of myasthenic crisis and a bigger threat than any drug here. If no alternative exists, give the drug, tell the patient and the team why, and monitor single-breath count and FVC every 4 hours for 48 hours with an airway plan in place.

Contraindications on the labels of the drugs this page recommends:

  • Pyridostigmine — mechanical intestinal or urinary obstruction; caution in bronchial asthma.
  • Eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan — do not initiate in unresolved serious meningococcal infection.
  • Inebilizumab — active hepatitis B; active or untreated latent TB.
  • Methotrexate — pregnancy (absolute, for non-neoplastic disease).
  • Prednisone — systemic fungal infection.
  • Glycopyrrolate / hyoscyamine — labelled contraindicated in myasthenia gravis itself.

Checkpoint-inhibitor myasthenia is a different disease — and the patient dies of the heart

Not a cautionary drug interaction. A distinct, fulminant entity that a covering provider meets in an oncology patient with no MG history.

  • Median onset ~3 weeks after the first dose (usually within 6 weeks).
  • It overlaps with myocarditis and myositis — the "triple-M" syndrome — in a large minority, with in-hospital mortality around 38%.
  • In any patient on pembrolizumab, nivolumab or ipilimumab with new ptosis, diplopia, bulbar or proximal weakness: send troponin, CK and an ECG, and put them on a monitor.
  • AChR antibody is often negative or low-titre — a negative panel does not exclude it.
  • Stop the ICI and start high-dose corticosteroids on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation; add IVIG/PLEX for bulbar or respiratory involvement. Escalate to cardiology and oncology the same night.

IV magnesium, eclampsia, and pregnancy

Treat IV magnesium as contraindicated in MG — it blocks neuromuscular transmission and can precipitate or deepen crisis. The situation where a provider feels forced to give it is eclampsia or pre-eclampsia prophylaxis.

  • Discuss alternative seizure prophylaxis (e.g. levetiracetam) with OB and neurology before giving magnesium.
  • If magnesium is judged unavoidable, give it only with an airway plan, continuous respiratory monitoring, IV calcium gluconate immediately available, and reduced dosing with serial magnesium levels.
  • Oral magnesium-containing antacids and laxatives are also best avoided.
  • Pregnancy and the first postpartum months are a high-risk exacerbation window. MG in pregnancy is a co-managed, hospital-delivery, no-surprises situation — and remember that mycophenolate and methotrexate are contraindicated, so review the regimen before conception.

TRICARE — MG prescribing

Pyridostigmine, prednisone, azathioprine, and mycophenolate are generic/formulary. The targeted biologics (all FcRn inhibitors, all complement inhibitors, inebilizumab) are high-cost specialty drugs, PA-gated. Expect a specialist-prescriber or neurologist-consultation requirement and documentation of serostatus and failed conventional therapy.

  • Start with the generics and document them. Pyridostigmine, prednisone, and azathioprine or mycophenolate are the conventional trials every biologic PA will ask you to have failed — record drug, dose, and duration for each from the first visit, not retrospectively.
  • Serostatus drives coverage as well as efficacy. Complement C5 inhibitors are FDA-labeled for AChR-antibody-positive gMG only, and payer criteria generally track the label — expect an AChR+ requirement on any complement request and route the MuSK patient accordingly. Efgartigimod is now the exception: its all-serotype label (May 2026) removes the serostatus argument entirely, which matters most for MuSK and seronegative patients. Published criteria for this class typically also require MGFA class II–IV and failure of or contraindication to ≥2 conventional therapies, and bar concurrent use of two gMG biologics.
  • Rituximab is off-label in MG — argue it as off-label, not as formulary. TRICARE evaluates off-label use on medical necessity plus support from medical literature and national organizations, not on formulary tier. For MuSK disease that argument is available: cite the 2020 International Consensus Guidance, the MuSK-specific response data, and the mechanistic reason complement inhibitors are unavailable.
  • Benefit split decides where the drug is given and who bills. Infused agents (eculizumab, ravulizumab, inebilizumab, IV nipocalimab, IV efgartigimod) typically run through the medical benefit; self-administered SC agents (zilucoplan, SC efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) through specialty pharmacy, which sets the copay tier.
  • Eculizumab is a biosimilar market now (BKEMV, interchangeable; EPYSQLI) — both carry the adult AChR+ gMG indication and cost substantially less, so expect step-therapy through one. The meningococcal boxed warning and REMS apply identically to all three.
  • IVIG — split the two settings. Inpatient crisis IVIG runs under the inpatient benefit; do not delay it for an authorization. Outpatient maintenance or bridging IVIG is a medical-benefit authorization — open it the day you decide the patient will need it, because the lag is unprotected time.
  • Verify every agent and its criteria at the TRICARE Formulary Search before counseling — the DoD P&T Committee revises tiers and PA criteria without notice. The specifics above are the general payer pattern; TRICARE-specific criteria were not independently verified for this page.

Military medicine — myasthenia gravis

Framework — verify against current AR 40-501, DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2, DoDI 1332.18, and service aeromedical policy. See Profiles, MEB/MAR2 & deployability.

  • Retention — and the carve-out that decides the case. AR 40-501 para 3-31c lists myasthenia gravis, "Unless clinically restricted to extraocular muscles." The DoD floor is DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.l, "myasthenia gravis, unless only involving extraocular muscles." Both retain purely ocular disease and disqualify generalized disease — but they are not structurally identical, and the difference matters:
    • MG is not an "upon diagnosis" condition. Unlike epilepsy (5.26.k) and dementia (5.26.d), which carry "Paragraph 5.26.a. does not apply," MG stays gated by 5.26.a: the condition must persist despite appropriate treatment and preclude satisfactory performance of required duties. Document both prongs explicitly — a board memo that skips them is the mis-cited document.
    • Add the AR 40-501 3-1 criteria generalized MG most readily meets: 3-1b (medication requiring frequent physician monitoring) and 3-1d (dependence on frequent special treatments or clinical monitoring).
  • The ocular carve-out does not end the retention analysis. Check and document three more standards before concluding "retains": AR 40-501 3-7b / DoDI 6130.03 V2 5.4.e (binocular diplopia "not correctable by surgery, that is severe, constant, and in a zone less than 20 degrees from primary position" — in MG the fluctuating character usually defeats "constant," so say so rather than leaving it unaddressed); 3-31k, residual symptoms after adequate treatment meeting the para 3-1 definition; and 3-1b/3-1d, which chronic immunotherapy or scheduled infusion can meet even in ocular-only disease.
  • Deployability: generalized MG is non-deployable, on multiple independent grounds:
    • Crisis risk — a respiratory emergency that needs IVIG/PLEX and an ICU is incompatible with an austere or afloat environment.
    • Infusion/monitoring-dependent therapy and immunosuppression.
    • Cold chain is the hard constraint. Every approved biologic here — and IVIG — requires continuous 2–8 °C storage. That fails before the infusion schedule does.
    • Live vaccines vs immunosuppression. Theater-entry immunization requirements commonly include live vaccines that are contraindicated on immunosuppressive therapy — a theater-entry blocker independent of how well the MG is controlled.
    • Complement inhibitors create a standing meningococcal risk (boxed warning, REMS, revaccination schedule) that is hard to manage forward and dangerous in a crowded field environment.
    • Nerve-agent pretreatment conflict. A Soldier already on therapeutic pyridostigmine cannot take standard pyridostigmine bromide pretreatment and is hypersensitive to cholinesterase inhibition generally — see nerve agent / organophosphate. Raise it before a CBRN-threat assignment.
    • Heat, exertion, and sleep deprivation all worsen fatigable weakness — the operational environment is a direct provocation.
    • A long list of common field/formulary drugs are contraindicated (fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides especially) — a real constraint on deployed medical support.
    • If retention is being contemplated, zilucoplan is the only self-administered daily SC regimen and the only one with any field plausibility — and it still needs the cold chain.
  • Profile (DA Form 3349). MG profiles on the P factor (DA Pam 40-502 4-3c(1) — nervous system falls under physical capacity/stamina); add E where there is visual impairment.
    • Temporary during induction, titration, or post-thymectomy recovery — ≤90 days per instrument, and link every extension so the days-on-profile count is real.
    • Convert to permanent at clinical MRDP or the 12-month administrative MRDP, whichever comes first. Generalized disease → permanent P-3 (a permanent 3 or 4 is itself the DES referral, AR 40-501 3-4). Jumping straight to permanent invites a premature referral.
    • Section 4 limits should be functional and specific: no sustained overhead or repetitive exertion; no sustained load-carriage; no duty requiring uninterrupted alertness or reliable speech/swallow; no high-heat exposure; no sustained wear of a protective mask where respiratory reserve is reduced.
  • Ocular-only: retain on a documented surveillance plan, not on an assumption. Roughly 4 in 10 generalize (fewer in treated cohorts), most within 1–2 years. Carry the Soldier on a linked temporary profile through that window at a stated interval — q3 months for 24 months, matching the DA Pam 40-502 3-month functional-reassessment requirement — recording at each visit baseline and serial FVC and single-breath count, a bulbar screen (speech, swallow, chew, neck flexion), limb fatigability, and repeat serology if initially seronegative. Conversion triggers — any bulbar or respiratory symptom, any limb fatigability, a falling FVC, or a crisis — end the carve-out: the disease is no longer "clinically restricted to extraocular muscles," 3-31c applies, and you write the permanent P-3.
  • EPTS / LOD — and the 6-month fork. MG symptoms often predate diagnosis by years; date the first attributable symptom (fluctuating ptosis/diplopia, chewing fatigue, exertional dyspnea) and review pre-accession records. AR 40-501 3-2, Note: for conditions predating enlistment, accession standards govern the first 6 months of AD (separation via EPSBD); after 6 months Chapter 3 retention standards govern. This matters more in MG than almost anywhere else, because the two standards do not match — DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 6.26.q disqualifies a history of MG with no extraocular exception, while AR 40-501 3-31c retains ocular-only disease. Also check 3-3c: a condition known and waived at accession, essentially unchanged in severity and not meeting para 3-1, is not a DES referral. If the diagnosis was made in service, state LOD affirmatively and say what you reviewed.
  • MEB/DES: refer generalized MG. Document serostatus, crisis history, respiratory function (FVC), medication trials, and duty impact. A first crisis is a sentinel event — crisis is respiratory or bulbar by definition, so the disease is no longer "clinically restricted to extraocular muscles" and the 3-31c carve-out is unavailable as a matter of text. Whether the Soldier is ultimately found fit is the PEB's decision, not yours — write the standard and the evidence, not the outcome.
  • Aeromedical: disqualifying for flying duty — and the retention carve-out does not carry over. AR 40-501 Chapter 4 never names myasthenia gravis. The chain is 4-27 (Neurological) → "the causes in the accession standards plus the following" → the accession standard DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 para 6.26.q, which disqualifies a history of myasthenia gravis with no extraocular exception. So a Soldier retained under the 3-31c ocular carve-out is still aeromedically disqualified — on the history alone, with or without current diplopia. 4-24 (systemic) and 4-24a (therapeutic medications; see the medication APLs) apply independently, as do the ocular-motility standards at 4-4g. Disposition and any waiver run through USAAMA and the applicable Aeromedical Policy Letters (4-1c), not through Chapter 3. Non-Army Services follow their own aeromedical policy — confirm before counseling.
  • Vaccination collides with every drug on this page. Get all live vaccines done before starting — inebilizumab requires them ≥4 weeks ahead and none afterwards until B-cell repletion; FcRn agents and rituximab exclude live vaccines during treatment. For complement inhibitors the requirement runs the other way: MenACWY + MenB ≥2 weeks before the first dose. Non-live vaccine responses are blunted on FcRn blockade — time them to the end of a cycle, and re-evaluate vaccine status before each new cycle.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
The lesion is the endplate. In AChR-positive MG, antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor drive complement-mediated destruction of the postsynaptic membrane — the folds flatten, receptor density falls, and the safety factor of neuromuscular transmission collapses, so repeated firing fails progressively. That complement mechanism is exactly why C5 inhibitors work in AChR disease. MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and act differently — they disrupt the MuSK–LRP4 clustering pathway that maintains the receptor array without prominent complement activation, which is precisely why complement inhibitors fail in MuSK disease while B-cell depletion (rituximab) works so well. The serostatus is not a label; it is the mechanism, and it predicts which drug will work.

A decade that transformed the refractory patient. For most of MG's history, the patient who failed steroids and azathioprine had few options. Since 2017, three mechanistic classes have arrived: complement inhibition (eculizumab, then ravulizumab and zilucoplan), FcRn blockade (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab, and nipocalimab, which recycles less pathogenic IgG), and now anti-CD19 depletion (inebilizumab, approved for gMG in December 2025). Refractory MG went from a management dead-end to a menu — the harder question now is sequencing and cost, not whether an option exists.

And in 2026 the last serostatus wall came down. Every targeted agent had been gated by antibody status, which left the triple-seronegative patient — perhaps 10–15% of generalized MG — with nothing approved. On 8 May 2026 the FDA removed efgartigimod's AChR-positive restriction, on the strength of ADAPT SERON, making it the only approved therapy covering MuSK-positive, LRP4-positive and seronegative disease alike. Before reaching for it, though, send a clustered-AChR cell-based assay: most "seronegative" patients are assay-negative rather than antibody-negative, and finding the antibody reopens every other option.

Not every immune target works at the endplate. The winners are easy to list; the failures are the more useful lesson. Since 2024, IL-6 blockade (satralizumab — statistically positive but clinically marginal, development halted), oral factor D inhibition (vemircopan — missed every endpoint, terminated early), and BTK inhibition (tolebrutinib — phase 3 discontinued) have all fallen out. Batoclimab succeeded in phase 3 and was then abandoned commercially in favour of a next-generation molecule. The classes that work are the ones that remove IgG or block terminal complement.

No class has beaten another head-to-head. A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis of 27 randomized trials (n=2,318) found FcRn inhibitors, C5 inhibitors and CD19 depletion comparable on QMG and MG-ADL, and a real-world propensity-matched comparison agreed — while noting insufficient response in 20–49% of patients in both arms. Sequencing is therefore driven by serostatus, route, dosing rhythm and cost. Two more complement agents are at the FDA door, and both would change the logistics rather than the efficacy: cemdisiran, an siRNA silencing hepatic C5 dosed subcutaneously every 12 weeks (FDA action date November 2026), and gefurulimab, a self-administered SC nanobody. Neither is approved.

Thymectomy earned its place by trial. MGTX was the randomized evidence that settled a decades-old practice: in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG, thymectomy plus prednisone beat prednisone alone, and the benefit — better disease control, less steroid, fewer exacerbations — held through 5 years.

Key evidence:

  • MGTX (NEJM 2016; Lancet Neurology 2019 extension) — thymectomy + prednisone superior to prednisone alone in non-thymomatous AChR+ generalized MG; benefit sustained to 5 years. Post hoc: no difference in patients ≥50.
  • REGAIN — eculizumab in refractory AChR+ gMG.
  • CHAMPION-MG — ravulizumab; RAISE — zilucoplan.
  • ADAPT — efgartigimod, the only pivotal gMG trial to enroll regardless of antibody status; ADAPT SERON — basis of the May 2026 all-serotype expansion.
  • MycarinG — rozanolixizumab; Vivacity-MG3 — nipocalimab.
  • MINT — inebilizumab in AChR+ or MuSK+ gMG (basis of the Dec 2025 approval); AChR+ benefit widened between weeks 26 and 52.
  • IMPACT-MG (2026) — first placebo-controlled trial of pyridostigmine, Class I evidence; and the negative arm showing amifampridine adds nothing on top of it.
  • Barth 2011 — the IVIG-vs-PLEX randomized head-to-head (69% vs 65%), in moderate-to-severe worsening MG, not intubated crisis.
  • Menon 2024 (Neurology) — 154-patient propensity-matched ocular MG cohort; immunosuppression associated with roughly halved generalization risk.
  • International Consensus Guidance for Management of MG, 2020 update (Narayanaswami et al., Neurology 2021) — still current, AAN-affirmed 14 Jul 2022. It has been supplemented, not replaced, by national guidance — and it predates nipocalimab, zilucoplan, rozanolixizumab and inebilizumab, so the biologic sequencing on this page reflects labels and trials, not guideline text.

docs.title: Related neuromuscular-junction disorders
docs.text:
MG is the postsynaptic, autoimmune prototype — but fatigable or acute weakness at the NMJ has other causes that are treated completely differently:

  • Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) — presynaptic antibody disease, often paraneoplastic. The MG mimic that is really a lung-cancer search.
  • Botulism — presynaptic toxin; descending paralysis, an antitoxin emergency.
  • Nerve agent / organophosphate toxicity — poisoning of the synaptic enzyme; a CBRN and pesticide emergency treated with atropine and pralidoxime.
