docs.title: Botulism
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

One-liner: a presynaptic toxin that cleaves the machinery of acetylcholine release, producing symmetric, descending, flaccid paralysis with prominent bulbar and autonomic features — and a normal sensorium throughout. The treatment is antitoxin, given on suspicion, plus ventilatory support.

Who this is for: the ED or ICU provider facing acute descending weakness. Botulism is rare, time-critical, and a reportable public-health and potential-bioterrorism event — recognizing it fast is the entire game.

🚩 Recognize it and treat before you confirm

The classic picture: an afebrile, alert patient with acute, symmetric, descending paralysis that starts with the bulbar "4 D's" — diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia — plus dilated, poorly reactive pupils, dry mouth, and progressive limb weakness, with normal sensation and normal mentation.

  • No fever (unless from a wound or aspiration), no sensory loss, preserved consciousness — these separate it from stroke, GBS, and encephalitis. Across 332 US cases: 99% afebrile, 93% descending, 91% normal mentation.
  • Descending (cranial nerves → arms → trunk → legs) and symmetric — the opposite of Guillain-Barré's ascending pattern.
  • Dilated, poorly reactive pupils are present in only ~50% — highly suggestive when there, not exclusionary when absent.
  • Antitoxin does not reverse established paralysis — it halts progression. Do not wait for laboratory confirmation, which takes days.
  • Call your state health department / CDC immediately — antitoxin is released only through public health, and reporting is mandatory.

Atypical features do NOT exclude botulism — this is the commonest way the diagnosis is missed

In the same 332-case series, 17% reported paresthesias, 13% had elevated CSF protein, and 7% of adequately documented cases were frankly atypical — unilateral cranial nerve findings, or even ascending paralysis. Those are exactly the features a clinician uses to talk themselves out of the diagnosis.

Botulism is the most-missed of the acute flaccid paralyses. Physicians' differentials in those cases named Guillain-Barré in 99 and myasthenia gravis in 76; in one restaurant outbreak all 28 patients were initially misdiagnosed, four of them as psychiatric illness. What actually distinguishes botulism is cranial nerve palsy disproportionate to the weakness below the neck, symmetry, and absent sensory findings.

docs.title: Forms — the route changes the antitoxin
docs.text:
Form Source Key points Foodborne Preformed toxin — home-canned/fermented foods Outbreak potential; investigate co-exposed contacts Wound C. botulinum in a wound producing toxin in vivo Injection drug use, esp. black-tar heroin. No GI prodrome; needs antibiotics + debridement in addition to antitoxin (avoid aminoglycosides) Infant Spore colonization of the gut (honey, soil/dust) The "floppy baby" — constipation, poor feeding, weak cry, hypotonia. Treat with BabyBIG, not equine antitoxin Iatrogenic Cosmetic or therapeutic botulinum toxin — overwhelmingly counterfeit or unlicensed product Now the fastest-growing category — see below. Mild and localized with authentic product at labelled doses; severe and systemic with counterfeit Inhalational Aerosolized toxin Not natural — implies bioterrorism. Botulinum neurotoxin is a CDC Category A bioterrorism agent and an HHS Tier 1 Select Agent (42 CFR Part 73) — two separate regimes. Presents as descending paralysis with diplopia, dysphagia, ptosis and pupillary dilation progressing to ventilatory failure, without fever or altered mentation

Iatrogenic botulism has changed character — ask every young patient about cosmetic injections

"Usually mild and localized" is still true for FDA-approved product at labelled doses by licensed injectors — typical cosmetic doses of 4–20 units sit orders of magnitude below the estimated systemic lethal dose (~40 U/kg). It is not true of the counterfeit and unlicensed market that now drives the case burden.

Where When Cases Severity Hebei, China (single centre) Jun–Jul 2024 195 26.2% severe, 16.4% mechanically ventilated, 44.6% still symptomatic at 30 days Guangzhou, China 2024–25 145 Bulbar-predominant, no deaths North East England Jun 2025 25 Seized vials assayed at 370 U/vial against a 200 U label Türkiye → 4 EU countries 2023 >80 Intragastric toxin for weight loss; ICU care US (NY, TX, WI) 2025 3 Self-injection of product bought online

It is product quality, not labelled dose, that produces systemic disease — counterfeit preparations of unknown potency, mislabelled potency, research-grade toxin, injection into highly vascular targets (intragastric for weight loss, calves for slimming), and underlying NMJ disease (myasthenia, LEMS) as a contraindication that is frequently ignored.

A young woman with acute bilateral cranial neuropathies and no food or injection-drug history should be asked directly about recent cosmetic injections — including product she bought and injected herself. Antitoxin is indicated, and delay to antitoxin was an independent predictor of poor 30-day outcome in the 195-case series.

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
• Clinical and immediate — the syndrome above drives treatment; confirmation is retrospective.
  • Confirmatory: toxin assay and culture from serum, stool, gastric contents, wound, or food — coordinated through public health. The mouse bioassay remains the reference standard, but CDC's Endopep-MS mass-spectrometry assay was validated for clinical specimens in 2024 with a limit of detection equal to or better than the bioassay and 100% inter-serotype specificity, intended for distribution to public health laboratories. Serum assays typically stay positive for up to ~16 days, and toxin has been detected 11–12 days after ingestion.
  • Incubation: 18–36 h foodborne, 4–14 days wound, ~6 h inhalational, and a median of 3 days for iatrogenic cases.

A negative electrodiagnostic study does not exclude botulism — and must never delay antitoxin

The classic triad is low baseline CMAP with facilitation on high-frequency (20–50 Hz) RNS, like other presynaptic disorders. But:

  • Facilitation appears in only 50–60% of patients, and is typically far less dramatic than in LEMS. In mild disease it may show only pseudofacilitation.
  • Sensitivity decays with time. Post-exercise facilitation and the 50 Hz increment fall progressively from the acute phase (days 4–8) through the late post-acute phase (days 66–80), and can vanish while clinical signs persist.
  • Single-fibre EMG is the sensitive test and was abnormal in every patient in a series where conventional studies were abnormal in only the most severe.

Use EDx to support the diagnosis and to exclude mimics — never to rule botulism out.

  • Rule out the mimics actively: Guillain-Barré / Miller Fisher (ascending, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation), myasthenic crisis, brainstem stroke, tick paralysis, organophosphate poisoning (which is the opposite autonomic picture — wet, not dry; see nerve agent).

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Recognize acute, symmetric, descending, afebrile flaccid paralysis with bulbar onset and clear sensorium.
  2. Protect the airway — serial FVC and bulbar assessment; intubate early for respiratory or bulbar failure. This is the intervention that saves lives.
  3. Call public health NOW for antitoxin release and reporting — in parallel with airway care.
  4. Give antitoxin on clinical suspicion — do not wait for confirmation.
  5. Address the source — wound debridement + antibiotics for wound botulism; supportive care.
  6. Report and investigate — outbreak and bioterrorism implications.

docs.title: Treatment
docs.text:
Step 1 — airway and supportive care

The airway fails before the bellows do. This is the single most important structural fact about botulism respiratory failure, and it is why the myasthenia numbers do not transfer cleanly: because paralysis is descending and bulbar-first, airway obstruction and aspiration usually precede hypoventilation. In infant botulism the principal indication for intubation was loss of protective airway reflexes, not hypoxaemia or hypercarbia.

  • Intubate for loss of gag or cough, inability to handle secretions, or pooling in the oropharynx — regardless of the numbers. A patient with an intact vital capacity and an absent gag needs a tube.
  • Then monitor numbers serially (q2–4 h while progressing): vital capacity <20 mL/kg, NIF worse than −30 cmH₂O, or a ≥30% fall from the patient's own baseline — treat any of these as a prompt to intubate now, not a threshold to wait for.
    • No botulism-specific study has validated any of these cutoffs. The 20/30/40 rule comes from a Guillain-Barré cohort; applying it here is extrapolation by analogy, and the JAMA consensus statement on botulinum toxin as a weapon deliberately gives no numeric cutoff and recommends anticipatory, controlled intubation instead.
  • The vital capacity you measure may be falsely low. Facial diplegia breaks the mouthpiece seal — face-mask versus mouthpiece spirometry differs by ~200 mL even in normal subjects. Use a facemask interface if there is facial weakness, and accept that some bulbar patients simply cannot perform the test.
  • Botulism-specific predictors of respiratory failure worth acting on: postprandial hypotension (adjusted OR 8.33), moderate-to-severe ptosis, dilated or fixed pupils, and a short incubation period. Sporadic single cases are sicker than outbreak cases — 85% vs 42% intubated.
  • The single-breath count is a validated triage adjunct for a mass-casualty botulism event, where spirometry will not be available for everyone.

Do not reach for BiPAP in botulism

Non-invasive ventilation should be actively discouraged here — the combination of bulbar failure, secretion burden and aspiration risk that defines botulism is exactly the profile in which NIV fails and becomes dangerous. This is a genuine difference from myasthenic crisis, where more than a third of NIV trials succeed. No botulism-specific NIV evidence exists, and no randomized trial of invasive versus non-invasive ventilation in neuromuscular disease exists at all.

  • Meticulous ICU supportive care — the paralysis is survivable with good support and is largely reversible over time. Expect weeks to months: mean ventilation is roughly 56 days for type A and 26 days for type B, though outbreak medians run shorter (14 days).

Step 2 — antitoxin, as fast as possible

Adults and children >1 year — heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (BAT/HBAT, equine F(ab')₂), covering toxin types A–G, US-licensed 2013, held in the Strategic National Stockpile and released only through CDC via the state health department, 24/7.

  • The adult dose is the entire contents of ONE vial as a single IV infusion — it is not weight-based. Exposure–response modelling predicts >95.9% survival across all seven serotypes after one vial.
  • Children 1–16 years receive a percentage of the adult vial scaled by age band; infants under 1 year a weight-based percentage. Transcribe that table from the package insert at the time of use — do not reproduce a paediatric percentage from memory.
  • Diluted 1:10 in 0.9% saline, infused slowly with stepwise rate increases; epinephrine 1:1000 and diphenhydramine at the bedside throughout, because the product is equine. Verify infusion parameters against the insert, which is the controlling document.

Do not delay BAT to perform skin testing — this is a change from older references

The AAAAI/CDC Botulism Clinical Treatment Guidelines Workgroup concluded that the data do not support delaying antitoxin for skin testing. Predictive values were poor for the older non-despeciated products (PPV 0–56%), anaphylaxis with modern BAT runs ~0.6–1.6%, and no fatal anaphylaxis has been reported with any botulinum antitoxin.

Registry safety in 162 patients: 19.1% any adverse event, 4.3% serious, 0.6% anaphylaxis. Note the historical 3.7% serum sickness figure comes from whole-IgG equine products and should not be quoted for the modern despeciated F(ab')₂ product.

  • A second dose is not routine and not labelled. But F(ab')₂ fragments clear faster than whole immunoglobulin, and rebound botulism has been documented 10 days after antitoxin in intestinal-colonization disease — where toxin production is ongoing. Re-progression after initial improvement, in wound or colonization botulism, is a CDC-consultation call, not a protocol.

Infants — human botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG), from the Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program, California Dept of Public Health (510-231-7600). Do not use equine antitoxin in infants if BabyBIG is available.

  • 1.0 mL/kg (50 mg/kg) as a single IV infusion. Reconstitute in 2 mL sterile water, start within 2 hours of reconstitution and complete within 4. Begin at 0.5 mL/kg/h; if no reaction after 15 minutes increase to 1.0 mL/kg/h and do not exceed that rate (total infusion ~68 minutes). Separate IV line with an in-line filter. Check BUN/creatinine before and after. Half-life ~28 days; one infusion neutralizes toxin for at least 6 months, so defer live virus vaccines (MMR, MMRV, varicella) for 6 months.
  • Labelled for toxin type A or B, in patients under one year. In practice it is given empirically before typing returns — which is correct. For a confirmed non-A/B infant case, BAT is the fallback (licensed A–G, and the registry included a 32-day-old), but that trades into equine sensitization and should be a joint IBTPP/CDC decision.
  • Give it on suspicion, not on confirmation — and the urgency is quantified: treating on hospital days 0–3 cut length of stay by 3.7 weeks, days 4–7 by 2.6 weeks, and days 8–10 by only 1 week (non-significant).

\"Too late\" is almost never the right call

No interval has been identified beyond which antitoxin stops being beneficial. Circulating toxin has been detected in serum 11–12 days after ingestion; wound and intestinal-colonization botulism involve ongoing toxin production, so the exposure is not a single bolus; and progressing paralysis is itself evidence that unbound toxin is still circulating.

Any antitoxin reduced mortality with an OR of 0.16; within 48 hours, OR 0.12. Treatment within 24 hours of onset gave a median of 0 ventilator days against 21. Documented benefit exists at day 7, day 9 and day 15 in iatrogenic cases.

Give antitoxin at any point while paralysis is progressing or exposure may be ongoing. Withhold only when the deficit has clearly plateaued after a single, finite, remote exposure — and even then, discuss with CDC.

Wound botulism specifics — and why the order matters

Antitoxin first, then antibiotics. This is not sequencing preference: antibiotic-induced lysis of vegetative C. botulinum releases preformed intracellular neurotoxin, which is only safe once neutralizing antitoxin is aboard.

  • Penicillin G 20 million units/day IV divided q4–6h (the labelled clostridial dose; penicillin G is FDA-labelled for botulism as adjunctive therapy to antitoxin).
  • Penicillin-allergic: metronidazole 15 mg/kg IV load (~1 g at 70 kg), then 7.5 mg/kg IV q6h (~500 mg); usual anaerobic course 7–10 days. Metronidazole reduces C. botulinum viability without enhancing neurotoxin production.
  • Early debridement is not optional — it removes the anaerobic niche sustaining toxin production. Duration is expert consensus, not trial-derived.
  • Avoid aminoglycosides, clindamycin, lincomycin, polymyxins and tetracyclines — all impair neuromuscular transmission and compound the toxin's presynaptic blockade. An infant with botulism became apnoeic and died on gentamicin. Extend this caution to any incidental antibiotic given for a coincidental pneumonia or UTI, not just the botulism-directed agent.
  • Think of it in people who inject drugs — especially black-tar heroin. Wound botulism is under-recognized because it looks like opioid intoxication.

Antibiotics are NOT indicated in foodborne or infant botulism

Foodborne disease is preformed toxin — there is no infection to treat. In infant botulism, empirical antimicrobials made things worse: hospitalization 20 days vs 12 in a multicentre series. Treat the toxin, not a culture.

docs.title: Prognosis — and what to tell the patient afterwards
docs.text:
Survival is now the expectation. Untreated case-fatality was 40–50%; with modern critical care it is around 4%, and deaths in the antitoxin programmes were attributed to underlying illness rather than the drug.

Intubation rate 67% type A · 52% type B · 39% type E; ~34% across foodborne outbreaks Ventilation duration mean ~56 days (type A), ~26 days (type B); median 14 days in outbreak settings Effect of early antitoxin treatment <24 h → median 0 ventilator days and 10 hospital days; >24 h → 21 and 41; none → 28 and 56 Tracheostomy in infants essentially unnecessary — 0 of 60 in a 10-year series despite mean intubation of 21 days

Recovery starts long before it finishes, and the page's readers will be asked about this. Improvement in strength begins at a median of ~5 days after antitoxin, but ventilatory and upper airway muscle strength recovers mostly over the first 12 weeks and continues improving to 1 year. Resolution of half the original symptoms took an average of 5 months, and 13 of 14 patients still reported symptoms at 13 months.

Long-term morbidity is real and is the most under-counselled part of this illness. At a median of 4.3 years after illness, 68% of 217 patients reported worse health than before, against 17% of controls (matched OR 17.6) — and mechanical ventilation during the acute illness independently predicted worse long-term health. A systematic review of sequelae found fatigue in 66%, general weakness in 57%, and dyspnoea in 43%, with psychosocial dysfunction outlasting physical impairment.

Mechanistically, recovery is biphasic: nerve terminal sprouts appear within days and carry transmission by ~4 weeks, then a second phase returns vesicle turnover to the original parent terminals and eliminates the sprouts. Serotype sets the duration — type A is the longest, type E the shortest. Single-fibre EMG jitter persists beyond clinical recovery.

Infant botulism — supportive care that actually changes outcome

  • Nasogastric or nasojejunal feeding is standard — 43 of 44 patients in one series needed it; transpyloric placement reduces aspiration risk given the impaired gag and ileus.
  • Avoid cathartics and enemas — glycerin contamination renders toxin assays inconclusive, and treatment must not be delayed to obtain a specimen.
  • Watch for SIADH (18% in one series) and for autonomic instability, which outlasts apparent motor recovery — heart-rate variability stays abnormal for weeks after the infant looks better. The one death in that series was progressive bradycardia despite adequate ventilation.
  • Discharge on full oral intake with a strong gag and cough, not on extubation.
  • Organism excretion in stool persists a median of 5.9 weeks (type A) after clinical recovery — relevant to infection control, not to treatment.

Military medicine — botulism

Framework — verify against current AR 40-501, DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2, and applicable force-health-protection / CBRN guidance. See Profiles, MEB/MAR2 & deployability.

  • There is no botulism vaccine — say this out loud, because the record may suggest otherwise. The investigational pentavalent (ABCDE) botulinum toxoid given to at-risk laboratory and Army personnel under IND 161 (CDC) and IND 3723 (US Army) was discontinued by CDC effective 30 November 2011 — falling immunogenicity of several serotype components, rising local reactogenicity on boosting, and a manufacture more than thirty years old. No FDA-licensed botulism vaccine exists. The recombinant rBV A/B successor completed Phase I/II, is not licensed, and today mainly immunizes plasma donors for BabyBIG.
    • Do not treat a documented toxoid series as protection. It does not raise the threshold for suspicion and it does not delay antitoxin by one minute.
    • AR 40-562 (7 Oct 2013), the joint immunization regulation, contains no botulinum toxoid entry — there is nothing to enforce, waive, or counsel against. Force health protection here is entirely non-pharmaceutical: detection, avoidance, respiratory protection, food and water surveillance, and post-exposure antitoxin.
  • This is an operational and public-health event before it is a disposition question. Botulinum neurotoxin is a CDC Category A bioterrorism agent and an HHS Tier 1 Select Agent (42 CFR Part 73) — two separate regimes, and the second one creates independent reporting obligations. A single case is a sentinel event.
    • What says "release" rather than "home canning": any case of inhalational botulism (it does not occur naturally); a cluster of acute flaccid paralysis with prominent bulbar palsy — CDC's syndromic indicator of intentional release; a common-source cluster with no shared food; or an unusual toxin type.
    • Notify in parallel with treating: the servicing MTF and its preventive-medicine / public-health element; the Public Health Emergency Officer; the chain as a reportable medical event; and, where intentional release is in question, medical intelligence via the National Center for Medical Intelligence (NCMI). A suspected laboratory exposure adds a Federal Select Agent Program report, separate from the clinical one.
    • How the Soldier actually gets antitoxin: BAT is not stocked at your pharmacy and is not ordered. It is held in the Strategic National Stockpile and released by CDC through the state or territorial health department, 24/7. Call the state health department first; CDC's Emergency Operations Center is the backstop. Make that call in parallel with airway management, not after it.
    • OCONUS and deployed: work the same request through the servicing MTF and the combatant command surgeon. The specific OCONUS pathway and any theater-held stocks are not in publicly releasable doctrine — confirm locally before you need it.
    • A planning note. Open-source global surveillance for 2017–2024 attributes 56% of human botulism outbreaks to Ukraine — food preservation and cold-chain disruption under wartime conditions. Supporting operations in or near that AOR means knowing the antitoxin request pathway before you need it.
  • Retention — the hook is 3-31k, not a bare "3-31," and it turns entirely on residual deficit. Botulism is named in no military medical standard — it appears nowhere in AR 40-501 or in either volume of DoDI 6130.03. Cite it as a reasoned analogy and say so.
    • AR 40-501 para 3-31k, "Other neurologic conditions" is the catch-all — "any other neurologic conditions when, after adequate treatment, there remain residual symptoms and impairments such as … weakness, paralysis, or atrophy of important muscle groups … as to meet the definition … as in paragraph 3-1." Name the 3-1 limb you actually meet — normally 3-1a (duty interference substantiated by the commander). 3-1b and 3-1d are usually NOT met — there is no maintenance drug, no infusion schedule, no indefinite monitoring. Do not pad the memo.
    • DoD floor: DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.i — "peripheral neuropathy or paralytic disorders resulting in permanent functional impairment." Its permanence qualifier, which works against you in LEMS, is the right fit here, because residual deficit at MRDP is precisely the question. Do not cite 5.26.c — botulism is peripheral and the sensorium is normal.
    • Not an "upon diagnosis" condition. Only 5.26.d (dementia) and 5.26.k (epilepsy) carry "Paragraph 5.26.a. does not apply." Document both 5.26.a prongs — but here "persists despite appropriate treatment" means a documented rehabilitation plateau after antitoxin and supportive care, not a failed drug trial.
    • The structural difference from MG and LEMS: the diagnosis carries no retention consequence at all. A Soldier who recovers fully has no permanent profile, no MEB and no MAR2 — the temporary profile closes and the episode ends there.
  • Profile (DA Form 3349) — the convalescence is the disposition, so write it properly. Profiles on the P factor; add E while accommodative paresis, mydriasis or blurred near vision persist (prominent in botulism and late to resolve), and L/U for residual girdle weakness.
    • Temporary through ICU care, weaning, and all of rehabilitation. ≤90 days per instrument; link every extension so the days-on-profile count is real.
    • Do not close the profile at extubation. Ventilation alone averages ~56 days in type A and ~26 in type B, and 68% of survivors report worse health at a median 4.3 years, with mechanical ventilation independently predicting worse long-term health. Close on documented functional recovery — FVC and NIF back to baseline, exercise tolerance restored, orthostasis and accommodation resolved — not on the ventilator being gone.
    • Expect the 12-month clock to matter more than the diagnosis. A long ventilator course plus a fatigue and dysautonomia tail will often run out the administrative MRDP. Anticipate it at the first extension, and watch the 120 / 180 / 240-day review gates.
    • Section 4 limits, functionally written: no sustained load-carriage or road march; no duty requiring reliable respiratory reserve or sustained protective-mask wear; no unrestricted work in high heat; no duty requiring sharp near vision or reliable accommodation (weapons sighting, NVD use, ATC/UAS consoles); no prolonged standing in formation while orthostasis persists; no duty requiring reliable speech or swallow while bulbar weakness persists.
  • EPTS / LOD — EPTS is a non-issue here; LOD may not be. Botulism is an acute intoxication with a datable exposure and onset, so there is nothing to date back to pre-accession and the 6-month accession/retention fork does not arise. State LOD affirmatively and record the exposure factually — food source, wound, procedure, date, co-exposed personnel, duty status, and the antitoxin product, serotype coverage, lot and date.
    • Anticipate the misconduct question in three settings, and document neutrally rather than conclusorily: wound botulism associated with injection drug use; foodborne botulism acquired off duty; and iatrogenic botulism after an elective cosmetic injection. Off-duty is not the same as not-in-line-of-duty — the LOD authority adjudicates that, not you. Your job is a clean, dated exposure history.
    • A slow LOD is not excludable time on the IDES clock.
    • Record the antitoxin as a durable fact. BAT is equine-derived — flag the equine exposure for any future re-administration, and watch for serum sickness roughly 1–2 weeks out, after the patient has left the ICU and may be back at their unit. A delayed febrile rash with arthralgias in a botulism survivor is not a new infection until proven otherwise.
  • MEB / MAR2 — run the fork, and expect the answer to be "neither."
    • Full recovery, the usual outcome: no board. Close the linked temporary profile on documented functional recovery. Do not write a permanent profile to "document the history."
    • Residual deficit at MRDP, still meets retention standards but cannot perform the PMOS → MAR2, an administrative review.
    • Residual deficit meeting 3-31k / para 3-1 → DES. The permanent P-3 in e-Profile is the referral (AR 40-501 3-4).
    • Do not refer before MRDP — rehabilitation must have plateaued or the 12-month clock must have run. Premature referrals get bounced and delay the Soldier.
    • Document increments a board can act on: serial FVC/NIF, ventilator days, weaning and ambulation dates, timed walk or exercise tolerance, and objective autonomic findings. Botulism recovery is gradual and cannot be reconstructed retrospectively.
  • Aeromedical — temporary suspension, not disqualification. Do not copy the MG/LEMS chain. AR 40-501 4-27 names no botulism or peripheral-intoxication standard, and DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 6.26.q is the wrong hook — it requires a chronic nervous system disorder. The accession hook that feeds 4-27 is 6.26.n, "history of paralysis, weakness, lack of coordination … or other specified paralytic syndromes, including, but not limited to, Guillain-Barré Syndrome" — GBS being named makes it the closest published analogy for an acute paralytic illness that recovers.
    • Use 4-27g as the structural model: for Classes 2, 2F, 2P, 3 and 4 its disposition is "until complete recovery without residual neurological deficits or other sequelae." So: ground on suspicion, treat it as a temporary medical suspension from aviation service pending complete recovery.
    • USAAMA reviews and recommends "qualified, qualified with waiver, or medical suspension from aviation service" and issues the governing Aeromedical Policy Letters — send the case rather than deciding it. Any condition producing a PULHES code greater than 1 requires a complete work-up per the APLs.
    • What keeps an aircrew member grounded after the limbs recover is ocular and autonomic — accommodative paresis, mydriasis, blurred near vision, orthostatic intolerance. If binocular diplopia persists, check AR 40-501 3-7b separately. The same findings are decisive for ATC and UAS operators (4-34).
  • Deployability — time-limited, not permanent, and that is the difference from every other page in this section. Non-deployable through the acute illness and all of rehabilitation. What actually fails downrange, and outlasts limb strength:
    • Impaired sweating from cholinergic autonomic blockade → reduced thermoregulation and real heat-injury risk in a hot AOR, invisible on a strength exam.
    • Reduced respiratory reserve vs sustained protective-mask wear.
    • Accommodative paresis, mydriasis, blurred near vision — weapons sighting, NVD use, console and map work.
    • Orthostatic intolerance under load and in formation; dry mouth and dry eyes in a desert or high-particulate environment.
    • What does not fail: no maintenance drug, no cold chain, no infusion schedule, no immunosuppression, no live-vaccine conflict, and nothing that has to be monitored forward. Once recovery is documented, full deployability is the expected endpoint — reassess against sweating, respiratory reserve, accommodation and orthostasis, not against ventilator status alone.

TRICARE — botulism: the access path is public health, not pharmacy

There is nothing here to look up on the formulary. BAT is not prescribed, not ordered, and not purchased. It is a Strategic National Stockpile product released by CDC through the state or territorial health department, 24/7, at no cost to the patient. No TRICARE tier, no prior authorization, no pharmacy-versus-medical-benefit split to reason about. Do not spend a minute of the therapeutic window looking for a way to order it — make the public health call.

  • BabyBIG is different. It comes only from the CDPH Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program, and the program bills for the product — for a TRICARE-eligible dependent infant that is a coverage question, not a formulary one. Involve the MTF or regional contractor early, and treat first. Current BabyBIG pricing and TRICARE billing treatment were not verified for this page — confirm with the IBTPP and the regional contractor.
  • The rest of the episode is inpatient benefit — ICU care, ventilation, and debridement plus antibiotics for wound botulism. Do not delay any of it for an authorization.
  • Nothing here is a maintenance prescription. The post-acute cost centre is rehabilitation, which is where the authorization effort actually belongs.
  • Verify current coverage at the TRICARE Formulary Search and with the regional contractor before you counsel.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
One of the most potent toxins known, with a precise molecular target. Botulinum neurotoxin is taken up by cholinergic nerve terminals, where its light chain is a protease that cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, syntaxin, synaptobrevin) — the fusion machinery that docks acetylcholine vesicles to the presynaptic membrane. With SNARE cleaved, no acetylcholine is released, and the muscle is chemically denervated. Recovery is not a matter of clearing the toxin; it requires the terminal to sprout and rebuild new release sites, which is why paralysis lasts weeks to months even after antitoxin. The same mechanism, dosed and localized, is what makes botulinum toxin a therapeutic — from chronic migraine to cervical dystonia — and what makes MG a contraindication to receiving it.

Why "treat on suspicion" is not just caution. Antitoxin can only neutralize toxin that is still circulating and unbound. Once toxin has entered the nerve terminal, no antibody can retrieve it. Every hour of diagnostic delay converts reversible circulating toxin into fixed, bound toxin — so the therapeutic window is measured against the clock, and the decision to treat is made clinically, before any test returns.

There is no licensed botulism vaccine, and this is not widely known. The investigational pentavalent (ABCDE) botulinum toxoid was discontinued by CDC on 30 November 2011 — declining immunogenicity of some serotype components, rising local reactogenicity with boosters, and manufacture more than thirty years earlier. It had been given under IND 161 (CDC, at-risk laboratory workers) and IND 3723 (US Army). Its successor, recombinant rBV A/B, completed Phase I and II but has never been licensed; its current job is immunizing the plasma donors who supply BabyBIG rather than protecting anyone directly. Previously immunized personnel must not be assumed protected.

The treatment pipeline is real but nowhere near the bedside. Four oligoclonal human monoclonal antibody antitoxins have completed Phase 1 with no drug-related serious adverse events — and a nine-antibody formulation covering A, B and E is lyophilized and stable at 50 °C for a year, which is operationally striking for austere storage. None has entered Phase 2 and none is available. Separately, 3,4-diaminopyridine — already approved for LEMS — has strong preclinical repurposing data, reversing respiratory depression at terminal stages in mice and, combined with antitoxin, extending the therapeutic window past the point where antitoxin alone did nothing. No human trial in botulism has been reported. Watch this space; do not prescribe from it.

Key references:

  • CDC Clinical Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of Botulism, 2021 (MMWR Recomm Rep) — still in force, with no formal update identified.
  • Heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (BAT) — types A–G, equine F(ab')₂, US-licensed 2013.
  • BabyBIG — human botulism immune globulin for infant botulism (California IBTPP). Now derived from plasma of donors immunized with recombinant rBV A/B rather than the original pentavalent toxoid; indication and dosing unchanged.
  • AAAAI/CDC workgroup systematic review — skin testing should not delay antitoxin.
  • Endopep-MS — mass-spectrometric toxin detection, validated for clinical specimens 2024.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rao AK, Sobel J, Chatham-Stephens K, Luquez C. Clinical guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of botulism, 2021. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2021;70(2):1-30. MMWR
  2. Botulism Antitoxin Heptavalent (A–G, equine) — FDA label — the controlling document for the paediatric percentage table and infusion parameters.
  3. BabyBIG FDA label, effective 2025-12-08 — 1.0 mL/kg (50 mg/kg), infusion rates, type A/B and <1 year indication. DailyMed
  4. Arnon SS, Schechter R, Inglesby TV, et al. Botulinum toxin as a biological weapon: medical and public health management. JAMA. 2001;285(8):1059-1070. PubMed — the source of "airway obstruction usually precedes hypoventilation," and of the deliberate refusal to give numeric intubation cutoffs.
  5. Rao AK, Lin NH, Jackson KA, Mody RK, Griffin PM. Clinical characteristics and ancillary test results among patients with botulism — United States, 2002–2015. Clin Infect Dis. 2017. PubMed — the 332-case series, and the 17% paresthesias / 13% raised CSF protein / 7% atypical figures.
  6. Schussler E, Sobel J, Hsu J, et al. Allergic reactions to botulinum antitoxin: a systematic review (AAAAI/CDC workgroup). Clin Infect Dis. 2017. PubMed — skin testing must not delay treatment.
  7. O'Horo JC, Harper EP, El Rafei A, et al. Efficacy of antitoxin therapy in foodborne botulism: systematic review and meta-analysis, 1923–2016. Clin Infect Dis. 2017. PubMed — no interval identified beyond which antitoxin is not beneficial.
  8. Arnon SS, Schechter R, Maslanka SE, Jewell NP, Hatheway CL. Human botulism immune globulin for the treatment of infant botulism. N Engl J Med. 2006;354:462-471. PubMed — the pivotal RCT.
  9. Gottlieb SL, Kretsinger K, Tarkhashvili N, et al. Long-term outcomes of 217 botulism cases in the Republic of Georgia. Clin Infect Dis. 2007. PubMed — 68% worse health at median 4.3 years.
  10. An Y, Lv B, Zheng T, et al. Clinical challenges and prognostic risk factors for 195 cases of iatrogenic botulism in China. Clin Toxicol. 2025 — the series that retires "usually mild."
  11. AR 40-501 para 3-31 (residual deficit); applicable CBRN / force-health-protection guidance for the operational response.

Verified August 2026: BabyBIG dosing, infusion rates, reconstitution, and the type A/B and under-one-year indication boundaries are taken from the current FDA label (effective 2025-12-08), not from memory. BAT is deliberately not dosed numerically here beyond the one-vial adult rule: it is absent from the openFDA drug-label API, its paediatric dosing is an age-band percentage table, and reproducing that from a secondary source is a realistic route to a paediatric overdose — the package insert is the controlling document at the time of use. Three positions were corrected outright. Skin testing must not delay antitoxin (AAAAI/CDC workgroup) — older references mandate it. There is no interval beyond which antitoxin stops being beneficial; toxin has been detected in serum 11–12 days after ingestion, and the page previously implied a closing window. And iatrogenic botulism is no longer "usually mild" — a single Chinese centre saw 195 cases in two months with 16.4% ventilated, driven by counterfeit product of unknown potency rather than by labelled dose.

The airway section was rewritten around the fact that airway obstruction and aspiration precede hypoventilation in botulism, so the myasthenia thresholds do not transfer cleanly: no botulism-specific cutoff has ever been validated, vital capacity is unreliable when facial diplegia breaks the mouthpiece seal, and NIV should be actively discouraged — a real difference from myasthenic crisis. The diagnosis section now states that 17% of patients report paresthesias, 13% have raised CSF protein, and 7% are frankly atypical, because those are the findings clinicians use to talk themselves out of the diagnosis, and that a negative electrodiagnostic study cannot exclude botulism (facilitation appears in only 50–60%, and sensitivity decays with time).

Not independently verified:* BAT paediatric percentages and infusion parameters (consult the insert); stockpile and release logistics at any given installation; and the long-term morbidity figures, which come from a single large cohort in the Republic of Georgia and may not generalize. Botulism is not a named retention condition* — disposition follows residual deficit, and the military box states its citations and their limits explicitly.

docs.title: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

One-liner: an antibody attack on presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels that throttles acetylcholine release — proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and hyporeflexia. Half the time it is the first sign of a small-cell lung cancer.

Who this is for: anyone working up proximal weakness that looks like myasthenia but isn't behaving — and the reason the page exists is that finding LEMS means starting a cancer hunt.

🚩 LEMS is a paraneoplastic red flag until proven otherwise

~50–60% of LEMS is paraneoplastic, and the tumor is almost always small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). The neurologic syndrome frequently precedes the cancer diagnosis by months to years — so a new LEMS diagnosis is a mandate to search, and to keep searching if the first scan is clean.

  • Screen with thoracic CT and FDG-PET/CT — not PET only if CT is negative. CT sensitivity falls for central and mediastinal tumors, where PET was positive in 100% of cases against 50% for CT. (CT-first-then-PET is a reasonable resource-constrained fallback; know that you are making that trade.) Chest radiograph is not a screening test — 51% sensitivity vs 83% for CT at first screen.
  • Repeat imaging every 4–6 months for 2 years if the initial search is negative (2021 PNS-Care criteria for high-risk phenotypes) — the tumor may not yet be radiologically visible.
  • Two years is the right stopping point: 91–92% of SCLCs are found within 3 months of the LEMS diagnosis and 96% within 1 year. Detections beyond 2 years occurred almost entirely in patients who had been screened inadequately.
  • The strongest single risk factor is smoking. A smoker with LEMS has SCLC until proven otherwise.

docs.title: The triad that separates it from MG
docs.text:
Feature LEMS Myasthenia gravis Weakness pattern Proximal, legs > arms; gait first Ocular/bulbar first; fatigable On brief exercise Transiently improves (post-exercise facilitation) Worsens Reflexes Reduced or absent — and may return after exercise Normal Autonomic features Prominent — dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, constipation, orthostasis Absent Ocular involvement Mild or late Common, early Antibody P/Q-type VGCC (~90%; near 100% in SCLC-associated disease) AChR / MuSK Cancer link SCLC in ~50–60% Thymoma in 10–15%

The counterintuitive sign: strength and reflexes that improve after a few seconds of exercise (facilitation) point to LEMS, not MG. Dry mouth is the most consistent autonomic clue and is easy to ask about.

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
• Serology — P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibody, positive in ~90% (range 85–95%; approaching 100% in SCLC-associated disease, ~91% in non-cancer LEMS).
    • Do not order N-type VGCC antibody — it lacks diagnostic value in LEMS.
    • P/Q-type positivity does not distinguish paraneoplastic from non-paraneoplastic disease and has no role in cancer risk stratification. SOX1 antibody does — 95% specific but only 65% sensitive for SCLC-LEMS, so a positive result is informative and a negative one is not.
  • Electrodiagnostics are characteristic and confirmatory:
    • Low baseline CMAP amplitude.
    • Decrement on low-frequency (2–5 Hz, usually 3 Hz) RNS, ≥10% — like MG, present in 94–98% but not specific.
    • But marked facilitation — CMAP amplitude increase ≥60% after 10 seconds of maximal exercise or after 20 Hz stimulation. Use ≥60% as the operating threshold (97% sensitive, 99% specific); the older ≥100% cut-off is more specific but misses 4–16%. This post-exercise facilitation is the signature and distinguishes it from MG.
    • High-frequency (20–50 Hz) stimulation works but is very painful — avoid it when post-exercise testing is feasible.
    • A subtler discriminator: on low-frequency RNS the decrement nadir falls at the 7th–10th stimulus in LEMS vs the 4th–5th in MG (cut-off 6.5, AUC 0.90).

  • The DELTA-P score stratifies SCLC risk and guides how aggressively to hunt — 1 point each, maximum 6, assessed at onset or within 3 months:

    Component Age at onset ≥50 years 1 Smoking at diagnosis 1 Weight loss ≥5% 1 Bulbar involvement 1 Erectile dysfunction (males) 1 Karnofsky performance status <70 1

    0–1 → 0–2.6% probability of SCLC; 4–6 → 83.9–100%. Prospective validation AUC 82.5% (the 94% figure comes from the derivation cohort and overstates real-world performance). The score shortens the surveillance interval — it never cancels the search. Every LEMS patient is screened regardless of score.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Recognize the triad — proximal weakness + autonomic features + hyporeflexia, with facilitation.
  2. Confirm — VGCC antibody + EDx showing post-exercise facilitation.
  3. Hunt for cancer — this is the priority. CT chest and PET/CT → serial imaging every 4–6 months for 2 years. Score DELTA-P to set the interval, not to decide whether to look.
  4. Treat symptoms — amifampridine, divided 3–5× daily, titrated toward 50–80 mg/day.
  5. Treat the cause — the tumor (paraneoplastic) or immunotherapy (autoimmune/non-tumor).
  6. Military disposition — and note that a paraneoplastic LEMS is a cancer diagnosis first.

docs.title: Treatment
docs.text:
Step 1 — symptomatic: amifampridine

Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine; Firdapse) — the FDA-approved first-line symptomatic therapy (2018; label covers adults and children ≥6 years). A potassium-channel blocker that prolongs the presynaptic action potential, increasing calcium influx and ACh release.

Adults / ≥45 kg Children <45 kg Start 15–30 mg/day 5–15 mg/day Titrate +5 mg/day every 3–4 days +2.5 mg/day every 3–4 days Max single dose 20 mg 10 mg Max daily 100 mg (US label) 50 mg
  • Divided dosing is mandatory, not stylistic — 3–5 times daily. The half-life is 1.8–2.5 hours (Tmax 20 min–1 h), so twice-daily dosing produces symptomatic troughs. Patients feel each dose within the hour.
  • The ceiling you should actually work to is 80 mg/day. The US label maximum is 100 mg/day, but 80 mg/day is both the EMA ceiling and the widely adopted expert cap on seizure-risk grounds — these are two different numbers, not a range. Real-world dosing sits well below either: mean 50.5 mg/day in the pivotal run-in and 66 mg/day long-term. Target 50–80 mg/day divided 3–4×.
  • Lower the starting dose in renal impairment (CLcr 15–90), any hepatic impairment, age ≥65, and — most importantly — NAT2 poor metabolizers. No dosing recommendation exists for ESRD or dialysis; it has not been studied.
  • NAT2 status matters more than renal function, and it is not a rare edge case. Poor acetylators have 3.5–4.5× the Cmax and 5.6–9× the AUC of rapid acetylators. Prevalence is 40–60% in White and African American populations, 10–30% in Japanese, Chinese and Korean populations. Start low.
  • Seizures occur in ~2% of patients without prior history and are dose-dependent; a prior seizure is an absolute contraindication, as is aminopyridine hypersensitivity. The reported seizures clustered at 100 mg/day, in a patient with brain metastases, and in one on high-dose theophylline — concomitant threshold-lowering drugs matter more than the absolute dose. A dedicated QTc study found no clinically relevant prolongation, so routine ECG monitoring is not required.
  • Expect paresthesia — it is the commonest adverse effect at 62%. Perioral and digital, starting within minutes of a ≥10 mg dose and lasting 5–10 minutes. Warn the patient in advance; most come to treat it as a marker that the dose has landed rather than a reason to stop. Also >10%: URI 33%; abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, elevated LFTs and back pain ~14% each.
  • In children, watch weight — clinically significant weight loss occurred at doses ≥60 mg/day.

Pyridostigmine — not a substitute, but worth a trial as an add-on

The page used to say it "adds little," which is stronger than the evidence supports. The only randomized trial was intravenous, single-dose, and enrolled 9 patients (pyridostigmine alone was no better than placebo, and adding it to IV 3,4-DAP conferred no extra benefit). Chronic oral co-administration has never been randomized, and the observational signal runs the other way: 68% of a long-term cohort used it and 67% reported subjective benefit, and 13 of 25 patients in an open-label extension improved further when it was added.

Reasonable position: amifampridine first and always; a trial of oral pyridostigmine is justified in incomplete responders, where the risk is low and the potential benefit real.

Step 2 — treat the underlying driver

Paraneoplastic LEMS: treat the SCLC. Cancer treatment improves the neurologic syndrome — 7 of 11 patients surviving >2 months after tumor therapy improved substantially, one to complete remission at 7 years, though in 3 the improvement was transient. A pretreatment CMAP amplitude >3.0 mV predicts a better neurologic outcome. Expect 6–12 months, not weeks.

Non-tumor (autoimmune) LEMS: immunotherapy. Be honest with yourself about the evidence — no randomized trial exists for any oral immunosuppressant, or for plasma exchange, in LEMS.

  • Prednisone + azathioprine — first-line immunosuppression, open-label evidence only. Needed in 70% of non-tumor LEMS vs 44% of SCLC-LEMS. The regimen behind the best-reported results is prednisolone 60–100 mg on alternate days plus azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day (near-complete remission in 3 of 6 non-cancer patients within 6–12 months). Check TPMT and NUDT15 before azathioprine, and monitor CBC — see the MG page for the full monitoring schedule and the allopurinol interaction. Mycophenolate mofetil 1,000 mg PO BID is a reasonable substitute if azathioprine is not tolerated, but has no LEMS-specific data at all — and carries a boxed warning for embryofetal toxicity.
  • IVIG 2 g/kg over 2 days — the one crossover RCT (n=9) showed significant limb, bulbar and respiratory gains with a fall in VGCC titre; peak at 2–4 weeks, declining by 8. An acute or bridging therapy, not maintenance.
  • Plasma exchange — open-label only; 8 of 9 responded, peak at 10–15 days. For acute severe or rapidly progressive weakness.
  • Rituximab — fourth-line, for refractory disease, on case-level evidence only. No LEMS-specific protocol exists; the borrowed MG regimens are 375 mg/m² IV weekly × 4 or 1 g IV × 2 doses two weeks apart. Off-label. Screen HBsAg and anti-HBc before the first dose — boxed warning.
  • Give it time. Treatment effect on functional scales is generally reached at 6–12 months; escalating before then is usually premature. Treatment is typically indefinite, but sustained remission does occur — 5 of 63 patients stopped everything at a median of 4 years and stayed in remission for a median of 12 — so a cautious withdrawal trial is reasonable in durable remission.

Do not extrapolate the myasthenia biologics to LEMS

None of the agents that reorganized MG care has been trialed in LEMS. For complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) this is a mechanistic mismatch, not merely a gap in the evidence — LEMS neuromuscular junctions do not show complement deposits, LEMS IgG works just as well in C5-deficient mice, and complement-incapable F(ab')₂ fragments transfer the phenotype. The mechanism is cross-linking and depletion of calcium channels, not membrane attack complex. Complement inhibition should not be expected to work here.

FcRn inhibitors have a better theoretical rationale, since LEMS is IgG-mediated — but remain untested in LEMS. Anti-CD19 CAR T has two case reports in MG/LEMS overlap: striking (wheelchair to full mobility in 2 months) and investigational, n=2.

Two exposures that catch LEMS patients out

  • Anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade. LEMS patients are markedly sensitive to neuromuscular blocking drugs. In a series of 37 patients across 60 operations, 4 (11%) had respiratory complications — and 3 of those were undiagnosed or untreated at the time. The risk concentrates in the patient nobody knew had LEMS. Tell anesthesia before any procedure, especially before thoracic surgery in a paraneoplastic case.
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors can worsen pre-existing LEMS and have been reported to trigger de novo LEMS in neurologically asymptomatic SCLC patients. The causal evidence is graded low and rests largely on case reports — treat it as grounds for vigilance, not an established causal link. It matters increasingly, because checkpoint inhibitors are standard in exactly this population.

Same NMJ-drug cautions as MG

LEMS shares MG's sensitivity to neuromuscular-blocking drugs — aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can all worsen it. If a paraneoplastic patient is heading for thoracic surgery or chemotherapy, flag the NMJ sensitivity to the anesthesia and oncology teams. See the MG precipitant list.

Military medicine — LEMS

Framework — verify against current AR 40-501, DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 and Vol 2, DoDI 1332.18, and service aeromedical policy. See Profiles, MEB/MAR2 & deployability.

LEMS is named in no military medical standard. Every citation below is a reasoned choice among analogies — cite them that way in a memo, and say so.

  • Retention (non-paraneoplastic) — the Army hook is 3-31k, not a bare "3-31." AR 40-501 para 3-31k, "Other neurologic conditions," is the only subparagraph that reaches an unnamed condition: "…there remain residual symptoms and impairments such as … weakness, paralysis, or atrophy of important muscle groups … as to meet the definition of a disqualifying medical condition … as in paragraph 3-1." Proximal girdle weakness is that, on the face of the text.
    • Do not cite 3-31b (all primary muscle disorders — LEMS is a presynaptic junctionopathy, not a myopathy) or 3-31c (myasthenia gravis; its extraocular carve-out does not transfer).
    • Because 3-31k closes on para 3-1, name the limbs actually met: 3-1b (medication requiring frequent physician monitoring), 3-1d (dependence on medication, frequent special treatments, or frequent clinical monitoring — amifampridine dependence, immunotherapy, 2-year serial cancer surveillance), and 3-1a (duty interference substantiated by the commander).
  • DoD floor — lead with 5.26.e, and do not use 5.26.i. DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.26.e, "Neuromuscular disorders and muscular dystrophy including, but not limited to…" — the enumerated examples are dystrophies, but the lead-in is expressly non-exhaustive and LEMS is by definition a neuromuscular disorder.
    • 5.26.i ("peripheral neuropathy or paralytic disorders resulting in permanent functional impairment") works against you. It is the only 5.26 subparagraph carrying its own permanence qualifier on top of the 5.26.a gate, so citing it raises the bar and invites the reply that a Soldier responding to amifampridine has no permanent impairment. Use it only as a secondary citation where permanent impairment is documented — and never describe LEMS as a peripheral neuropathy.
    • 5.26.n — "Recurrent, neurogenic, or unexplained syncope or near syncope that interferes with duty" — is a genuinely named standard the dysautonomia engages directly, without analogy. Cite it when the autonomic burden is documented.
  • LEMS is not an "upon diagnosis" condition — 5.26.a gates it. Only 5.26.d (dementia) and 5.26.k (epilepsy) carry "Paragraph 5.26.a. does not apply." Document both prongs: the condition persists despite appropriate treatment (name drug, dose, duration — amifampridine titrated to maximum tolerated, ± immunotherapy) and it impairs function so as to preclude satisfactory performance of duty. A well-controlled Soldier has not met the neurologic standard on the neuro hook alone; the case is then carried by 3-1b/3-1d, by 5.26.n if there is near-syncope, or by the malignancy standard.
  • Paraneoplastic LEMS — cite the malignancy standard by paragraph, and lead with it. AR 40-501 para 3-34a: "Malignant neoplasms that are unresponsive to therapy. Or when therapy is such as to require prolonged, intensive medical supervision, or when the residuals of treatment themselves meet the definition… as in paragraph 3-1." SCLC therapy meets the second limb on its face — you do not wait for the cancer to fail treatment, which is the point most memos miss. 3-34c covers an inadequate post-treatment observation period. DoD floor: DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 para 5.29 (its own persist-despite-treatment gate in the lead-in; 5.29.a surveillance, 5.29.b residuals).
    • Cite both standards in the same memo. The malignancy paragraphs carry the case; the neurologic paragraphs document the residual deficit that persists after the tumour is treated — which in LEMS is common, and is exactly the "residuals" language in 3-34a and 5.29.b.
  • EPTS / LOD — onset-dating is the contested question here. Symptoms commonly predate diagnosis by months to years (proximal leg weakness written off as deconditioning, dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, constipation). Date the first attributable symptom, not the serology. Say what you reviewed — pre-accession records, prior PHAs, ACFT trend, sick-call notes for "leg weakness." AR 40-501 3-2, Note: accession standards govern the first 6 months of AD (separation via EPSBD); after 6 months, chapter 3 governs. Accession counterparts: DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 6.26.q (history of chronic nervous system disorders — non-exhaustive) and 6.26.n (history of paralysis, weakness, lack of coordination), plus 6.29.b (history of malignancy) in a paraneoplastic case. Check 3-3c before referring: a condition waived at accession, essentially unchanged and not meeting para 3-1, is not a DES referral. If diagnosed in service, state LOD affirmatively — a missing LOD is not excludable time.
  • Profile (DA Form 3349). LEMS profiles on the P factor; add L/U only where documented girdle weakness limits extremity function (E is rarely engaged — ocular involvement is mild or late).
    • Temporary through diagnostic work-up, amifampridine titration, immunotherapy induction, and — if paraneoplastic — staging and oncologic treatment. ≤90 days per instrument, and link every extension so the days-on-profile count is real.
    • Convert to permanent at clinical MRDP or the 12-month administrative MRDP, whichever comes first. Generalized disease at MRDP → permanent P-3, which is the DES referral (AR 40-501 3-4).
    • Section 4 limits, written functionally: no sustained load-carriage or road march; no repeated stair or ladder climbing; no sustained overhead work; no duty requiring rapid unaided rise from prone; no prolonged standing in formation (orthostasis); no unrestricted work in high heat; no duty requiring reliable independent egress under load.
  • MEB / MAR2 — run the fork, do not default to "refer." Refer to the DES when MRDP is reached and the Soldier fails retention standards under 3-31k → 3-1 (or 3-34 if paraneoplastic). If the Soldier meets retention standards on well-controlled disease but cannot perform their PMOS, that is a MAR2 — an administrative review, not a disability process — and sending it to DES gets the packet bounced. Do not refer before MRDP. The permanent 3/4 profile in e-Profile is the referral; the approval authority's second signature starts the clock.
    • Document: first attributable symptom date, VGCC serostatus, EDx (baseline CMAP, decrement, post-exercise facilitation), amifampridine dose and response, immunotherapy by drug/dose/duration, autonomic burden, objective strength and timed measures, the cancer-surveillance schedule and findings, and commander-corroborated duty impact.
    • Whether the Soldier is found fit is the PEB's decision, not yours — write the standard and the evidence, not the outcome. Put the oncologist's staging and prognosis in the packet as evidence, not in the profile as a prediction.
  • Deployability — what actually fails forward:
    • NMBA hypersensitivity is the deployment-defining hazard. A Soldier needing emergency anaesthesia forward — trauma laparotomy, appendicectomy, airway — risks prolonged post-operative ventilation at a Role 2 with no ICU and no spare ventilator. Carry it on the medical alert documentation, not just the neurology note.
    • Amifampridine has no theatre supply line. Orphan drug, specialty-pharmacy distribution, not on any theatre formulary, not locally resupplyable, not substitutable — and dosed in multiple divided doses across the day, so a delayed shipment converts to weakness within days.
    • It lowers the seizure threshold, which interacts badly with heat, sleep deprivation, exertional hyponatraemia, and other threshold-lowering agents in the deployed formulary.
    • Autonomic failure is operational, not merely clinical — orthostasis in formation, under load, and in armour; impaired sweating in a heat-injury environment.
    • On prednisone plus a steroid-sparing agent, live vaccines required for theatre entry are contraindicated — a theatre-entry blocker independent of disease control.
    • Rescue therapy is unavailable downrange — IVIG needs continuous 2–8 °C cold chain; PLEX does not exist below Role 3.
    • Paraneoplastic cases are non-deployable on the cancer alone — active SCLC, treatment cycles, and 4–6 monthly imaging for 2 years are, in the words of 3-34a, "prolonged, intensive medical supervision."
    • Field/formulary drugs that worsen NMJ transmission — aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium — constrain deployed medical support.
  • Aeromedical: disqualifying — by import, and categorically if paraneoplastic. AR 40-501 Chapter 4 never names LEMS. Para 4-27 (Neurological) makes the flying-duty standard "the causes in the accession standards plus the following" → DoDI 6130.03 Vol 1 6.26.q and 6.26.n, neither with a carve-out. In a paraneoplastic case the answer is categorical and independent of the neurology: AR 40-501 para 4-30b, "History of any malignant tumor" — a history of SCLC ends flying-duty qualification on its own terms, whether or not the LEMS improves. Waivers run through USAAMA and the applicable Aeromedical Policy Letters (4-1c); amifampridine is not an approved aviation medication and a seizure-threshold-lowering agent will not be treated as one. Non-Army Services follow their own policy — confirm before counselling.

TRICARE — LEMS prescribing

Amifampridine (Firdapse) is an orphan specialty drug — assume it is prior-authorisation-gated. Expect the PA to require a documented LEMS diagnosis (VGCC seropositivity and/or the characteristic electrodiagnostic study), a neurologist prescriber, and dispensing through the specialty / home-delivery channel rather than a retail counter. Start the authorisation the day you make the diagnosis — this is not a drug an MTF pharmacy keeps on the shelf.

Know which benefit you are billing — LEMS treatment spans both sides. Oral amifampridine runs through the pharmacy benefit (Express Scripts; an approval applies at military pharmacies, network pharmacies, and home delivery). IVIG and plasma exchange run through the medical benefit, at an infusion or apheresis site, under a different authorisation path. That split decides who authorises, who pays, and where the patient is treated — and it is the commonest reason a LEMS treatment plan stalls.

Verify current tier and criteria at the TRICARE Formulary Search before you counsel a patient — DoD P&T revises formulary status and PA criteria without notice. Firdapse's actual TRICARE tier and PA criteria text could not be confirmed from public sources for this page; treat the expectations above as expectations, not as TRICARE rules.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Presynaptic, not postsynaptic — and that is the whole story. In LEMS, antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the motor nerve terminal reduce the calcium influx that triggers acetylcholine vesicle release. Fewer quanta are released per impulse, so the first contraction is weak — but a burst of activity transiently loads the terminal with calcium, briefly increasing release and producing the facilitation that defines the syndrome on exam and on EMG. The same channels sit on autonomic terminals, which is why dry mouth and orthostasis travel with the weakness. It is the mirror image of myasthenia gravis, where the defect is postsynaptic receptor loss and repeated activity only worsens transmission.

The tumor connection is mechanistic. Small-cell lung cancer expresses functional voltage-gated calcium channels, and the anti-tumor immune response cross-reacts with the identical channels at the neuromuscular junction. LEMS is, in a real sense, the immune system finding the cancer before the radiologist does — which is exactly why the neurologic diagnosis obligates the search.

And that immune response appears to help. SCLC with LEMS carries substantially better survival than SCLC alone — median 17 vs 7 months in the Dutch registry and 18 vs 9.5 in a prospective UK cohort, with 5-year survival 21% vs 4.4%. The advantage persists in extensive disease and survives adjustment for stage, age, sex, performance status and sodium, so it is not simply lead-time bias from earlier detection. Tellingly, SCLC patients with low-titre VGCC antibodies but no clinical LEMS get no survival benefit — it appears to be the functionally pathogenic antibody response that matters. NCCN states plainly that the presence of LEMS does not imply metastatic or incurable disease. Counsel the patient accordingly; a paraneoplastic diagnosis here is not the worst version of an SCLC diagnosis.

But do not use the LEMS as a tumor monitor. This is the counterintuitive correction to a tempting assumption. Of 9 patients followed through tumor recurrence, only 2 had simultaneous worsening of their LEMS, and in both the link was questionable. The syndrome frequently does not flare when the cancer comes back. Oncologic surveillance runs on its own schedule; neurologic stability is not reassurance.

Key evidence:

  • Firdapse (amifampridine) FDA approval, 2018, expanded to children ≥6 years — the only amifampridine product now marketed in the US.
  • P/Q-type VGCC antibody — the confirmatory serology (~90%); SOX1 for cancer risk.
  • DELTA-P score — stratifies SCLC risk at diagnosis (prospective AUC 82.5%).
  • 2021 PNS-Care criteria — 4–6 monthly surveillance for 2 years in high-risk phenotypes.
  • Wirtz 2009 — the only randomized pyridostigmine trial (IV, n=9), and the reason the oral-add-on question is still open.
  • Amifampridine failed in myasthenia gravis (2026) — a negative randomized crossover trial of amifampridine added to pyridostigmine in AChR-positive MG. The presynaptic drug does not transfer to the postsynaptic disease, which is a neat confirmation of the mechanism.
